World.title: A dispute about fact vs. fiction at the trial over Tupac Shakur's 1996 killing
World.content:
A dispute about fact vs. fiction at the trial over Tupac Shakur's 1996 killing

toggle caption Steve Marcus/POOL Reuters via AP

LAS VEGAS — A prosecutor said Monday that while few have been willing to speak about the 1996 killing of Tupac Shakur, Duane "Keffe D" Davis is the "one person who has a hard time being silent."

"Let's be clear, Duane Davis did not pull the trigger. But he did plan the shooting in retaliation of the beating of his nephew," Chief Deputy District Attorney Binu Palal told jurors at the start of Davis' Las Vegas trial. "Remarkably, you will learn that from Duane Davis himself."

Davis, 63, could get life in prison if he's convicted of murder with a deadly weapon with the intent to promote, further or assist a criminal gang. He has pleaded not guilty. His lawyer in the defense opening called the prosecution's narrative "fiction."

Sponsor Message

Palal showed jurors video of Shakur's entourage attacking Davis' nephew Orlando "Baby Lane" Anderson outside the boxing match at the MGM Grand hours before the shooting on Sept. 7, 1996.

Davis spent the next two hours planning how to get even, said Palal, and Shakur was gunned down "in an act of revenge."

Shakur remains a cultural icon and is considered one of the most influential and versatile rappers of all time, despite dying at 25.

What he told the FBI and investigators

In a 2008 interview with a federal task force investigating the killing of Shakur's rival, the Notorious B.I.G., Davis instead talked about the Shakur shooting. He described handing a gun to the men in the backseat of a white Cadillac that fired on a black BMW with Shakur and Marion "Suge" Knight inside.

As prosecutors played audio of Davis explaining the moment Shakur was shot, members of Shakur's family, including his stepbrother Maurice "Mopreme" Shakur, stared ahead and listened intently from the audience.

Palal told jurors Davis held onto a visceral hatred for Shakur for decades that drove him to speak.

He said the defendant talked to the FBI in 1998 and again in 1999, admitting he had been in Las Vegas at the time of the shooting.

In 2009, he admitted to his role in the killing in an interview with Las Vegas police, Palal said.

"And now 30 years later, we're going to ask you to finally hold Duane Davis accountable," Palal said.

He also showed jurors the 2019 memoir that Davis co-authored, "Compton Street Legend," that the prosecution will use and that the defense fought to keep out of the trial, along with several of the defendant's interviews.

Sponsor Message

How Davis' legal team is defending him

Davis, wearing a blue suit and tie, sat quietly with his hands folded on the table in front of him, occasionally nodding along as his attorney gave his opening, and often scanned the room during testimony to see who was in the gallery.

toggle caption Steve Marcus/Pool Reuters via AP

"What they are telling you, they are representing as fact, when it's really fiction," Michael Sanft said. "There's no facts."

He said Davis wasn't previously charged because law enforcement knew that he was "full of crap."

The defense attorney also pointed to missing documents in the original investigation and distrust between police departments.

He called one detective's work "biased," "sloppy" and "incomplete."

Sanft said outside court at the end of the day that he thought the 30 years that had elapsed would help Davis.

"The length of time is going to be a huge problem for people trying to recall things, to remember things," the lawyer said. "That's just not how it works."

Asked about the oddity of calling his client "full of crap" and similar things, he said, "We all have a family member who's like that."

Briefly a suspect in Notorious B.I.G.'s death

Former Los Angeles Police Department detective Fred Miller — assigned to the investigation of the 1997 shooting death of the Notorious B.I.G., born Christopher Wallace — testified remotely and said that Davis had briefly been suspected in that shooting.

Davis admitted to being present at a party at the Petersen Automotive Museum in Los Angeles where Wallace and Sean "Diddy" Combs were guests. Wallace was shot as he was leaving.

Sanft objected to the inclusion of the testimony. The judge, with prosecutors' agreement, told jurors that police do not believe Davis was involved.

Most eyewitnesses are no longer alive

The story of the drive-by shooting has long gripped the hip-hop community, partly because no one was charged until Davis was indicted in 2023.

toggle caption Steve Marcus//POOL Reuters via AP

The other three men riding in the Cadillac have all died in the years since.

Sponsor Message

Retired Las Vegas police officer Garry Dale was the first of the 35 to 45 witnesses the prosecution plans to call at the trial expected to last about a month.

He testified that he and another officer stopped Knight and Shakur's car for missing a license plate, warned them and let them go.

About 10 minutes later the officers responded to a shooting call and found EMTs pulling Shakur from the car. Dale said Knight had been grazed by bullets, but told the officers to take care of Shakur.

Dale jumped in the ambulance and asked Shakur who shot him. The retired officer said that Shakur said something like "no, we'll take care of it."

Brent Becker, a former Las Vegas homicide detective, testified that Knight showed up to a police interview with attorneys, which he thought was odd because Knight was a victim. Knight was timid, his interview was practiced and he told investigators he knew nothing, Becker said.

"I thought he lied to us," Becker said in video testimony.

Becker said it was difficult to get other witnesses to talk and they "were leaning on" Davis, Anderson, Deandrae "Freaky" Smith and Terry "Bubble Up" Brown as the men in the Cadillac, but had no living witnesses who could identify them.

Witnesses describe the night Tupac was shot

Ingrid Stokes testified that she and her friends were heading home from Las Vegas when they encountered Shakur and Knight, who were friends with a woman in Stokes' group.

Knight invited them to a nightclub, she said, and they decided to meet them there.

The car Stokes was riding in was one lane over and a car length ahead of Knight's vehicle, when they heard gunshots.

Stokes said they drove off in fear and almost hit a white four-door vehicle in the process.

When they returned to the scene, police made them sit on the sidewalk and treated them like suspects, she said. Stokes was scared to be seen in public talking about the case, worried about poor treatment from law enforcement and the potential for retribution.

Sponsor Message

"Snitches get stitches," she said.

World.title: Hoekstra's missteps in Canada are mild compared to some of Trump's ambassadors
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The U.S. ambassador to Canada's behaviour has clearly rubbed many Canadians the wrong way.

Over 100,000 of them signed a House of Commons petition to declare Pete Hoekstra persona non grata — the rarely used diplomatic lever to kick an ambassador out of the country.

Jeremy Kinsman, who held important posts including ambassador to Moscow, London and the EU during his career as a Canadian diplomat, says Hoekstra's actions don't rise to the level that would normally lead to such a step.

"PNG is for egregious behaviour" such as malfeasance and direct interference in Canadian affairs, he said. But that doesn't mean Kinsman is an admirer of Hoekstra's.

WATCH | More about the petition: Why Canadians are targeting Trump’s U.S. ambassador | About That | Duration 2:24 More than 100,000 Canadians have signed a petition calling for the expulsion of Pete Hoekstra, the U.S. ambassador to Canada. Avneet Dhillon explains the reasons behind the petition, which comes as the latest trade deadline approaches. (Photo credits: The Canadian Press, Reuters, Adobe Stock and Getty Images)

In diplomacy, said Kinsman, it's important to separate the messenger from the message. The problem of the Trump administration — embodied by Hoekstra — is that an already unpalatable message is being delivered by an undiplomatic messenger.

"[Hoekstra] does express frustration, exasperation, grievance with Canada that Canadians find bizarre.… Seemingly we're supposed to submit, quietly, docilely and accept all this stuff," Kinsman said.

"What the president of the United States thinks is offensive, it's hostile, it's aggressive, it's uninformed, it's untruthful. And [Hoekstra] radiates it."

The U.S. Embassy has declined to comment on the petition beyond acknowledging its existence.

No desire to explain

Some American career diplomats have observed the Trump era with dismay.

John Dinkelman ended a 37-year career last year, and was elected by his peers to head the American Foreign Service Association — essentially the diplomats' union.

Being a diplomat is not about being nice, said Dinkelman, but it is also not about gratuitously alienating your hosts.

"The idea behind diplomacy is to actually arrive at a point where your foreign interlocutor sees the logic your way and you are actually perceived to be doing — if not effectively doing — things for the betterment of all," he said.

"You've got to at least explain for your audience — the Canadian public — the context of it. He doesn't do that," Kinsman said.

Kinsman says Hoekstra's attitude has echoes of Chinese ambassador Lu Shaye, who picked several fights with his hosts during a low-water mark in Canada-China relations, including accusing the country of " white supremacy " over the arrest of Huawei executive Meng Wanzhou.

Lu had already moderated his tone somewhat by the time he left Canada in 2019, and today, China seems to have decided the aggressive "wolf warrior" diplomacy he represented isn't that effective.

U.S. ambassadors, said Kinsman, are now the ones throwing their weight around and offending hosts.

"In Europe where their ambassadors are doing this sort of stuff, the United States is held in esteem today in percentage terms at about half of what Europeans now hold for China. What kind of a win is that?" he said.

Hoekstra has certainly fared no worse in Canada than he did as ambassador to the Netherlands during Trump's first term, when he found himself having to apologize after making false claims about Muslim "no-go zones" and politicians being set on fire .

And he's hardly unique among political ambassadors of the Trump era. Nor is Canada alone in having a petition to refuse credentials. Iceland had one after its new ambassador-designate, former Missouri congressman Billy Long, joked that he would turn the country into the 52nd state with himself as its governor.

He later apologized , something not all Trump ambassadors have elected to do.

Trump's ambassador to Chile, former U.S. Border Patrol agent Brandon Judd, made it his business to condemn Chileans who criticize Trump or his policies, including Chile's former left-wing president Gabriel Boric, and to attack ministers in the new right-wing government of José Antonio Kast who dared to criticize U.S. tariffs.

"He knows nothing about diplomacy," commented former Chilean foreign minister José Miguel Insulza this month.

When Ambassador Tom Rose began his tenure in Warsaw in late 2025, President Donald Tusk greeted him as "a true friend of Poland" who "understands our external and internal situation very well."

Two months later, Tusk was tweeting , "Mr. Ambassador Rose, allies should respect, not lecture, each other. At least that is how we, here in Poland, understand partnership."

That was after Rose announced that the U.S. would have "no further dealings, contacts, or communications" with the Speaker of Poland's legislature, for expressing the view that Trump didn't deserve the Nobel Peace Prize.

Ambassador barred from meeting French officials

Though it's perhaps the U.S. ambassador to France, Charles Kushner, who has most upset his hosts.

Kushner, a convicted fraudster and the father of Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, wrote an open letter last summer accusing France of tolerating antisemitism and chiding it for moving toward the recognition of Palestine, saying "antizionism is antisemitism, pure and simple."

France responded that Kushner's "allegations are unacceptable" and "contravene international law" by interfering in domestic affairs. Kushner was summoned to the French diplomatic headquarters in Paris, the Quai D'Orsay, but failed to show.

U.S. President Donald Trump speaks with U.S. Ambassador to France Charles Kushner in June. Kushner was twice summoned by the French government over the last year. (Mandel Ngan/AFP/Getty Images)

He ignored a second summons two months later when the U.S. Embassy spoke out about "violent radical leftism" after the killing of French neo-fascist activist Quentin Deranque.

France has since banned Kushner from meeting any French official, citing his "misunderstanding of the basic expectations of an ambassador who has the honour of representing his country."

Next door in Belgium, the country's foreign minister responded angrily earlier this year to U.S. Ambassador Bill White's "personal attacks" around laws requiring medical certification for circumcision , saying his actions "violate basic diplomatic norms."

Then there's Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, who is popular with his Israeli hosts, but who managed to offend every other government in the Middle East by saying that the Bible gives to the Jews all the land "from the Nile to the Euphrates, which is, once again, basically the entire Middle East," and adding "it would be fine if they took it all."

Key posts left unfilled

What troubles professional diplomats like Dinkelman is that when Trump doesn't appoint obnoxious ambassadors, he often appoints no ambassador at all.

About half of all U.S. ambassadors' posts are currently vacant — even though Dinkelman says there are experienced, ready and willing diplomats to take those roles.

"It's quite painful for someone like myself who spent 38 years in the diplomatic corps to see the diminished importance of having the people on the ground where you need them, when you need them," he said.

U.S. President Donald Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff has been involved in many of the administration's most high-stakes foreign negotiations. (Daniel Heuer/Reuters)

Only 13 of 54 countries in Africa now have a U.S. ambassador. Russia has no U.S. ambassador, and neither does Ukraine.

Key allies in the Middle East, including Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, also have no ambassador.

Instead, the U.S. has come to rely more and more on "special envoys," the most prominent of whom is a private citizen who once said he would have no role in the second Trump administration: Jared Kushner.

Kushner was unable to obtain a security clearance to work in the U.S. government until the White House interceded. Today he and New York real estate investor Steve Witkoff are the duo that conduct the most sensitive foreign affairs missions, including negotiations with Russia, Israel and Hamas, which would normally be the purview of U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

Witkoff has at times appeared to try to exclude Rubio from meetings, or speak to world leaders before Rubio can . Rubio's State Department has complained about Witkoff's use of insecure communications.

On Sunday, Kushner met with Hamas political leader Khalil al-Hayya in Egypt, and on Monday again it was Kushner, not a U.S. diplomat or even government employee, who met with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu .

While governments might normally wish to avoid employing envoys with close personal ties to their foreign interlocutors, no such concerns seem to have impeded Kushner's role as go-between with Netanyahu, a family friend who was a guest at the their home in New Jersey and once even slept in Jared's bed .

Reporting directly to Trump, Kushner and Witkoff allow the president to circumvent the normal channels of U.S. diplomacy and restrict the circle of knowledge of what is actually being discussed and agreed upon.

"One of the biggest complaints from some of the most respected professional diplomats from this nation is that the diplomats are not even in the room when decisions are being made or negotiations are taking place," said Dinkelman.

"That speaks volumes."

World.title: 'Owners are afraid': New tariffs could cut sales in half for some Canadian businesses
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

With only hours to spare for Canada to strike a trade deal with the United States, a wide swath of Canadian businesses are on edge — with some expecting as much as half of their sales could disappear if the punishing new levies take hold.

The latest round of U.S. tariffs are set to take effect Wednesday unless a last-minute deal is reached. They would layer on top of existing U.S. trade sanctions, adding another duty to $28 billion worth of Canadian products including electronics, dairy, alcohol, wood and more.

Negotiations are coming down to the wire. Canadian officials could see U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer again before Prime Minister Mark Carney and U.S. President Donald Trump speak ahead of Wednesday's tariff deadline, a source with direct knowledge of the talks told CBC News. America's top trade negotiator has made it clear that it will be Trump who ultimately makes the final decision on any deal.

CBC News is not identifying the source because they were not authorized to publicly discuss the talks.

For some Canadian businesses, the new proposed tariffs wouldn’t just raise prices on American customers. They say shipping across the border will become uneconomical.

Todd Stafford, president of Brockville, Ont.-based Northern Cables, says his company counts on U.S. buyers for about half of its sales. The company manufactures copper and aluminum power cables for commercial and industrial use.

WATCH | Canada-U.S. trade talks stuck as Washington, provinces refuse to budge: Canada-U.S. trade talks stuck as Washington, provinces refuse to budge | Duration 5:14 Sources tell CBC News that Canadian negotiators fear looming new U.S. tariffs may be unavoidable as Washington continues to demand an end to provincial bans on U.S. alcohol — which provinces refuse to do. Canada's push for greater tariff relief on key sectors like lumber is also stalled.

“We ship 50 per cent of our production to the U.S. We have seven warehouses in the U.S.,” he told CBC News on Monday. “At the announced level of 50 per cent tariffs, we would lose all of that business immediately.”

Stafford says if the new U.S. tariffs kick in on Wednesday, "we can’t have a single tractor-trailer cross the border.

"We’re hoping cooler heads prevail, or maybe there'll be some kind of time extension," he added.

The company, which has 320 employees in Brockville, has avoided layoffs for the last 26 years. Stafford said he worries the tariffs will compound problems at home, like slowing condo construction and competition from cheaper Chinese-made products.

“We wouldn’t [lose] 50 per cent of the people,” he said. “But it would be very close to that.”

Shield of CUSMA won't apply

From auto parts to lumber, steel and aluminum, U.S. President Donald Trump has targeted key sectors of Canada’s economy since his second term started in January 2025.

However, the vast majority of cross-border trade has been exempt under the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement (CUSMA), a trade deal Trump formally signed in 2020. This has significantly blunted the trade war's impact on Canada’s economy.

The new tariffs set to take effect on Wednesday would change that, impacting about five per cent of the overall trade Canada does with the U.S. The list of affected Canadian exports is long, including items like hockey sticks, certain flowers and antiques.

Canadian hockey equipment is pictured at a sports retailer in Vancouver, B.C., in July. (Ethan Cairns/CBC)

Energy, potash and critical minerals are set to remain exempt.

“To say business owners are afraid is an understatement,” Canadian Federation of Independent Business (CFIB) vice-president of national affairs Jasmin Guénette said on Monday. “You cannot lose 50 per cent of your revenue without feeling the impact.”

“CUSMA has been providing a shield for many sectors and many businesses,” Guénette added.

Cindy Baldassi runs a Calgary-based company called CindyLouWho2 that sells handmade jewelry. Baldassi said she is worried she might lose half of her business.

"I have now shut down U.S. shipping on my website and my Etsy shop,” she said on Monday. “I’m going to spend the rest of the day adding 50 per cent to a substantial amount of my items.”

Baldassi’s business was briefly hit by earlier rounds of tariffs until she was able to keep shipping tariff-free to the U.S. by proving her products were CUSMA-compliant. That option doesn't exist this time.

WATCH | Owner of jewelry business braced for the impact of new tariffs: Calgary jewelry seller fears new U.S. tariffs could cut her business in half | Duration 7:38 Cindy Baldassi, who sells handmade jewelry out of Calgary, is among the Canadian business owners bracing for a new round of U.S. tariffs that would impose a 50 per cent levy on various products as of Wednesday. Baldassi says she was able to mostly avoid an earlier round of tariffs by proving her products were CUSMA-compliant, but that option won't exist this time.

She said she's been able to increase marketing in Canada over the past year and sell more domestically, but about three-quarters of customers to her Etsy shop were American. She notes her one-person business doesn't have a marketing team or big budget to help expand.

"We often have to really scrape to get what traffic we can to our websites. And I don't have a lot of control over where Google tends to show me or where Etsy wants to show me," Baldassi said.

Guénette said pursuing customers in non-U.S. markets is a common theme these days.

“Many businesses in Canada don’t feel the U.S. is a reliable trade partner anymore,” he said.

Businesses already burned by tariff threat

Even if the new swath of tariffs don't come to pass, some business leaders say they've already had an impact.

Randy Williams, director of sales and marketing for Monterey Textiles, says his business has longstanding operations on both sides of the Canada-U.S. border. In recent years, they've ensured all of their products can be made in factories in either country to limit international shipping.

He says business on the Canadian side is strong, so Monterey will be all right. But, as a board member with the Canadian Textile Industry Association, Williams said he is aware of other textile makers who have already made tough choices as a result of the mere threat of new tariffs.

“People have already been laid off. Orders aren't coming in. U.S. customers are possibly searching for other suppliers,” said Williams.

"The threat of them being put in place had a significant impact already."

WATCH | Alberta honey farmers bracing for new tariffs: Home to Canada’s largest honey crop, Alberta is bracing itself for U.S. tariffs | Duration 3:20 As an Aug. 19 deadline looms, Albertan beekeepers are bracing for a proposed 50 per cent U.S. tariff on its product. As CBC's Nadeer Hashmi reports, the new tax could be devastating for the industry.

In Alberta, beekeeper and owner of Gull Lake Honey, Lorne Prins, says he's aware of other producers that have been racing to ship honey to the U.S. as soon as it's extracted in order to get ahead of the deadline.

Prins sells most of his honey locally and sends some of it to a large buyer in Alberta. But if new tariffs prevent other honey producers from selling to the U.S., that could stick Canada with tonnes of surplus honey, impacting the price at which he sells his product.

"It will strand an enormous amount of honey on the Prairies and it could be really, really damaging to our price this year," Prins said.

If the tariffs do go through, he's hoping Canadians can pick up the Buy Canadian movement again in order to support local businesses that will need the help.

World.title: Ambassador Bridge 'aggressively' pursued trucking clients amid Gordie Howe delay: industry rep
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

As uncertainty swelled in recent months around the long-awaited opening of the Gordie Howe International Bridge, representatives from the privately-owned Ambassador Bridge up the Detroit River were “aggressively” pursuing trucking companies in an apparent bid to retain their business, according to an industry representative.

Lak Shoan, director of policy for the Ontario Trucking Association, said his organization started hearing from a “handful of members” about the bridge’s efforts around springtime.

“It wasn't something that they came to us with or anything like that,” he said. “It would just come up in conversations sort of, you know, ‘Have you heard that the Ambassador Bridge has been, you know, reaching out to more companies?’ And that's when we started hearing from a few more folks that this was occurring.”

Lak Shoan is the director of policy for the Ontario Trucking Association. He said his organization started hearing from a “handful of members” about the bridge’s efforts around springtime. (Submitted by Lak Shoan)

CBC Windsor contacted several Canadian trucking companies with cross-border operations to ask if the Ambassador Bridge had approached them with toll rate offers. Those who answered said they couldn’t discuss private business agreements, while others simply did not respond.

But in a now-deleted post from late July, a U.S. trucking union official ordered his members not to use the new publicly-owned crossing because of a contract with the Ambassador Bridge in which they were saving $240,000 on tolls per month.

“If we wanted to begin using the Gordie Howe bridge, the Ambassador Bridge would first have to be notified that we intend to terminate the current contract,” wrote UAW Local 212 Chair JT Barrett, who represents FCA Transport (Stellantis) drivers.

Toll rates and revenue were a key part of the months-long political saga to open the $6.4 billion Gordie Howe bridge, which the Canadian government paid for in full. The deal to open the crossing contains a provision giving the U.S. government the ability to block the new bridge from lowering tolls “below the average of comparable regional crossings.”

The wealthy Moroun family of Michigan, which has owned the Ambassador Bridge since 1979, ramped up its political influence efforts in the months before U.S. President Donald Trump suddenly threatened to block the new crossing from opening.

Though the bridge eventually opened to traffic on July 27, it came after a June opening was scrapped at the request of the U.S. government, according to Prime Minister Mark Carney .

A poster attributed to UAW Local 212 Chair JT Barrett published in late July 2026, after the opening of the Gordie Howe bridge. (Screenshot/Facebook)

Trump has been accused of trying to block the new bridge’s opening to benefit the Morouns.

Representatives for the Ambassador Bridge did not respond to questions before publication time. But a notice on their website suggests there is a cheaper toll program available to some trucking companies.

“Commercial customers with over 150 expected monthly crossings are eligible for new A-Pass Subscription Accounts,” the page reads. “These feature fixed monthly rates, determined based on expected crossings.”

Shoan said the trucking association doesn’t know the exact details of what the bridge was offering companies, but he believes “it was around retention or trying to attract fleets to use the Ambassador Bridge.”

He said his group welcomes “healthy competition” between the bridges, which can lead to lower toll costs for trucking companies.

Barrett’s Facebook post provided some financial specifics about the deal he said FCA Transport has with the Ambassador Bridge.

“Under that contract, we pay a flat rate of $160,000 per month, regardless of how many crossings are made,” he said.

The first wave of vehicles cross the newly-opened Gordie Howe International Bridge, connecting Windsor, Ont., and Detroit, Mich., on July 27, 2026. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

“Before this contract, we were paying north of $400,000 per month on a per-crossing basis,” he continued.

Barrett did not respond to a request for comment. Stellantis declined to confirm whether its FCA Transport drivers are under an exclusive toll contract with the Ambassador Bridge.

“The opening of the Gordie Howe International Bridge strengthens the single most important border crossing in North America,” the global automaker said in a statement. “We are looking forward to using this additional crossing to support our just-in-time operations across our manufacturing operations in both countries, improving the flow of goods for an integrated industry that depends on seamless logistics. As a matter of company policy, Stellantis does not comment on proprietary information."

Shoan said the uncertainty around the Gordie Howe bridge’s opening would have made any deals offered by the Ambassador Bridge appealing to trucking firms.

“If you look at the current economic climate, which has been unsettled over the last several months, businesses are looking for certainty wherever you can find it,” he said. “If there's an opportunity to look for certainty from a cost perspective, [...] most business owners would definitely take that peace of mind.”

World.title: This summer camp kept an instructor who pleaded guilty to assaulting kids. Ontario law allows it
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

For weeks this summer, a lead instructor at a Kawartha Lakes hockey camp was a man who recently pleaded guilty to charges of assaulting children. As CBC's Christian D'Avino explains, there is currently no Ontario legislation that requires summer camps to screen staff that work with children.

KL Hockey i n Kawartha Lakes, which offers day and overnight programming for children in July and August, aims “to bring the best to campers everyday — on and off the ice,” its website reads.

But for weeks this summer, one of its lead instructors was a man who recently pleaded guilty to charges of assaulting children.

Bradley Gibbs, who is a Durham Regional Police officer, pleaded guilty in April to two charges of assaulting children who were known to him, his lawyer confirmed. CBC News cannot provide further details due to a court publication ban.

Gibbs is currently described on the camp’s website as “an active coach and mentor to many in the Kawartha Lakes region.” However, he chose to step down on Wednesday afternoon, according to an email that was sent to the camp's parents one day after CBC News contacted Gibbs and the camp for this story.

Camp leadership told parents in the email they have supported Gibbs as he dealt with a personal legal matter over the past year. But they did not say whether they knew about the guilty pleas, or why he was allowed to stay on despite them.

There is currently no Ontario legislation that requires summer camps to screen staff that work with children. Camps are not required to get criminal record checks or more extensive vulnerable sector checks from their employees.

The Ontario Camps Association (OCA) requires its 400-plus accredited members to vet staff with criminal record checks. But membership in the non-profit organization is voluntary, meaning summer camps that aren’t part of the OCA — including KL Hockey Camp — don’t have to meet any standards when it comes to vetting staff.

Bradley Gibbs (pictured far left) in an undated photo posted on the KL Hockey website 'About Us' section. Gibbs posted the same image on his personal Facebook page in October 2022. (KL Hockey)

The camp’s director Amanda Tayles said in a statement that Gibbs “has publicly taken accountability for his personal actions.”

“Our focus remains entirely on maintaining a safe, supportive, and positive environment for our summer camp players,” she wrote.

CBC News reached out to Gibbs for comment, but he did not respond before deadline. He is expected to appear in court in September for sentencing.

Gibbs is still employed at Durham Regional Police Services, where he’s currently redeployed from frontline patrol duties to an administrative role, a police spokesperson said. Any potential internal disciplinary proceedings will be informed partly “by the outcome of the ongoing criminal matter, including the sentencing,” Const. Nicholas Gluckstein said in an email.

‘Big gap’ in Ontario legislation for summer camps: lawyer

One of Gibbs’ victims, who is now an adult, spoke with CBC News before Gibbs announced his departure.

“If I had sent my kid to [KL Hockey], I’d be really concerned,” said the victim, whose identity is protected under the court publication ban.

WATCH | Some families struggling to afford summer camp expenses: Can't afford your kids' summer camp anymore? You're not alone | Duration 1:58 More Canadian families are simply finding it too expensive to send their kids to summer camps, as the affordability crisis drives up costs, prompting calls for governments to help with funding.

They said Gibbs co-founded the camp with his friends and that camp leadership are aware of the guilty pleas. CBC News has asked the camp if leadership knew about Gibbs’ pleas, but they did not directly respond to the question.

The lack of legislated requirements for summer camps is a “big gap,” said Puneet Tiwari, an employment litigator and partner at Levitt LLP in Toronto.

He said the province should consider legislation that requires summer camps to get vulnerable sector checks from their employees.

Vulnerable sector checks are for people who intend to work with groups considered vulnerable, such as children.

According to the province’s website, they include the same information as a criminal record check, but may also have additional details on outstanding charges, arrest warrants, absolute and conditional discharges and information about charges that didn’t result in a conviction.

The Durham Regional Police Service website provides examples of who might require vulnerable sector checks, which include coaches and parent volunteers for sports or school trips.

An image from the KL Hockey website. The camp offers day and overnight programming for children in July and August. (KL Hockey)

CBC News asked the Ministry of the Solicitor General whether the province would consider creating legislation that requires summer camps to get vulnerable sector checks from their employees, but did not receive a response.

The Ministry of Education does require “day camps” for children under four to get a child-care license and make their staff complete a vulnerable sector check, according to its website . But camps for children over the age of four aren’t considered child-care centres, and don’t fall under the ministry’s scope.

The Ministry of Education declined to comment for this story.

Still, Tiwari said it's common sense for camps to require vulnerable sector checks when they’ve been entrusted with children, regardless of the law.

“[Camps] bear the responsibility to screen, supervise and act on relevant information,” he said.

KL Hockey ‘supported’ Gibbs through challenging period

In the email sent to parents on Wednesday, KL Hockey’s camp director Amanda Tayles wrote that Gibbs decided to step away from camp due to "recent attention" about a personal legal matter.

“KL Hockey is aware of Brad’s personal legal matter, which is unrelated to camp operations or his law enforcement duties, and has supported him through a difficult and challenging period in his personal life,” she wrote.

The email doesn't say that Gibbs was criminally charged, or that he pleaded guilty to those charges in April.

KL Hockey’s Facebook account posted a video on August 3, recapping its first week of activities, that shows Gibbs at a campsite. CBC has censored faces of children in the screenshot. (KL Hockey)

The same email includes a letter from Gibbs, where he writes that he’s taken full responsibility in court for a personal legal matter “and accepted accountability for my lapse in judgment.”

He said he made the decision to remove himself from all KL Hockey duties “out of respect for our players, families and the integrity of our summer camp.”

Gibbs wrote he was “deeply sorry to our community, our campers, our staff, our board, and the families who have placed their trust in me.”

“My focus right now is on continuing to take responsibility, learn from this experience, and rebuild that trust over time.”

KL Hockey’s Facebook account posted a video on Aug. 3, recapping its first week of activities, that shows Gibbs at a campsite. Two people who know Gibbs confirmed it was him.

Gibbs is also pictured on the camp’s “About Us” webpage. Several posts on his personal Facebook reference the camp, most recently from November 2024.

Gibbs is described as a lead instructor on the KL Hockey website. (KL Hockey)

KL Hockey's day programming runs out of the Lindsay Recreation Complex, which is owned by the City of Kawartha Lakes. The city doesn’t require camps that use its facilities to request criminal record checks or vulnerable sector checks from their staff, the director of community services, Jenn Johnson, said in an email.

The camp’s overnight accommodations are located at Camp Endobanah, a non-profit camp available for rent that’s also in Kawartha Lakes. CBC News asked Camp Endobanah about its vetting process for camps that rent its facilities, but did not hear back before deadline.

Parents advised to ask about camp staff vetting

It’s unclear what vetting standards KL Hockey has for its staff, since it is not a member of the OCA. The provincial camp association has a publicly-available document of over 600 standards for its members, reviewed annually.

Those standards include a mandatory requirement that camps obtain a criminal record check from each staff member over 18 before employing them.

Puneet Tiwari, an employment litigator and partner at Levitt LLP in Toronto, said the lack of legislated requirements for summer camps is a 'big gap.' (CBC News)

Camps have discretion over how they use information from criminal record checks, said Rankin Middlebrook, who is on the OCA board of directors and former chair of its standards review committee.

He said individual camps should determine appropriate steps based on the information in a check and the surrounding context.

The OCA also has an optional standard that camps request criminal record checks once every three years from returning staff members.

Middlebrook said he doesn’t think camps have to be OCA-accredited to be a “good camp,” but accredited camps must follow a higher standard. He said parents can review the OCA standards document so they can make an informed decision when picking a camp for their children.

Meanwhile, Tiwari said parents should do their due diligence by inquiring how summer camps are vetting their staff. But he added parents are entitled to expect a “safe system” and aren’t expected to become private investigators.

If a camp chooses to keep a staff member despite concerns, Tiwari said parents’ options are limited, due to the lack of legislation in this area.

“There's really nothing that can be done, other than parents demanding a refund or pulling their kids and speaking with their wallets,” he said.

World.title: What the Churchill Falls deal means for Quebec – and the provincial election
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Prime Minister Mark Carney was in St. John’s on Monday to announce a new agreement on Churchill Falls and other electricity projects in Labrador, alongside N.L. Premier Tony Wakeham and Quebec Premier Christine Fréchette.

It is being touted as the largest clean energy investment in North American history, valued at nearly $70 billion with Ottawa chipping in $10 billion in federal financing.

That money would go towards upgrading and expanding the Churchill Falls generating station, developing the Gull Island hydroelectric project, building transmission lines and implementing a 2,000 megawatts onshore wind energy project in Labrador.

It will increase the current generating capacity of Churchill Falls, with enough power to light, heat and cool all the homes in Toronto, Montreal and Vancouver combined.

Here’s a closer look at the deal, what it could mean for Quebec, Premier Fréchette and the looming provincial election campaign.

Is it really a done deal?

Not quite.

The agreed-upon framework announced on Monday will hold until March 2027.

A definitive agreement still needs to be signed and the parties involved hope that happens by the end of the year.

The provincial election is scheduled for Oct. 5. That means there could be a change of government before the deal is officially signed.

WATCH | Opposition leaders in N.L., Innu nation leader react: Opposition leaders, Innu grand chief await the fine print on new Churchill Falls deal | Duration 2:48 Quebec and Newfoundland and Labrador have a new agreement on Churchill Falls. While Premier Tony Wakeham calls it a better deal than the previously announced 2024 MOU, the Liberals and NDP aren't sold on it just yet. The CBC's Cameron Kilfoy reports.

What does it mean for Quebec's electricity needs?

Under this deal, the province would have access to over 10,000 megawatts, representing more than a quarter of Hydro-Québec's total current output.

In comparison, the 2024 Churchill Falls Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) — which was rejected by Wakeham shortly after he became premier —provided for a total potential of 7,200 megawatts.

The electricity produced at Churchill Falls would be sold to Quebec at an average price of 6.2 cents per kilowatt-hour, which Fréchette said could lead to savings of $200 billion over the course of the deal.

Yvan Cliche, a fellow specialist in the energy sector at the Université de Montréal’s centre for international studies, called it a “historic landmark agreement for Quebec.”

Cliche believes the deal will benefit not only the energy sector but consumers in Quebec, by allowing Hydro-Québec to keep its rates as low as possible.

Prime Minister Mark Carney, centre, signs a new agreement on the Churchill Falls generating station and the launch of new hydro, wind and transmission projects, premiers Wakeham and Fréchette. (Paul Daly/The Canadian Press)

What does it mean for Fréchette?

For Fréchette, the agreement represents a win ahead of the start of the campaign — and a chance to demonstrate her economic credentials.

On Monday, the premier and leader of Coalition Avenir Québec (CAQ) described the deal as a partnership that ensures Quebec's energy security for the next 50 years and create thousands of jobs.

If her party stays in power come October — a third straight CAQ election victory but a first under Fréchette — she will follow through to make sure the Churchill Falls deal is made official.

“Because it brings to Quebec thousands of new megawatts and we need those megawatts for residents, for businesses, for every region in Quebec," Fréchette said.

Carney said the time was right for the deal — even if it is so close to the start of the election period. He said negotiations began four months ago, soon after Frechette took over as premier.

Others were more critical — even before the deal was announced.

Jonathan Shetush, the chief of the Innu nation of Uashat mak Mani-utenam issued a joint statement with the chief of Matimekush-Lac John stating there can be no official deal without their communities being consulted. (Shushan Bacon/Radio-Canada)

The leaders of the Innu nations Matimekush - Lac John and Uashat mak Mani-utenam, both located in Quebec's Côte-Nord region, issued a joint statement emphasizing that they had not been consulted.

"Our participation and consent are mandatory for any agreement to the Churchill Falls megaproject," reads the statement.

They also highlighted that the initial project was carried out on their traditional land — the Nitassinan — and that their case for reparations is still before Quebec courts.

WATCH | Experts react to the new deal: What the new Churchill Falls deal means for Quebecers — and their Hydro bill | Duration 2:11 Hydro-Québec is set to invest $45 billion into the project and receive about $6.5 billion from the federal government. For Quebecers, that means their electricity bills are set to go up between two to five per cent starting in 2029.

What does it mean for Quebec's election campaign?

The campaign is expected to launch sometime next week.

Days of speculation leading into Monday put a spotlight on Fréchette — who came took over as premier in April — and made her a target for criticism from opposition parties.

In a social media post last week, Parti Québécois (PQ) Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon said Fréchette doesn’t have the legitimacy to make such a deal right before the campaign that will bind Quebec for 50 years and there was no need to make a deal now.

On Monday, the two exchanged words, with Fréchette stating during the news conference that St-Pierre Plamondon would tear up the agreement if elected.

On X, the PQ leader shot back, saying that was "simply a falsehood" and accused her of rushing a deal for electoral reasons.

PQ leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, seen here in a photo taken in January earlier this year, says Fréchette is trying to score political points by rushing this deal. (Sylvain Roy Roussel)

What are other parties saying?

Éric Duhaime, leader of the Quebec Conservatives, mad e similar accusations as did Québec Solidaire (QS).

In a written statement, Duhaime said Fréchette is trying to distract Quebecers from “eight long years of disastrous management of our public finances" under the CAQ.

He said his party supports increasing energy production in Quebec and would look to maximize the province's natural resources, including hydroelectricity, natural gas "and, possibly, nuclear power."

Ruba Ghazal, the parliamentary leader for Québec Solidaire, was among those accused Fréchette of serving her own political interests with the Churchill Falls deal and not those of Quebecers. (Sylvain Roy Roussel/Radio-Canada)

Ruba Ghazal, the parliamentary leader for QS, said a deal of this magnitude should serve the interests of Quebecers for the next half century, "not the electoral interests of the CAQ."

Charles Milliard, the leader of the Quebec Liberal Party, said it wouldn't make sense to start from scratch and saluted the work accomplished by Hydro-Québec.

He said, however, the agreement would have short-term impacts on public finances and on the rates for Quebecers and that if elected, his government would "fully analyze it before ratifying it."

Fréchette had a message to opposition parties Monday: What deal are you proposing?

"Where will they find the 10,000 megawatts we are bringing to Quebec with that agreement? At what cost will they bring new megawatts? Where will they take them? How will they create 20,000 jobs?” she asked.

“Because this is what is in that agreement. It's 23,000 jobs for Newfoundland and Quebec."

World.title: Drug trafficker, associates convicted after investigation Winnipeg police feared was undermined by corrupt cop
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A high-level cocaine trafficker, a nightclub owner working as a drug courier and a recently divorced father have pleaded guilty to various roles in a drug bust Winnipeg police once worried had been compromised by a corrupt officer.

Mohamed Ali, Abdullah Khan and Ahmed Dini were charged in 2024 as part of Project Roasted, a months-long investigation into a drug trafficking network. It culminated in one of the accused being arrested at his home and the other two being taken into custody as they left Stella's on Pembina Highway with about two kilograms of cocaine in one of their cars.

Months later, police got a warrant to search one of the men's seized cellphones because of "concerns that the drug investigation had been compromised" and a belief the phone data would establish a link between Ali, his associates and then-Winnipeg police officer Elston Bostock, an agreed statement of facts filed during Bostock's sentencing said.

"I believe that Ali and other members of the organized crime world in Winnipeg are receiving police information from … Bostock," a detective sergeant wrote in a warrant document filed to search Ali's phones.

Bostock, then a veteran constable, was sentenced this year to seven years in prison after admitting to a long list of corruption-related offences, including providing confidential police information to people outside the force.

When police went through the cellphone data, they found photos of Bostock with people the agreed facts described as "criminal associates" and text messages between Ali and others referencing Bostock looking up police information for them.

While few details about those targeted in Project Roasted were previously shared, recent court hearings shed light on the three men who have now been convicted in the case — and how some of them became involved in the drug operation.

Cocaine in Winnipeg, Niverville

A federal prosecutor told Court of King's Bench Justice Shawn Greenberg during a hearing in June that information about Ali's cocaine trafficking activities sparked Project Roasted.

The ensuing investigation included search warrants that allowed police to do repeated covert entries at Ali's home in Niverville, Man., south of Winnipeg. Investigators found cocaine, cutting agents, large amounts of cash and other drug-related items throughout the house and garage, in addition to the two kilograms later seized after Ali and Khan were arrested outside Stella's.

While Khan was moving the drugs around, Ali was the one directing those meetings, court heard.

"The accused was a high-level cocaine trafficker with some decision-making authority or responsibility," Deniset said.

Ali admitted to possessing cocaine for the purposes of trafficking in Winnipeg and Niverville from October 2023 to February 2024. Deniset said lawyers plan to jointly recommend he get eight years in prison at a sentencing expected to happen early next year.

Club owner's involvement 'baffling': judge

During Khan's sentencing in May, court heard the drug courier was the owner of the Moonlight Lounge nightclub on Osborne Street at the time of the investigation and had no criminal record.

His lawyer, Brett Gladstone, said he believed Khan's "poverty-related concerns," debts and other financial challenges contributed to the decisions his client made in the drug case and another incident he was later charged in.

Khan admitted to picking up a load of 20 kilograms of cocaine and delivering some of it before he was arrested with two kilos still in his car. He pleaded guilty to possession for the purpose of trafficking.

Khan also pleaded guilty to attempting to obstruct justice in a separate case, after he misled police following a shooting at his nightclub last year. He was sentenced to a total of seven years during an emotional hearing in May, where Khan apologized through tears for his actions.

"It's an individual who simply wants to do better," Gladstone said. "He regrets deeply the choices that he's made."

Provincial court Judge Kael McKenzie said it was "baffling" why Khan, who court heard is almost 50, was involved in the drug operation — but said it wasn't lost on him that the accused was running a nightclub at the time.

"I don't know if this is where you made these acquaintances," McKenzie said. "But it's probably not unusual, from where I sit, that people who are involved in nightclubs come across people who are involved in other things."

While a spokesperson for the Liquor, Gaming and Cannabis Authority of Manitoba previously said Moonlight Lounge's liquor licence was suspended in February 2025, the authority said this week it later got notice the business had been sold, with a request to withdraw its licence effective May 1, 2025.

'Regretted every day since'

In a sentencing in August 2025, court heard Ahmed Dini, described as a hard-working father in his 40s who'd spent years working with people with developmental disabilities, was also among those arrested in Project Roasted.

Court heard the same day police arrested Ali and Khan outside of Stella's, they did a search of Dini's apartment and found 213 rocks of crack cocaine stashed in a dresser drawer. His lawyer, Eric Wach, said Dini agreed to keep drugs there while at the "lowest point" of his life, as he dealt with a divorce and hard financial times.

"A friend of his said, 'Hey, there's an opportunity to make some money and, you know, stash some drugs and so forth,'" Wach said. "He took that opportunity, and it's something that he's regretted every day since. He talks about praying every day for forgiveness."

Provincial court Judge Lisa LaBossiere said she was "puzzled" why, despite Dini's financial circumstances, he'd involve himself "in something like this" as a father of eight children.

"The repercussions, even on your family alone, are significant," she said.

Dini was given a roughly two-year conditional sentence, to be followed by two years of supervised probation, as part of a joint recommendation from lawyers.

Charges against two other co-accused in Project Roasted were stayed last year. A spokesperson for federal prosecutors declined to provide specific reasons for the decisions to stay those charges.

World.title: Could an explosive drone at a German airport signal a growing Russian threat to NATO?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

As German authorities investigate a drone laden with explosives and a detonator found at Leipzig airport, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has signalled Moscow's intent to step up retaliation against countries helping Ukraine.

"We will adopt much harsher methods to destroy everything that enables the West to fuel Kyiv's war machine," Lavrov said in an interview with VGTRK, Russia's state media. "We are already doing this."

German investigators said an airport employee found a drone carrying an unknown explosive device in the security area of the cargo operations zone near the south runway of Leipzig airport, a facility classified as "critical infrastructure."

Leipzig is a strategic NATO airport used to deliver armaments, ammunition, weapons and other military equipment to Ukraine on flights operated by Ukrainian cargo companies.

The discovery of the drone, which was spotted beside one of those Ukrainian cargo planes, marks "a new level of danger" for Germany, according to Germany's interior minister.

Alexander Dobrindt said the incident did not appear to be the work of amateurs and that investigators were treating it as part of a "professional hybrid threat scenario."

German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said Germany is the target of daily hybrid warfare attacks, and the country is increasingly facing new threats. (Fabrizio Bensch/Reuters)

German authorities are investigating the incident and have not said where they believe the drone came from. Late last week, U.S. intelligence officials told the Wall Street Journal that intelligence reports indicated the drone likely belonged to the Russian government.

Berlin is responding cautiously, strengthening anti-drone capabilities while avoiding premature attribution.

"We are right in the middle of establishing the facts," Dobrindt said. "We are at the investigation stage and it would not be appropriate for a federal minister to prematurely comment on this."

But officials warn that Russia is already using drones, espionage, sabotage and influence operations across Europe — including ahead of upcoming regional elections in Germany.

"We are facing new threats," Dobrindt said in the days following the drone incident. "We are facing a serious threat situation we are confronted with every day."

Escalations in hybrid warfare

Dobrindt says Germany is the "daily target" of hybrid warfare, including "espionage, sabotage, cyber attacks and covert actions by foreign powers aimed at destabilizing Germany, causing harm to our country and bringing about political and social change as well."

In 2024, U.S. and western intelligence uncovered a Russian plot to assassinate Armin Papperger, CEO of German defence contractor Rheinmetall. The company is responsible for heavy military production and is a major supplier of armaments to Ukraine.

In March, German federal prosecutors arrested a man suspected of spying for Russia and scouting sabotage targets. The intelligence he gathered reportedly included details about Berlin's military support for Ukraine and information about the country's defence industry, particularly companies developing drones and robotics.

The Institute for Strategic Dialogue (ISD), a London-based think-tank specializing in counter-extremism and digital policy, has been tracking the ways it says Russia is interfering in Germany online, through a campaign known as Operation Overload.

The ISD says the campaign aims to exploit "emerging controversies within NATO member countries and Ukraine," with a focus on Germany, France and Ukraine. The group said its messaging centres on undermining Ukraine's war effort and destabilizing democracies.

The latest phase of the campaign, according to the ISD, included videos impersonating news organizations, law enforcement agencies and academics.

"It is apparent that there are attempts to influence German politics and society," Dobrindt said. "I'd say we all have a pretty good sense that such disinformation attempts take place especially in such upcoming regional elections. Thus we must assume they too are a target of our adversaries."

Hans-Jakob Schindler, senior director of the Counter Extremism Project, said Russia is testing how much Germany is willing tolerate, calling the drone incident in Leipzig an "aggressive escalation" of such interference.

A police officer in protective clothing works at Leipzig/Halle Airport in Schkeuditz, Germany, on August 5, after the police said explosives experts examined a drone near a runway. (Axel Schmidt/Reuters)

"Very clearly, Russia is trying to test how far Germany is willing to accept [these attacks], going from hacks and lower level sabotage to something that has turned into quite serious plots to kill CEOs of German companies, disruption of critical infrastructure and now this very aggressive attack in Leipzig."

For Schindler, these increasingly physical tactics raise urgent questions about where defence ends and direct conflict begins.

"There has to be a point that its made very clear to Russia that there is a limit.... Where does it stop being hybrid and where does it start to be a conventional attack?" Schindler said. "In this case, it looked like they were willing to exert a lot of damage. People could have been killed or hurt on German soil if it worked."

Schindler said Lavrov's comments mark a shift from the Kremlin's past denials about Russia's interference in Western countries.

"In addition to being as close as it will ever get to an admission of guilt by Russia in any hybrid warfare operation, the statement by Russian Minister Lavrov is also a threat and a warning that the campaign against Europe, against the west and against NATO is going to be more aggressive," he said.

World.title: 50% tariffs might mean U.S. businessowners have no choice but to leave their Canadian suppliers
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Late last August, Julia Hallman and her husband road-tripped from their home in Massachusetts to spend time with one of their Canadian suppliers at Fromagerie La Station in Quebec.

Hallman sat on the back porch at the farmstead in Compton and watched the grazing cows that would eventually provide the milk for one of her shop's best-selling cheeses: the supple Alfred le Fermier. She's determined to keep buying the cheese to sell at her shop not only because her customers love it, but also because she counts the family as her friends.

"At the end of the day, we want to help support them and get more money into their hands," said Hallman, who owns Formaggio Kitchen, a specialty cheese and artisan goods shop in Cambridge.

Hallman is one of the innumerable businessowners in Canada and the U.S. waiting to hear whether the Trump administration will impose steep new levies on a long list of Canadian goods on Wednesday. Entrepreneurs south of the border say sustained, 50 per cent tariffs would force them to make the choice they've been trying to avoid for more than a year and a half: breaking away from longstanding, good-faith relationships with Canadian suppliers for the sake of their finances.

Hallman, left, at Fromagerie La Station in Compton, Que., last summer. (Submitted by Julia Hallman)

Businesses can only handle so much: owner

Imported products from cheeses to chocolates to spices and spreads account for roughly half of the stock at Formaggio Kitchen, with Canadian products making up roughly 15 per cent of those goods.

Hallman has managed tariffs on Canadian dairy in the past by sacrificing profit, raising prices for customers or both. She would like to continue that way, but says a rate of 50 per cent would eventually be too much to handle.

"There will come a point in time when we do have to make some hard choices," she said in an interview on Monday. "That's the challenge: we don't want to sacrifice the friendships that we've made. But we also have a threshold of what we can handle as a business and what our customers are willing to pay."

WATCH | Trade talks stuck at an impasse with days to go: Canada-U.S. trade talks stuck as Washington, provinces refuse to budge | Duration 5:14 Sources tell CBC News that Canadian negotiators fear looming new U.S. tariffs may be unavoidable as Washington continues to demand an end to provincial bans on U.S. alcohol — which provinces refuse to do. Canada's push for greater tariff relief on key sectors like lumber is also stalled.

Like Hallman, Sarah Paxton is worried the new rate will force her to move away from the suppliers her business has used in Ontario and Quebec for decades — one of which, Amisco, offered to meet her in the middle by covering the cost of tariffs until a certain date. She said she could manage the new fees herself for a while, but not forever.

"We're going to try and continue if we can. Fifty per cent, though, that's a pretty high number," said Paxton, who co-owns a contemporary furniture store in Richmond, Va., called LaDIFF.

"If you can imagine somebody reaching into your wallet and taking half of what you've got, that would be pretty tough."

The latest round of U.S. tariffs are set to hit $28-billion worth of Canadian goods just after midnight unless the two governments come to a last-minute deal.

Canadian entrepreneurs are worried about tariffs taking a massive bite out of their profits if American buyers like Hallman and Paxton — the ones who ultimately pay the bill when they bring Canadian goods across the border — have to source elsewhere.

Representatives from Canada and the U.S. met on Monday for what was expected to be the final meeting at the ministerial level. The Prime Minister's office confirmed to CBC News that Mark Carney spoke to U.S. President Donald Trump that afternoon about the "ongoing trade negotiations."

WATCH | Carney on the state of the negotiations as of Monday afternoon: Carney expects to speak with Trump before Aug. 19 tariff deadline | Duration 1:33 Prime Minister Mark Carney says he'll have 'opportunities over the next 48 hours' to speak to U.S. President Donald Trump before his threat to raise tariffs on a number of Canadian goods takes effect. Carney was speaking to reporters after announcing $10 billion in federal financing for the Churchill Falls hydroelectric agreement between Quebec and Newfoundland and Labrador.

Waiting to see whether another threat would come to pass, Hallman stocked her shop's basement "cheese cave" with as many non-perishable goods as she could before the deadline. The cost of tariffs, she said, is just as emotional as it is financial.

"We're pretty stubborn," said Hallman. "We bring these products in intentionally. We bring them in because we love them. We don't want somebody to say, essentially, that we can't import them. That's what they're doing by putting a tariff that egregious [in place.]"

"It's a pretty loud and clear message."

World.title: Colombia says 377 still missing three days after 7.4M earthquake
World.content:
The director of Colombia’s disaster management agency UNGRD said Thursday that at least 273 people died and that 377 were missing from the region that was struck by a 7.4M earthquake on Monday.

According to UNGRD director David Tamayo, the earthquake affected a total of 97,515 people.

So far, rescue workers and neighbors were able to rescue 348 people from the rubble alive and 3,826 people were injured.

The earthquake, which was the strongest in a decade, destroyed 12,563 homes and damaged another 75,654.

At least 172 apartment buildings collapsed, said Tamayo.

Damaged public infrastructure

217 health centers and hospitals

2,206 educational facilities

825 community centers

226 roads

71 aqueducts

24 vehicular bridges

8 pedestrian bridges

5 airports

The disaster triggered President Abelardo de la Espriella to declare an economic emergency in the disaster area, and in the southern Putumayo and the eastern Norte de Santander province where no damages were reported.

This State of Exception allows the president to govern by decree when it comes to matters related to disaster relief and reconstruction in the affected area.

The State of Exception will last three months and can be extended by another three with congressional approval.

World.title: Colombia declares economic emergency to rebuild after earthquake
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella said he would declare an economic emergency and create a reconstruction fund for homes and small businesses that were destroyed in Monday’s earthquake.

In a press statement, De la Espriella said that the government would initially support victims with temporary relief and will declare an economic emergency to find the funds for reconstruction.

Finance Minister Miguel Gomez said the government was not yet considering raising taxes to find the approximately COP20 trillion ($6.4 billion) that would at least be needed for reconstruction.

The president said his government would initially prioritize relief for the estimated 24,000 families from the west of the country who have lost their homes or businesses.

The temporary relief measures would include:

The payment of public services for affected families by the government.

Housing rent subsidies for those who lost their homes.

Tax and financial relief measures.

Economic support for the most vulnerable families.

Support mechanisms for merchants and small business owners who have been affected by the earthquake.

As part of the emergency, De la Espriella announced the creation of a “Miracle Fund, an entity that will channel national and international contributions destined for the reconstruction of hospitals, educational centers, properties, roads, and airports that suffered damage from the earthquake.”

“The state of emergency must encompass economic reactivation measures that stimulate investment, reduce obstacles to project development, and generate more jobs in the affected areas,” said the president.

An economic emergency gives the president three months to issue decrees related to the cause of the emergency without having to go through Congress.

The legal validity of the decree declaring an emergency and those that follow will only be tested by the Constitutional Court.

At the time of publication the President’s Office had yet to issue its first decree.

World.title: Colombia asked US to carry out joint military operations: Hegseth
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella asked the US Government for joint military operations “to destroy terrorists and terror networks,” said US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth Wednesday.

At an event of the so-called Americas Counter Cartel Coalition (ACCC) in Panama, Hegseth said that “Colombia will join the ACCC, becoming the 19th member.”

Through the newly inaugurated president, as our president likes to say “President El Tigre,” Colombia has already requested that our department of war join Colombia in its fight against narcoterrorism. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth

Hegseth’s announcement was rejected by leftist opposition party Historic Pact, whose Senate chief Ivan Cepeda said that “the US citizen Abelardo de la Espriella wants to surrender our government, our territory and our sovereignty to the strategic interests of the United States.

Cepeda stressed that Colombia’s constitution allows only the Senate to permit the entry of foreign troops to the country.

Colombia’s sovereignty is not up for negotiation, it is not to be surrendered, and it cannot be subordinated to the military interests of any foreign power. To defend it is to defend the dignity of the nation, the independence of the Republic, and the right of the Colombian people to freely decide on their territory and their destiny. Senator Ivan Cepeda

Ahead of taking office on Friday, De la Espriella said that he would join US-led alliances that allegedly seek to combat drug trafficking.

In his inaugural speech, the president said he intends to “defeat, without truce, narco-terrorism and all criminal organizations that threaten the freedom of Colombia.”

The State Department last week announced that it would seek to send a $1 billion military aid package to Colombia to “support the De la Espriella Administration’s efforts to defeat the vicious narcoterrorist and criminal organizations that threaten US, Colombian, and hemispheric security and economic prosperity.”

World.title: Controversy in Colombia over refusal to allow foreign search and rescue teams
World.content:
The government of President Abelardo de la Espriella has been criticized over its refusal to accept foreign search and rescue workers in the crucial hours after Monday’s earthquake.

One of the first to raise the alarm was China’s ambassador to Bogota, Zhu Jingyang, who called on the government on Tuesday to “release the name of the official and his or her designated contact person to coordinate international aid for the earthquake victims.”

El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele said that he was told that Colombia’s “rescue teams, medical personnel, and other emergency responders are on the scene and handling the situation” and “they do not require personnel support.”

Mexico’s President Caudia Sheinbaum said that her government was waiting for approval to send a team of 225 rescue workers to look for survivors, but was waiting for a “formal invitation” from Bogota.

In a response to growing pressure, newspaper El Tiempo said Colombia didn’t need foreign search and rescue teams because “the country has 23 teams with personnel that is part of the global elite.”

The Foreign Ministry said on Tuesday evening that it had “called on the international community to provide support in addressing the emergency, in order to tackle the most severely affected areas and mitigate the disaster.”

But social leader Leonard Renteria from Buenaventura said Wednesday that “as of yesterday, we still didn’t know anything about the arrival of rescue workers” in the partially destroyed port city.

“On the streets, we’ve seen people from the neighborhoods with the firefighters and civil defense personnel,” Renteria posted on social media platform X.

Fifty hours after Monday’s disaster, the US Department of State said it had “mobilized urban search-and-rescue (USAR) technical teams from Fairfax County, Virginia, and Los Angeles County, California to support Colombia’s search and rescue efforts.”

With chances of finding people alive rapidly decreasing, pressure on the government to respond increased online.

“I would really like to know the technical reason for rejecting assistance from teams that specialize in this type of disaster. There are many affected areas and plenty of evidence of technical inadequacies,” said civil engineer Gina Villalobos on X.

According to opposition congresswoman Maria Fernanda Carrascal, “it was an ideological decision, they only wanted rescue workers from Israel and the United States to enter while the Mexicans have been ready since Monday.”

On Wednesday afternoon, newly appointed disaster response chief David Tamayo said the government would also allow search and rescue workers from Ecuador and El Salvador “that can guarantee the provision of search and rescue teams and that are recognized by their own governments as meeting international search and rescue standards.”

These teams would come to search for hundreds of people who are feared to be under the rubble of buildings that collapsed in the worst earthquake in 10 years.

World.title: West Colombia earthquake killed more than 227 people, say local authorities
World.content:
Local and regional authorities have said that at least 227 people were confirmed killed in Monday’s earthquake while search and rescue teams continue to look for survivors.

So far, 120 people were confirmed dead in Valle del Cauca where locals said that entire towns in the north of the province were all but destroyed by the 7.4 magnitude earthquake that struck the Choco province on Monday.

In Cali, the capital of Valle del Cauca, rescue workers continued to look for survivors under the rubble of apartment buildings that collapsed. Cali Mayor Alejandro Eder imposed a curfew in the city after locals chased him away from a search and rescue operation.

Choco Governor Nubia Carolina Cordoba said that mayors from the capital Quibdo and 22 affected towns reported 14 deaths and 140 injuries.

Multiple parts of the western province have yet to be contacted, however, as the local energy and telephone grid were destroyed by the earthquake, said Cordoba.

In Pereira, a city located at only 60 kilometers of the earthquake’s epicenter, and the surrounding Risaralda province, at least 88 people had died and dozens were still missing.

All major cities in the coffee region, Choco and Valle del Cauca declared an emergency to deal with the hundreds of injured that required medical attention at one of the cities’ hospitals.

President Abelardo de la Espriella said Tuesday morning that the earthquake destroyed more than 5,000 homes and that 188 people were missing.

The National Army and fire brigades from across Colombia sent teams to the cities in the disaster area to help with local search and rescue missions.

The US Department of State said it had committed $15.5 million “in funding for emergency shelter, food, protection, and earthquake assessments” for Colombia.

The Chinese embassy in Bogota said that Chinese companies that operate in Colombia were “sending heavy equipment to the most affected areas of the earthquake, participating in rescue efforts and the clearing of debris, in order to rescue the affected population using all available means.”

World.title: Colombia declares national disaster after devastating earthquake
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella declared a national disaster and sent his ministers to the west of Colombia to coordinate rescue operations in response to a 7.4M earthquake.

Following an emergency meeting at disaster management agency UNGRD, De la Espriella said he would travel to Pereira, one of the worst hit cities, to further coordinate the government response.

Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara would coordinate rescue operations for the rest of the coffee region, the health and defense ministers would travel to the Choco and Transport Minister Elsa Noguera would coordinate efforts in Valle del Cauca from Cali.

De la Espriella canceled plans he had to visit La Guajira, a northern province that wasn’t affected by the earthquake.

Throughout the morning, local and regional media reported dozens of collapsed buildings in multiple cities in Valle del Cauca, the coffee region and Choco.

More than 110 people were killed and dozens were injured because of the earthquake, De la Espriella said at a press conference.

The earthquake damaged more than 1,500 homes and destroyed 37. Sixty-one buildings collapsed and 18 healthcare centers suffered damage as well as 52 schools and 17 community centers.

The roof of the Pereira airport also came down and five other airports in western Colombia reported damages, said the president.

According to the National Police, road travel has been complicated because of landslides and fallen trees.

The government has yet to report on missing persons.

“Right now, the most important thing is to protect lives, rescue those who remain trapped, treat the injured, and bring aid to the hardest-hit communities,” said Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo.

“United we will overcome this emergency,” Restrepo added.

The vice-president, together with Foreign Minister Omar Bula, will coordinate foreign aid.

According to the Colombian Geological Service, the earthquake was the strongest in Colombia of the past decade and the strongest in the west of the country since 1979.

World.title: 7.4M earthquake hits western Colombia: at least 110 killed, dozens of buildings collapsed
World.content:
An M7.4 earthquake hit western Colombia on Monday, killing at least 110 people and injuring hundreds.

The earthquake struck around 7:30 and had its epicenter in San Jose del Palmar, a municipality in the Choco province.

In the hour that followed, locals began reporting collapsed buildings in the cities of Cali, Pereira and Manizales, where a tower of the cathedral and a dozen other buildings fully or partially collapsed, according to Mayor Jorge Eduardo Rojas.

In a first report on fatalities, Risaralda Governor Juan Diego Patiño said that at least 40 people were killed in the capital Perira. Another three would have been killed in Manizales.

In Cali, an unknown number of people would be trapped under the rubble of multiple buildings. At least 27 people would be killed in the Valle del Cauca province.
