Por una parte, en Moscú, una cámara de apelación del Tribunal Supremo confirmó la sentencia, ya dictada por el alto tribunal el 10 de agosto, que excluía a Yábloko de los comicios parlamentarios del próximo septiembre. El partido, sin representación en la Duma Estatal (Cámara baja del Parlamento ruso) desde 2003, ya había recibido el visto bueno de la Comisión Electoral Central pero, tras su registro, su popularidad comenzó a crecer en las encuestas. Como resultado de la denuncia de un contrincante electoral (el partido Ródina), las autoridades rusas reconsideraron la decisión de permitirle competir con otras diez fuerzas, todas las cuales aprueban el rumbo militarista del Kremlin. Entre los motivos por los que Yábloko ha sido excluido está el haber transgredido la legislación sobre derechos de autor, al reproducir unas estrofas de una popular canción soviética.

Por otra parte, un tribunal municipal en la ciudad de Pskov (a 730 kilómetros al noroeste de Moscú) condenó el lunes a once años y un mes de prisión a Lev Schlosberg, de 63 años, periodista, historiador y vicepresidente de Yábloko. Schlosberg, que fue un brillante parlamentario en el parlamento regional de Pskov, fue declarado culpable de “desacreditar repetidamente al Ejército” y también de difundir bulos sobre esta institución. Los hechos por los que le han juzgado son, por una parte, la difusión de una caricatura aparecida en el diario británico Daily Mail en la que se representaba al presidente Vladímir Putin asiendo a una mujer ensangrentada (supuestamente Ucrania) con el lema “La sangre de ella; las manos de él”. Además, Schlosberg fue declarado culpable de haberse manifestado a favor del alto el fuego y de negociaciones inmediatas para concluir con el derramamiento de sangre y la guerra en Ucrania, durante un debate radiofónico. Se da la circunstancia de que la caricatura apareció antes de que entraran en vigor, en marzo de 2022, las enmiendas legislativas que permiten al aparato de Justicia ruso castigar las manifestaciones pacifistas con penas administrativas y de prisión.

En Moscú, durante la apelación en el Tribunal Supremo la policía dispersó a jóvenes que se habían concentrado en la calle en espera del veredicto definitivo. A lo largo de la jornada, se practicaron unas 70 detenciones, según datos de Yábloko.

En Pskov, la sentencia contra Schlosberg fue recibida con gritos de “vergüenza”, “vergüenza”. El presidente de Yábloko, Nikolái Ribakov, y el fundador del partido, Grigori Yavlinski, consideraron la decisión judicial como “la tragedia de la desintegración de la justicia rusa moderna”. Desde Francia, adonde huyó recientemente, el político ruso Boris Nadezhdin ha dicho que “muchos asesinos y violadores reciben sentencias más cortas”. Nadezhdin, que ha sido declarado “agente extranjero” y privado así de la posibilidad de competir en las legislativas (por distrito mayoritario) no consiguió registrarse como candidato a la presidencia del Estado en enero de 2024 pese a las multitudes que lo apoyaban.

El caso de Yábloko repite pautas que se dieron en el caso de Nadezhdin, a saber, el reflejo hostil de la Administración rusa cuando un contrincante aceptado inicialmente como inofensivo pasa a ser percibido como un peligro por quienes controlan hoy el Estado. En ambos casos hay que deslindar el miedo a perder el control y a correr riesgos de los poderosos y el peligro real que para ellos representan quienes los desafían.

Las últimas palabras de Schlosberg ante el tribunal que le juzgaba el pasado viernes, fueron un alegato a favor del alto el fuego inmediato y del inicio de negociaciones en la guerra contra Ucrania. Sus palabras fueron también la denuncia de un sistema donde los órganos de seguridad han tomado el poder y recurren a leyes anticonstitucionales para mantenerlo y para reprimir la disidencia pacífica y sembrar el miedo en la sociedad, incluidos los jueces. “Desde 2021, los organismos de seguridad del país han recibido de hecho las competencias del poder político, lo que ha provocado un fuerte aumento de la anarquía, la ausencia de garantías legales y la arbitrariedad”, dijo. “La entrega de poder político a las fuerzas de seguridad y su derecho de hecho a tomar decisiones políticas han privado a los tribunales rusos de su independencia”, agregó. “Privar a los tribunales de su independencia lleva a la destrucción del poder judicial como rama suprema del poder”, sentenció el acusado, que era interrumpido una y otra vez por la presidenta del tribunal, Victoria Maliamova, quien intentaba impedirle que hablara de la guerra y transformara el juicio en un alegato contra el sistema dirigido por Vladímir Putin y contra el tribunal que le juzgaba, en tanto que parte de ese sistema.

Según Schlosberg, nunca en toda la época postsoviética en Rusia la “ley” y el “derecho” habían estado tan distanciados como hoy y las leyes se han convertido en “armas para la persecución ilegal de los ciudadanos por parte del Estado”. “Las leyes ilegales destruyen el Estado más deprisa que la corrosión destruye el metal”. “Nos encontramos en un proceso político incoado contra mí por encargo de personas que tienen poder político y que actúan por motivaciones personales, políticas, ideológicas y cuyo fin es acabar con mi actividad política en interés de los ciudadanos de Rusia y de nuestro mismo Estado”, señaló, para concluir que “este no es un asunto del tribunal municipal de Pskov o de los tribunales regionales de Pskov, sino un proceso penal político de toda Rusia que indicará en qué dirección se mueve Rusia como país en el futuro próximo”.

World.title: El giro ético: cómo cambiar el capitalismo salvaje desde dentro para hacer el bien
World.content:
La reflexión ética no está de moda en un mundo despiadado, pero varios autores proponen ideas para, sin caer en la ingenuidad y ser tachados de ‘buenistas’, transformar la sociedad y construir una vida mejor

Pueden acusarle a usted de buenista o de naíf. Pensar en el bien común no está de moda. La especie humana atraviesa tiempos de guerra, odio y división, y un nutrido menú de amenazas existenciales hace el futuro temible. En esta desesperanza, algunos de los gobernantes y empresarios más poderosos del planeta se asemejan más a villanos de ficción que a los héroes que nos hicieron soñar: privilegian el poder desmedido y la fuerza bruta frente a la negociación, la cooperación y las reglas compartidas. El bien cotiza a la baja.

“La manera de salir de todas las amenazas y retos que se nos presentan será haciendo más cosas juntos y comprometiéndonos con una vida en común y más cohesionada. No queda otra alternativa”, dice a este periódico el politólogo Jorge Tamames. Si vuelven Dios y los pantalones de campana, ¿por qué no va a volver la ética? Ya hay quien se preocupa por ello. Es posible dicen, hacer el bien dentro del sistema, dentro de las empresas, en el trabajo de cada uno o, como veremos, estableciendo un servicio de cooperación social obligatorio. Varios ensayos recientes reivindican que la ética no es una reliquia, sino una necesidad política y social de nuestro tiempo. Se trata de recuperar el discurso en tiempos de cinismo, ironía, competición… y hasta malismo.

El filósofo alemán Markus Gabriel no es un revolucionario: no quiere derrumbar el sistema, como tantas veces se intentó para empeorar las cosas, sino conseguir implementar un capitalismo ético (no cree que sea oxímoron) en el que “el negocio de los negocios sea hacer el bien”. Es decir, no se trata de que la humanidad entre en una especie de modo angelical donde todo el mundo obre de manera virtuosa, sino de lograr una organización del mundo que haga que el bien sea rentable. Gabriel propone, nada menos, que una Nueva Ilustración basada en estos principios.

'El cambista y su mujer', de Marinus van Reymerswaele, muestra la faceta más mercantilista y obsesa del capitalismo.

Eso se lee en su libro Hacer el bien. Cómo el capitalismo ético puede crear un nuevo contrato social (Pasado & Presente), que sigue la senda de obras anteriores como Ética para tiempos oscuros. “Necesitamos una nueva ética (…) cuya función sea regular al alza nuestra economía para que satisfaga las necesidades humanas reales y las de sociedades futuras moralmente más progresistas”, escribe Gabriel. Es lo que llama la reconciliación del valor moral y el económico, en la que tiene mucho que decir la regulación estatal coercitiva (y no la bondad por arte de magia), pero también la autorregulación en las empresas. En algunos momentos recuerda al Green New Deal, que propone hacer de la lucha contra el cambio climático un motor económico, y también quiere aparejar el interés económico al interés moral.

Del “trabajo de mierda” a la ambición moral

Luego, en el sistema capitalista, hay “trabajos de mierda”, como acuñó muy famosamente el antropólogo anarquista David Graeber, que no son los que están mal pagados o tienen malas condiciones —que también—, sino esos muy bien pagados, con nombres rimbombantes, prestigiosos y deseados… pero que no aportan nada a la sociedad. Se basaba en una encuesta realizada por YouGov en Estados Unidos en 2015 en la que el 37% de los encuestados afirmaban que su trabajo no hacía ninguna contribución significativa al mundo.

Contra esta deriva hay quien nos incita a actuar para cambiar el mundo. Es el caso del ensayista neerlandés Rutger Bregman en Ambición moral (Península): se enfoca en la cantidad de personas inteligentes y preparadas que están desperdiciando su talento en busca de la riqueza o el prestigio —a veces haciendo el mal— cuando podrían contribuir a hacer un mundo mejor. “De todo lo que desperdiciamos en estos tiempos de desperdicio, lo más importante es el talento echado a perder”, escribe.

Una manifestación multitudinaria en la Puerta del Sol de Madrid, el 21 de mayo de 2011. LUCA PIERGIOVANNI (EFE)

Bregman apuesta por combinar, de forma ambiciosa, el desarrollo personal con la acción social. Si Markus Gabriel expone cómo las empresas pueden obtener beneficios haciendo el bien —el capitalismo ético—, Bregman lo traslada a nuestra actividad laboral y cotidiana: también podemos tener algo así como éxito laboral ético. No basta con ser bueno en la vida privada; podemos trabajar en el bien, algo que, según el escritor, no abunda en sectores como la banca, el marketing, la consultoría o la tecnología. Lo verdaderamente ambicioso no es trepar hasta lo más alto del escalafón social, sino hacerlo tratando de resolver los problemas que aquejan a la sociedad de nuestro tiempo.

Para ello es necesaria una compasión radical: “Queremos ampliar nuestra compasión a ayudar a tanta gente y animales como sea posible”, escribe Bregman en su decálogo para la ambición moral. “Como los abolicionistas [de la esclavitud] y las sufragistas antes que nosotros, intentamos mover las fronteras del círculo moral de la humanidad. Nos preocupan las futuras generaciones y queremos ser buenos ancestros”.

¿Por qué no lo hacemos juntos?

Si seguimos dentro del sistema, algunos proponen normativizar de algún modo ese compromiso con la sociedad. Es el caso del politólogo Jorge Tamames en Algo que hicimos juntos (Círculo de Bellas Artes / Lengua de Trapo), que parte de una pregunta sencilla: “¿Cuándo fue la última vez que hiciste algo útil y valioso por los demás?”. Inspirado en cosas tan dispares como la ciencia ficción de Ursula K. Leguin o el ensayo El amanecer de todo, de David Graeber y David Wengrow, y partiendo de su pregunta inicial, aboga por un “servicio civil universal y obligatorio” —una especie de mili social y solidaria— mediante el que la ciudadanía de a pie puede afrontar los cuidados colectivos o la crisis medioambiental.

Según lo plantea Tamames, tendría también algo de experiencia vital, donde “juntar a gente de orígenes diferentes, borrar las jerarquías y distinciones”. Trabajarían codo con codo, en igualdad de condiciones, el pobre y el rico, el jefe y el empleado, el de aquí y el de allá. En definitiva, no difiere mucho de los trabajos vecinales que se hacían en los pueblos. En su texto no obvia las posibles objeciones (algunas bastante cuñadas) que se le harían, desde el rechazo a la obligatoriedad hasta el calificativo de “mili woke”, pasando por las críticas desde la izquierda, que podría ver aquí una sustitución del Estado de bienestar. A todas responde. “Creo que el tono general de la época es bastante optimista, y quise escribir en un registro algo más utópico, aunque también pragmático y realista”, dice, no en vano el libro ganó el premio Utopías que caben en el BOE que busca eso mismo: utopías que se puedan aterrizar en nuestro día a día.

Bici eléctrica de carga en la Plaza Tetuan, Barcelona. Gianluca Battista

Son todas propuestas para actuar desde la reflexión ética y cambiar el sistema desde dentro y en el marco de lo posible. Aunque tal vez el ánimo social sea el contrario: el malismo (en oposición al buenismo), que el artista Mauro Entrialgo describió en un libro homónimo, Malismo (Capitán Swing, 2024). “Se trata de una estrategia de comunicación que consiste en confesar deseos o actos que tradicionalmente habrían sido reprobables con el fin de conseguir algún tipo de beneficio”, dice el autor.

Hay malismo de distintos grados: ahí mete desde el nombre de los bares “canallitas” y los jurados severos en los talent shows hasta las bandas de trolls de las redes sociales (perfecto caldo de cultivo del malismo), pasando, sobre todo, por la actitud de ciertos gobernantes sin complejos que se vanaglorian de tener comportamientos poco éticos, como no hacer “nada” por facilitar el acceso a la vivienda o desmantelar a la fuerza campamentos de personas sin hogar. No en vano muchos de los grandes personajes de los productos audiovisuales del s. XXI no son los héroes sino los villanos: tal vez de ahí salga el fervor malista.

En definitiva, puede pensarse que estas iniciativas por encarar el bien común, a pesar de su voluntad pragmática, son absurdas en un mundo superindividualista y desnortado (a la par que malista), pero quizá la verdadera ingenuidad consista en creer que los grandes problemas de nuestro tiempo se resolverán sin una renovada idea de bien común.

World.title: Polvo de verano: ‘Una noche en La Latina’, por Lucía Lijtmaer
World.content:
Tres amigas que comparten piso se preparan para salir a plena luz del día a un local de cuarentones divorciados. Visten leopardos, cuero y ‘minishorts’. Llegan a la pista de baile y comienza la acción.

Artículos estrictamente de opinión que responden al estilo propio del autor. Estos textos de opinión han de basarse en datos verificados y ser respetuosos con las personas aunque se critiquen sus actos. Todas las columnas de opinión de personas ajenas a la Redacción de EL PAÍS llevarán, tras la última línea, un pie de autor —por conocido que éste sea— donde se indique el cargo, título, militancia política (en su caso) u ocupación principal, o la que esté o estuvo relacionada con el tema abordado

No entiendo muy bien cómo se torció la cosa.

El fin de semana había empezado perfectamente y como tiene que ser, el jueves.

Las tres nos acabábamos de despertar, debían ser como las seis de la tarde, porque nos habíamos quedado viendo una teleserie de los ochenta que le encanta a Zenia, Belleza y poder. No entiendo por qué le fascina esa telenovela, no dirías que tiene nada que ver con ella. Todas las chicas de la serie son rubias de ojos azules, llevan sombra de ojos lila nacarada, perlas en las orejas y trajes de chaqueta colores pastel. Todas tienen problemas con hombres fornidos y altos y con pieles cubiertas de maquillaje terracota y, aun así, Zenia se queda embobada tragándose un capítulo tras otro.

Ella, que tiene la piel transparente, el pelo negro, los ojos del color del carbón y las piernas interminables. Un tatuaje de una serpiente le recorre de la cadera al tobillo y siempre viste de negro. Cuando se pone coqueta, a Zenia le encanta bailar haciendo que su serpiente ondee como si fuera real. Hace que todos los tíos se caigan de culo con su belleza.

A Zenia le flipa poner el aire a 13 grados, bajar las persianas hasta que no queda ni un hálito de sol y que toda luz llegue del tubo catódico. Me encanta esa especie de luz azulada y verdosa que nos tiñe a las tres la piel hasta que parecemos tres peces debajo de un río en pleno invierno, qué gusto. Una de las cosas que más me hace feliz de compartir piso con Zenia y Gradi es que ninguna de las tres tiene frío jamás. Es en esas cosas en las que se nota que somos parecidas. Una vez intentamos traer a una chica nueva y se empeñaba en que saliéramos a hacer el saludo al sol. Hablaba de salir a trotar por el Retiro y a hot yoga a primera hora de la mañana. Nos deshicimos de ella inmediatamente. Zenia, Gradi y yo somos el trío perfecto.

Gradi se desperezó y dijo que tenía hambre y que se aburría. Gradi siempre tiene hambre y siempre se aburre. Yo lo entiendo, de las tres es la más delgada y la más frágil, necesita comer al menos una vez al día. Zenia, que no suele tener ganas de salir de casa tan fácilmente, accedió a apagar la tele. Gradi empezaba a temblar un poquitín, así que le recordé a Zenia que ya habíamos visto las primeras 10 temporadas de la serie.

No es sencillo encontrar lugares oscuros para huir del calor a media tarde, así que nos tuvimos que decantar por uno de esos bares infectos de la zona de divorciados que practican el tardeo, qué asco, joder. Reservé por la app un coche de lujo con los vidrios tintados para que nos recogiera en una hora y puse música a todo lo que da. Empezó a sonar Metrika, que me encanta. Podría ser una de las nuestras. A veces creo que lo es. La música muy alta es nuestro código para empezar a arreglarnos, nos da subidón. Me enfundé un vestido de leopardo con botas de cuero pegadas al cuerpo. Gradi eligió una camisa blanca y un corsé de color carne que le dejaba a la vista las bragas a juego. Zenia no se cambió: shorts tan cortos que va enseñando medio culo y un bodi negro con cortes a ambos lados del ombligo. Las tres nos maquillamos mientras cantamos: “Con las botas de pelo, pla pla pla pla. Cuando me rebota el culo, pla pla pla pla. Estoy follando con las bota’ y suena, pla pla pla. Pla pla pla, pla pla pla”, y me entró la risa cuando Gradi se puso el eyeliner rojo que fosforecía en la negrura de nuestro baño con las luces apagadas. Me encanta.

Ya en la pista de baile del bar de divorciados distinguí a Gradi solo por el eyeliner, de lo oscuro que estaba todo. Apenas dos rayitas rojas paralelas que se movían de un lado para otro. El local era perfecto, porque alguien había echado las cortinas de terciopelo negro por dentro y había puesto la luz negra para disimular que eran las ocho de la tarde. Ahí fuera aún hacía sol y el asfalto emanaba 41 grados a la sombra. Zenia y yo bailamos para atraer a los grupos de cuarentones que llegaban al afterwork. Qué asco dan los tíos siempre, sudando el gin-tonic y aflojándose las corbatas. Aun así, sabíamos que no nos iba a costar elegir. Los oficinistas de verano son las piezas más fáciles, es como pescar salmones en un barril.

Yo me había decantado por uno grande y gordo, para que me saciara al menos un par de días, y me di cuenta de que Zenia estaba por la labor de compartir, así que nos empezamos a restregar a su alrededor como perras en celo. El tipo y sus amigos no daban crédito, como siempre, sentían que les había tocado el euromillones. Esa maniobra siempre nos sale perfecta a las dos, parecemos dos traperas de un videoclip. Le perreamos al tipo arriba y abajo, moviendo el culo mientras él parecía el rey de la pista y sus compañeros le miraban con envidia. Zenia y yo sabemos cómo no pasarnos porque hay que ser cautas: consiste en llamar un poco la atención pero que nadie se acuerde de nuestras caras. Cuando nos miramos a los ojos es la señal para llevar al tipo para el baño. Me acerqué a su cara grande y sudorosa. No debía tener más de 40 años. Le susurré al oído si quería venirse al baño con nosotras. Asintió y me gritó directamente al tímpano que tenía coca. Me dieron ganas de arrancarle la lengua de un tajo, pero en vez de eso le sonreí y le tiré de la camisa para que me siguiera.

Avanzamos por el interior del local, que tenía el color exacto del hígado, entre marrón y rojo, salpicado de las luces de espejo que daban vueltas. Todavía no se había puesto el sol pero noté la anticipación que se me agolpaba en las sienes en forma de un latido sordo y hueco. Me rechinaban los dientes y tragué algo de la saliva que se me estaba acumulando en la boca. El tío nos quería llevar al baño de hombres, que era apenas una puertecita batiente, pero Zenia le arrastró de la mano hacia el de mujeres diciendo: “Ahí hay más sitio”. Las dos teníamos ya las pupilas dilatadas, yo apenas podía contener las ganas y abrí la puerta del baño de un golpe fuerte mientras el tío balbuceaba un: “Tranquilas, nenas, que hay para todas”.

Apenas había transcurrido una milésima de segundo cuando el tío resbaló con algo húmedo que se derramaba por todo el suelo y cayó, como un fardo, quedando inmediatamente inconsciente. Primero pensé que había resbalado con agua o pis, pero en cuanto contemplé la escena en su totalidad, entendí. Gradi estaba tirada en el suelo con la boca chorreando sangre y un tío con la piel de color gris a su lado. Todo a su alrededor era sangre derramada.

—Joder, Gradi, no me lo puedo creer —soltó Zenia con resignación, mientras se agachaba para darle un par de bofetadas, a ver si espabilaba—. Te has vuelto a chupar a un yonqui.

Gradi abrió los ojos despacito, como si estuviera borracha, y susurró algo parecido a “teniamuschajambre”, pero no se le entendía del todo bien.

Es verdad que es para cabrearse, entiendo a Zenia. Gradi no tiene paciencia, es superansias con lo del comer.

—Ya, pero te tengo dicho que no te chupes a los tíos en los bares, y menos a los flacos. Que se te acaban en un suspiro. Y además que te puedes colocar de más dependiendo de lo que hayan tomado. A ver, saca la lengua —le pidió Zenia, en plan maternal.

Gradi abrió la boca, y apenas pudimos distinguir sus colmillos de color marfil y nácar.

—Me encuentro fatal —se quejó, superdespacito—. Creía que el tío iba de coca pero se ha metido keta.

—Lo que nos faltaba.

—¿Y ahora qué hacemos? —dije yo.

Se hizo un silencio, un poco largo. Yo sabía lo que pensaba Zenia. O nos llevábamos al gordo a casa o había que cargarse a todos los tíos del local. Las dos nos miramos, con la cara muy seria.

—¿Cuántos tíos hay? —preguntó Zenia.

—Unos 20.

—Joder. Otro barrio vetado por las ansias de la Gradi.

—Ya te digo.

Zenia suspiró justo antes de decir lo inevitable:

—Bueno, al lío, que tenemos faena.

World.title: Police get stop and search powers after shootings in Zuidoost
World.content:
Police will be able to stop and search anyone for weapons in part of Amsterdam-Zuidoost for a week from Thursday, after a long series of shooting and gun threats that the city says often involve minors.

The mayor, police and public prosecutor have designated the H-buurt, the K-buurt and the Nelson Mandelapark a security risk area until August 27. Inside it, police can search people without having any specific cause for suspicion.

Authorities recorded 18 firearm-related incidents in the area between June 1 and August 1, ranging from threats made at gunpoint to shootings that left people wounded.

In one case on August 3, a shot fired during a confrontation passed through a wall into a child’s bedroom. A minor was inside the house at the time, reported local broadcaster AT5.

Second summer running

It is the second summer in a row that Zuidoost has faced such a regime. Last year’s designation followed the fatal shooting of a 17-year-old and was extended into September.

Extra police patrols had already been deployed this summer, the city said, but had not been enough to restore calm.

Controversial tactics

Preventive searching has been used in Rotterdam for a long time. It was introduced there in 2002 and now covers large parts of Rotterdam-Zuid.

The tactic is controversial, with opposition and coalition parties on Rotterdam’s council having accused the city of ethnic profiling. Stop and searches in Rotterdam require at least three police officers at every search to guard against it.

Amsterdam dropped preventive searching in 2015, deeming it ineffective. The city has still used it repeatedly over the past year, in the red light district, over New Year and now twice in Zuidoost.

World.title: Budget talks offer no clear route to majority for Dutch cabinet
World.content:
The cabinet has begun talks with opposition parties to try to secure a majority for next month’s annual budget, with prime minister Rob Jetten setting a target of August 28 to secure a deal.

The three-party coalition of D66, VVD and CDA is 10 seats short of a majority in the lower house and holds less than one-third of the seats in the Senate.

Commentators say the choice boils down to two options: either do a deal with the main left-wing party Progressief Nederland (PRO) – which was formed by the merger of PvdA and GroenLinks – or try to forge a majority on the right with JA21. But neither route is straightforward.

PRO leader Jesse Klaver told NRC this week that he supported the cabinet’s plans to invest €2.1 billion extra in defence and €1 billion in education.

But his party wants to force the cabinet to scrap its proposed €6.5 billion cuts to social security and raise the money instead through higher taxes on wealth and corporations.

Klaver said he was prepared to drive a hard bargain on the welfare cuts even though they are not due to be introduced until next year’s budget. His stance is backed up by the trade union movement, which has called a national transport workers’ strike for September 9 to protest against the reforms.

“We won’t let people live with uncertainty about cuts in the future,” Klaver said. “These need to be taken off the table this autumn.

VVD reluctance

The right-wing liberal VVD says the cuts are non-negotiable because they are not prepared to increase borrowing or let the budget deficit exceed the European Union’s 3% limit.

The VVD has been reluctant to negotiate with PRO, which it explicitly ruled out as a coalition partner during last year’s general election campaign and in the negotiations to form the current cabinet at the start of this year.

But the path to a majority on the right is even more complicated. Support from PRO would give the cabinet a healthy majority in the lower house and a near majority in the Senate, where the government needs to find just two more votes from smaller parties.

JA21 has nine seats in the lower house – one fewer than the number needed for a majority – but only two senators. The party wants the cabinet to cut welfare even further and reduce taxes, including the so-called “freedom contribution” proposed by the Christian Democrats (CDA) to fund defence spending.

JA21: “Constructive”

Its leader, Joost Eerdmans, said a video call with Jetten and the two deputy prime ministers, Dilan Yesilgöz of the VVD and Bart van den Brink of the CDA, had been “good and constructive” and further discussions would follow, without disclosing further details.

Geert Wilders’ far-right PVV group and the even more extreme Forum voor Democratie (FVD), which have 25 seats between them, are refusing to lend the cabinet any support.

DNA, the splinter group of former PVV MPs led by Gidi Markuszower, is willing to co-operate with the cabinet, but has not been invited to the negotiating table.

Markuszower has warned he will demand a high price for his party’s support: “People at home are crying out for more money in their pocket, lower costs, more houses, more secuity and less asylum, but the cabinet is failing on all fronts.”

BBB shut out

The farmers’ party BBB has also been left off the guest list for this week’s talks, even though the party has 11 seats in the Senate.

The BBB has been unhappy with the government’s plans to impose more limits on the agriculture sector in order to cut nitrogen pollution, which has triggered a new wave of farmers’ protests over the summer.

The party has been riven by defections in both houses in the last year, particularly the upper house, where five BBB senators have left the party, including two who switched allegiance to its arch-nemesis, the progressive liberal party D66.

Heinen absent

Even more intriguing is the fact that finance minister Eelco Heinen, who will present the budget when parliament reconvenes on September 15, is not attending the first two days of negotiations.

Heinen excused himself on the basis that the focus of the talks was to secure “political commitment” rather than discuss the details of fiscal policy, but Klaver remarked: “I can’t remember a previous time when the finance minister wasn’t there for the budget process.”

The Christian parties ChristenUnie and SGP, as well as the pensioners’ party 50Plus, are also due to meet with ministers on Wednesday.

World.title: Water board call in police after drought inspectors face threats
World.content:
Water authorities in Noord-Brabant have contacted police after inspectors received threats for checking whether local residents were breaking drought restrictions.

The Brabantse Delta water board, which covers an area centred on Breda stretching from the Maas to the Belgian border, has imposed a ban on taking water from streams and ditches between 9am and 9pm.

Inspectors have been using drones equipped with cameras to monitor fields since the ban was introduced a month ago. But staff who were named in a recent article on news website Omroep Brabant about their work have since ben subjected to threats.

Water board chairman Joris Bengevoord would not go into detail about the threats, but said a criminal complaint had been filed with police so they could investigate.

“It’s very serious and goes way too far,” he told NOS. “It’s not OK that they’re being threatened, which is why I’m speaking out as water board chair.

“We are doing this with the best intentions and I stand behind my staff. They are in the midst of it day after day.”

World.title: Do you know “Lucky”? Police can’t ID foreign man in Amsterdam
World.content:
Amsterdam cold case police are appealing for help identifying a man known as “Lucky” who collapsed on the street three years ago after suffering a suspected brain haemorrhage or stroke.

Doctors believe he subsequently developed aphasia, which makes communication nearly impossible. No one has been able to work out who he is or where he came from.

He now lives in a care home in Amsterdam Zuidoost and the only words he still uses are English ones – “nonsense” and “definitely” – which he uses to confirm or deny things. He spoke in an American or Canadian accent, the police say. Beyond that, he cannot talk or communicate at all.

Detectives first began looking into the case in 2023 but every line of inquiry ran into a dead end. The search then passed to the force’s cold case team, where two retired members, named as Ruud and Nel, are now volunteering to find out who he is. Presumably, somewhere his family or friends are looking for him.

A public appeal for information has garnered an “overwhelming” response, police say, with more than 140 tip-offs reported on the first day. A DNA and fingerprints search on the missing persons and deceased database returned no matches, VRT News reported the police as saying.

Two nicknames, conflicting clues

Digging into his former social circle, the investigators found that he belonged to a Buddhist community on Middenweg, in the east of the city, where he was known as “Lucky”. They also learned that he would occasionally have a drink at Soep en Zo, a café on Waterlooplein, where regulars knew him by a different name again: “Chris the Canadian”.

People who knew him think he may have come from the US or Canada because of his accent. He also may have had a past in Nepal, VRT News said.

Investigators say a lot of the information they’ve gathered is conflicting. “He was supposedly filthy rich, but at the same time he was wandering the streets of Amsterdam,” according to Ruud.

But what the investigators cannot understand is how a person could leave so little trace. “I simply cannot believe that nobody knows who this man really is,” Nel said. “Isn’t it strange that you could perhaps live under the radar in the Netherlands for 20 years?”

“Every person has the right to an identity,” Ruud stressed, “and that includes this man.”

Anyone with potential information on the case can report it to the police here.

World.title: Campaigners call for Amsterdam to pull plug on giant data centre
World.content:
More than 500 people have joined a campaign to stop a huge data centre being built in Amsterdam-Zuid, arguing that it will bring “zero benefits to the area”.

The Dutch government has introduced restrictions on the size of data centres in recent years following criticism from provincial and municipal governments about the strain on the electricity network. Data centres accounted for 4.6% of all electricity use in the Netherlands in 2024.

But the plans to build a 24,000 m2 facility on Amsterdam’s Science Park were submitted by US firm Equinix before the ban, which only applies to new developments, took effect in 2022.

Local residents have also become increasingly vocal in opposing the construction of data centres, while campaign groups Geef Tegengas and Extinction Rebellion both staged demonstrations this summer against a Microsoft project in Amsterdam Sloterdijk.

“There are already enough data centres to keep everything running. This is becoming overkill,” Dylan Bakker of Stop Datacenter Zuidoost told NOS.

Amsterdam city council, which wants to build 8,000 homes in Zuidoost to help relieve the national housing shortage, has attached extra conditions to the site, such as requiring the residual heat from the plant to be used for domestic heating.

Water and electricity

There are also concerns about the strain on water supplies, which have been exacerbated by the summer drought. Equinix said in its planning application that it would need 274 million litres of water a year for the first stage of the project, rising to more than a billion litres when the data centre is complete in 2036.

But the municipality says it would face legal action and penalties if it tore up the permit to build the data center at this stage.

Equinix has said it will only build one of four planned 60-metre data towers initially, until electricity grid operator Tennet can supply enough power.

Tennet warned earlier this year that the network was nearing capacity, leading to a six-month moratorium on new connections in Utrecht.

The complete campus in Zuidoost will consume 779 kWh of electricity a year, almost as much as all the households Amsterdam combined, which currently use 869 kWh.

Michiel Eielts, director of Equinix Benelux, argued that the data centres were an essential part of modern infrastructure. “Every house needs the internet. We need data centres for the growth of our companies, our public services and our security,” he said.

World.title: Dutch men face Argentina in World Cup hockey, women win again
World.content:

The Dutch men’s hockey team are taking on Argentina in their second World Cup group match on Tuesday, with the winners set to take a giant step towards the knock-out rounds.

Both teams won their opening matches comfortably, with the Netherlands beating New Zealand 5-1 in Amstelveen while Argentina overcame Japan by a 3-0 scoreline at the same venue.

The Netherlands and Belgium are co-hosting the tournament, 12 years after the World Cup was held in The Hague. On that occasion the Dutch women’s team won their tournament while the men lost in the final to Australia.

The women’s team are on the brink of reaching the quarter-finals this time after coming through a tricky tie against Australia to win 4-2.

Goalkeeper Anne Veenendaal was kept busy in the opening period as the Dutch had to defend seven penalty corners before taking the lead when Yibbi Jansen scored from a penalty corner at the other end.

Joosje Burg made it two midway through the second period, but Australia hit back almost immediately through Stephanie Kershaw.

After a goalless third quarter, the Australians equalised when Abigail Wilson converted a penalty corner, but Burg restored the lead with her second before Marijn Veen rounded off a fine move to make sure of the points.

In an intriguing subplot, the Argentinian men’s team includes Nicolas Keenan, the fiancé of Dutch prime minister Rob Jetten.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by hockey.nl (@hockeynl)



Jetten wore an Argentina replica shirt as he cheered on his partner from the sidelines on Sunday’s match, but was evasive when asked by RTL which team he would be supporting on Tuesday.

“Hopefully it’ll be a draw so we don’t have to fall out at home,” he joked.

World.title: More Dutch adults are single or living apart, says CBS
World.content:
The amount of people in the Netherlands who are single is rising, and a growing number are in relationships with a partner they do not live with, new figures from statistics agency CBS show.

In 2025, 30% of adults said they had no long-term partner, up from 27% in 2013. A further 10% were in a so-called “living apart together” relationship – a couple who keep separate homes – compared with 8% in 2013. The remaining 60% lived with a partner.

At the start of 2025, 5.7 million adults did not live with a partner. Most of them, 4.4 million, were living alone, while 627,000 were single parents and others still lived with their own parents.

Single women happier

Single women were more likely to call themselves happy (82%) than single men (76%), the agency found. People in couples were happier still: 92% of those living with a partner said they were happy, whether married or not.

Women were slightly more likely to be single overall (32%) than men (28%). Among the under-25s, most were single (62%) or living apart from a partner (29%), and just 8% shared a home with one.

The pattern shifts with age. From 45 onwards single women outnumber single men, an effect CBS links partly to divorce, after which men more often find a new partner. Among divorced women, 68% were single, against 55% of divorced men.

By 75 and over, about 42% of people lived alone with no partner, mostly because a partner had died. Just over half were still living with someone.

World.title: Schools return as new Dutch and maths targets become law
World.content:
Schools in the north of the Netherlands are the first to go back after the summer holidays, and they return to a new set of legally binding targets for what pupils have to learn in Dutch and maths.

The updated core curriculum objectives (kerndoelen) were written into law this month for the first time, NOS reported on Monday. They set out the knowledge and skills pupils are expected to acquire in primary school and the first years of secondary education.

The previous objectives dated from 2006 and were criticised as out of date, vague, and non-committal. There are now fewer of them for Dutch, but what pupils should be able to do is described more concretely. Literature has a clearly defined role, and language development is to be built into other subjects as well.

Junior education minister Judith Tielen said the change was needed because of a serious decline in basic language and maths skills.

Falling standards

The Netherlands was previously seen internationally as one of the leaders in reading, but standards have dropped sharply in recent years.

Tielen wrote to MPs recently that no other European country has seen learning performance fall as far, and school inspectors have found year after year that many children cannot read, write, or do basic maths at the expected level.

Earlier attempts to turn this around – a masterplan on basic skills launched in 2022 and the national programme set up to make up for learning lost during the coronavirus closures – have not had the intended effect, Tielen said. She is working on a new approach prioritising language.

The objectives for the remaining subjects, including two new ones – digital literacy and citizenship – are due to be made law next summer. Schools have until 2031 to incorporate all of them into their teaching.

Ilja Cornelisz, an education researcher at the Vrije Universiteit in Amsterdam, said ambitious objectives do matter because basic skills are under pressure, but that more is needed to improve schooling.

The real task, he said, is giving teachers the professional room, the reliable knowledge, and the support to deliver the goals in their own classrooms, while leaving schools free to decide how they get there.

World.title: FedEx-led €7.8bn takeover of Polish delivery giant InPost wins EU approval

The European Commission has granted approval for a consortium led by American transportation conglomerate FedEx to take over Polish delivery giant InPost in a deal worth €7.8 billion (33.7 billion zloty). InPost, which operates in France, Spain, the UK, Portugal, Italy and the Benelux countries, as well as in its home market, confirmed on Tuesday that it had received the green light from the EU for the deal, which was announced in February. If it goes through, the takeover will see a consortium made up of FedEx along with existing InPost investors, Advent, A&R, and PPF, purchase all of the company’s shares at a price of €15.60 each. Konsorcjum inwestorów, w którym jednym z uczestników jest amerykański @FedEx, uzyskało bezwarunkową zgodę KE na nabycie wszystkich akcji @InPostPL @RBrzoska https://t.co/F4AleTCViO — WNP.PL (@wnppl) August 18, 2026 The group behind the deal says the aim is to help InPost continue its recent rapid expansion. The firm will retain its name, branding and Polish headquarters. Founder and CEO Rafał Brzoska will remain in place, as well as being a major shareholder through A&R, which is his investment vehicle. The deal will see Advent, an American private equity firm, and FedEx each hold 37% of InPost. A&R would have 16% and PPF, a Czech investment fund founded by the late billionaire Petr Kellner, 10%. Currently, PPF holds 28.75%, A&R 12.49%, and Advent 6.5%. The initial offer period for the consortium’s takeover was due to end on 27 July. However, on 22 July, it was extended until 18 September due to the fact that antitrust proceedings in the EU and Vietnam were still ongoing. In its announcement today of EU approval, InPost noted that it is still awaiting a green light from the Vietnam Competition Commission but expects a decision to be made by 8 September. Although the Polish company has no operations in Vietnam, FedEx has been present on the market since 1994. InPost has grown rapidly in recent years through its pioneering use of parcel lockers, first in Poland and then across western Europe. In the UK, it has established a network of over 14,000 parcel lockers, including in branches of the British Post Office. In June this year, French President Emannuel Macron thanked InPost for its latest investment in France, where the firm – which operates there through its subsidiary Mondial Relay – is planning to spend a further €500 million to expand its presence. In the first quarter of 2026, InPost saw its revenue rise 31% year-on-year to reach 3.9 billion zloty. That included 121% growth in the UK, 28% in the Eurozone and 9% in Poland itself. However, the group’s earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortisation (EBITDA), a measure of profitability of business operations, were down 4% to 902 million zloty. World.title: Twelve killed as Polish coach crashes in Hungary
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Twelve people have died after a bus carrying Polish pilgrims from Medjugorje in Bosnia and Herzegovina back to Poland crashed on a motorway in Hungary. Initial findings indicate that the cause of the accident was the driver of the coach falling asleep. Political leaders in both Poland and Hungary have offered condolences to the families of the victims, while the Polish foreign ministry has set up a special helpline for those affected. BREAKING: 12 people have been killed after a Polish tourist bus crashed on a motorway in Hungary https://t.co/PAiZ4D1jU3 📺 Sky 501, Virgin 602, Freeview 233 and YouTube pic.twitter.com/yxW9tBN5bw — Sky News (@SkyNews) August 16, 2026 The accident occurred at around 1 a.m. local time on the night of Saturday to Sunday on the M3 motorway in Hungary. Later on Sunday morning, Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar confirmed that 12 people had died and at least 10 were seriously injured. According to information from the Hungarian emergency services, 57 passengers and two drivers had been on the bus. “The driver probably fell asleep at the wheel”, resulting in the vehicle veering off the road and into a ditch, said police in a statement quoted by Polsat News. Polsat reports that the group is from around Strzyżów, a town in southeastern Poland. The owner of the local company that had been transporting them told Business Insider Polska that the coach “was driven by two experienced drivers”. Twelve people lost their lives and at least ten were seriously injured overnight when a bus carrying Polish tourists overturned and went off the road into a ditch on the M3 motorway. My sincere condolences to the families of the victims. I am grateful to all those who took part… — Magyar Péter (Ne féljetek) (@magyarpeterMP) August 16, 2026 Polish media outlets reported that the group in the bus were pilgrims on their way back to Poland from Medjugorje, which is a popular destination for Catholic pilgrimages due to a series of reported visions of the Virgin Mary that have occurred there. Polish foreign ministry spokesman Maciej Wewiór later confirmed to broadcaster TVN that “everything indicates they were returning from Medjugorje”. The authorities in Podkarpackie, the province of Poland where the group was from, also reported that they were pilgrims returning from Bosnia and Herzegovina. The accident on Sunday morning took place just after the end of celebrations of the Assumption of Mary on Saturday, which had included the unveiling in Poland of Europe’s tallest statue of Mary. Poland’s president, Karol Nawrocki, issued a statement on Sunday morning expressing his “deep sorrow…in the face of this unimaginable tragedy” and offering “prayer and profound compassion for the families and loved ones of the victims”. Prime Minister Donald Tusk likewise expressed his “deepest condolences to the families and loved ones of the victims” and thanked the Hungarian emergency services for undertaking the rescue operation. Andrii Sybiha, the foreign minister of Ukraine, which borders both Poland and Hungary, also offered his “heartfelt condolences” and said that “Ukraine stands in solidarity with the friendly Polish people and shares their grief”. The Polish embassy in Budapest has set up a special helpline for family members and loved ones of those involved in the crash. World.title: Europe’s biggest Virgin Mary statue – taller than Rio’s Christ the Redeemer – unveiled in Polish village
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The tallest statue of the Virgin Mary in Europe has been officially opened in the small village of Konotopie in central Poland. Towering over the rural landscape at 55.6 metres high, the monument, whose construction was funded by a wealthy local couple, is taller than the famous Christ the Redeemer statue in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. The new landmark, which is also the tallest religious statue of any kind in Europe, was unveiled on 15 August, when Catholics celebrate the assumption of Mary into heaven. The consecration ceremony was led by Krzysztof Wętkowski, bishop of the diocese of Włocławek in which Konotopie, which has a population of only around 130 people, is located. The local community hopes that the statue will become a major site of pilgrimage. Among those to attend the ceremony was former Polish president and Nobel Peace Prize winner Lech Wałęsa. “We sinners ask Our Lady of Mercy to take care of the whole nation,” wrote the 82-year-old in a post on social media, sharing photos of himself at the statue. Construction of the concrete statue took 18 months and reportedly cost around 100 million zloty (€23.2 million). Those costs were covered by the couple behind the project, Roman and Grażyna Karkosik. After making his fortune investing in undervalued companies during Poland’s post-communist transition in the 1990s, Roman Karkosik had by the early 21st century become one of Poland’s richest people, though his fortune has since diminished somewhat, according to estimates. The couple – who keep an extremely low profile, rarely giving interviews and never speaking publicly about the project to build the statue of Mary – live in a restored 18th-century palace around 2 kilometres away, from where they can see the new monument. Konotopie’s statue of Mary has now overtaken one in Miribel, France, as Europe’s tallest. But it is still some distance behind the tallest in the world, the 98-metre Mother of All Asia–Tower of Peace in Batangas City, Philippines. Until recently, Poland also had the tallest statue of Jesus in the world, the 33-metre-high Jesus Christ the King of the Universe monument, erected in the town of Świebodzin in 2010. However, in 2024, it was overtaken by a 61-metre-tall statue of Jesus in Indonesia. The design for the statue of Mary in Konotopie was originally conceived in the form of a two-metre-high model by sculptor Adam Jakub Matejkowski, who told the Polish edition of Forbes magazine that the Karkosiks had specifically requested that the statue be larger than Świebodzin’s Christ. Chief engineer Bartłomiej Niesłuchowski told broadcaster TVN that it took months to find a company willing and able to undertake such a project. Because no suppliers in Poland could produce the material needed for the unique mould into which the concrete would be poured, it had to be manufactured in Italy. The monument will be free for the public to access, including its observation deck, located 15 metres up on the pedestal upon which Mary stands. The site is expected to become a place of pilgrimage, with local authorities preparing for an influx of people. “We’re already seeing growing interest in investment plots, including restaurants,” Renata Gołębiewska, mayor of the nearby town of Kikoł, told the Rzeczpospolita daily. “But it’s too early to assess the impact.” Poland is one of Europe’s most religious countries. Just over 70% of the population identify as Catholic, according to the most recent national census, while around 30% attend Sunday mass. However, religiosity has been falling rapidly in recent years, especially among young Poles. The Catholic church in Poland has also been hit by a series of scandals relating to historical child sex abuse as well as accusations that it interferes in politics. The proportion of Catholics who attend Sunday mass in Poland has stabilised at around 30% after falling from a peak of 57%, new church data show. The proportion of children taking Catholic catechism in schools has continued to fall but remains a majority https://t.co/5bu35hzJ7c — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 17, 2025 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Polish opposition expels 40 lawmakers who formed breakaway caucus led by ex-PM Morawiecki
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s largest opposition party, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), has expelled 40 of its lawmakers in response to them forming a breakaway parliamentary caucus led by PiS deputy leader and former prime minister Mateusz Morawiecki. The decision formalises a split that began last month, when Morawiecki and his supporters refused to resign from a political association they had formed and sign a pledge of loyalty to PiS. They represented a more moderate faction that had long been unhappy with the party’s move in a hard-right direction. Koleżeński Sąd Dyscyplinarny PiS podjął decyzję o wykluczeniu z partii 38 posłów i 2 senatorów wchodzących w skład klubu Rozwój Plus, w tym byłego premiera Mateusza Morawieckiego – przekazał rzecznik dyscyplinarny PiS Karol Karski. https://t.co/Qe6KuPVUVZ — tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) August 13, 2026 On Thursday, PiS’s disciplinary spokesman, Karol Karski, announced that its disciplinary court had found that 38 MPs and two senators “seriously violated the PiS statute by leaving the PiS parliamentary caucus and joining a new caucus” founded by Morawiecki, called Development Plus (Rozwój Plus). Karski added that all 40, including Morawiecki, had been notified of the decision by email and been sent scans of the ruling. They have seven days to appeal. If no appeal is filed, they will officially cease to be PiS members, Karski said. A statement from the party’s disciplinary court, cited by news website Onet, also noted that Morawiecki had committed a further “serious violation” of the party’s statute by announcing last week that Development Plus would become a political party. Mateusz Morawiecki has confirmed that his Development Plus group, which is splitting from the national-conservative opposition PiS party, will soon form a party of its own. However, he categorically ruled out ever working with Prime Minister @donaldtusk https://t.co/J6mQaer4MA — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 4, 2026 Among those to be expelled are several former government ministers, including Janusz Cieszyński, Paweł Jabłoński, Olga Semeniuk-Patkowska and Szymon Szynkowski vel Sęk. Some of the ousted lawmakers expressed their disappointment at PiS’s decision. “Someone who has done everything for PiS is being expelled simply because he wanted to broaden the party’s voter base,” Grzegorz Puda, another former minister, told the Fakt daily. Another, Łukasz Schreiber, told news website Onet that, in reality, the decision to expel them had been taken when party leader Jarosław Kaczyński said in July they had effectively resigned by refusing to sign the loyalty pledge. “Everything else was just a formality.” Morawiecki served as prime minister from 2017 until 2023, when PiS lost power to the current government, a more liberal coalition led by Donald Tusk. The party has plunged into crisis this year, with its support in polls falling to the lowest level in over 15 years. In response to a growing challenge from the far right, Kaczyński has shifted PiS itself rightwards. That frustrated more moderate figures around Morawiecki, who founded the Development Plus association in April this year as a way of promoting their ideas. However, that prompted criticism from some other members of the party, who saw it as a step towards creating a breakaway group. The split in PiS is a blow to the party and its leader, Jarosław Kaczyński. But the potential emergence of a new centre-right party led by Mateusz Morawiecki could actually help the opposition win a majority at next year's elections, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/xMP7e4rOFf — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 31, 2026 Matters came to a head in July, when Morawiecki and his supporters refused to quit their association and sign the pledge of loyalty demanded by Kaczyński. They then formed their own caucus, which immediately became the third largest in parliament and meant that PiS’s was no longer the biggest. Last week, Morawiecki confirmed that his group would soon form a new party of its own. He laid out a vision of a more moderate, centre-right party that would focus on economic development rather than “ideological disputes”. Its first policy proposal was to establish a special “salary” for parents, equivalent to the minimum wage, that they would be paid for the first three years of a child’s life, with the aim of boosting Poland’s birth rate, which is one of the lowest in the world. According to poll aggregator eWybory.eu, Development Plus already has average support of 5.6% in polls, despite not yet being a party. Support for PiS has fallen to 20.3%, down from 24.4% in July. World.title: Poland seeks to boost investment with new tax-free personal accounts
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has introduced a new type of account that will allow individuals to invest up to 100,000 zloty (€23,200) without paying capital gains tax. The government says the scheme is designed to encourage Poles to build long-term savings and channel billions of zloty into the domestic financial market. Osobiste Konta Inwestycyjne to nowe narzędzie, które ułatwi inwestowanie i oszczędzanie na preferencyjnych warunkach podatkowych. Nowe przepisy wejdą w życie 1 stycznia 2027 r. Szczegóły w komunikacie ⤵️ https://t.co/Z6zEHKkQsY — Ministerstwo Finansów (@MF_GOV_PL) August 13, 2026 The new legislation, which was signed into law on Thursday by President Karol Nawrocki and will take effect on 1 January 2027, creates Personal Investment Accounts (OKI). All assets held in an OKI will be completely exempt from the usual 19% capital gains tax. Amounts up to 100,000 zloty, including up to 25,000 in savings assets such as bonds and deposits, will be completely tax free. Assets above 100,000 zloty will be subject to a new tax on their value. The government has said the tax will amount to 0.85% in 2027 and will be adjusted annually. Finance minister Andrzej Domański earlier described the introduction of OKI as “the biggest change in years for individual investors and the largest project aimed at building domestic capital to drive the development of the Polish economy”. While Nawrocki, who is aligned with the opposition, regularly clashes with the government and has vetoed a record number of laws, in this case he approved their idea, which he office said “could have a positive impact on both citizens and the state”. “Poles will gain a tool to promote family wealth building thanks to an attractive tax-free allowance and a guarantee of no account maintenance fees,” they added. Sejm przyjął ustawę o Osobistych Kontach Inwestycyjnych. Do 100 tys. zł bez podatku. To największa od lat zmiana dla indywidualnych inwestorów i największy projekt budowy krajowego kapitału napędzającego rozwój polskiej gospodarki. 🇵🇱 — Andrzej Domański (@Domanski_Andrz) July 3, 2026 The government estimates the scheme could result in about 74 billion zloty flowing to the Warsaw Stock Exchange by 2040. Kamil Gemra, an assistant professor at the Warsaw School of Economics, said he considered the projection realistic. “Society is getting wealthier; we have record amounts in our bank accounts. It would be enough for just a few per cent of that money to flow into the capital market for the figure cited by the finance ministry be achieved,” Gemra told the Polish Press Agency (PAP). The government also forecasts, however, that the tax exemption will reduce state budget revenues by nearly 9 billion zloty over 10 years, at a time when public finances are under increasing strain amid rapidly rising debt. Poland’s WIG20 stock market index has hit its highest ever level, surpassing a record that had stood for almost 19 years. The WIG20 has been Europe’s best-performing major blue-chip index so far this year, gaining almost 25% https://t.co/CBbv99v2Uk — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 4, 2026 Poland already has three mechanisms that allow people to accumulate assets with tax advantages: Individual Retirement Accounts (IKE), Individual Pension Schemes (IKZE), and Employee Capital Plans (PPK). However, in all three cases, the capital gains tax exemption is conditional on withdrawing funds after reaching retirement age. Despite the Polish stock market’s strong performance in recent years, Poles’ direct participation remains modest. Shares make up only 2.9% of household assets, the equivalent of 3% of GDP. That is well below the EU average of 8.2%. By contrast, households’ cash holdings are equivalent to 11.5% of GDP, well ahead of the EU average of 4.5% and behind only Slovenia (11.7%) and Germany (11.6%). World.title: Polish PM confirms he wants his “right-hand man” to be made constitutional court judge
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Prime Minister Donald Tusk has confirmed that he will seek to have Maciej Berek, a government minister who stepped down this week and whom Tusk calls his “right-hand man”, appointed as a judge on Poland’s constitutional court. The move has generated considerable controversy given that Tusk’s ruling coalition has repeatedly pledged to “depoliticise” the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) after the previous national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government appointed its former politicians to the court. At a press conference on Thursday, however, Tusk defended the idea, describing Berek as an “apolitical and nonpartisan” figure who would help “fix the Constitutional Tribunal” after it was rendered illegitimate by PiS. Premier @donaldtusk potwierdził, że @MaciejBerek – do tej pory minister ds. nadzoru nad wdrażaniem polityki rządu – będzie kandydatem na sędziego Trybunału Konstytucyjnego. – To jeden z najwybitniejszych polskich prawników – uzasadnił szef rządu.https://t.co/RsKLhLjHhC — PolsatNews.pl (@PolsatNewsPL) August 13, 2026 Berek is a longstanding associate of Tusk. During Tusk’s first period as prime minister, from 2007 to 2014, Berek was head of the Government Legislation Centre (RCL) while also serving as secretary of the cabinet. After Tusk returned to power in 2023, heading a coalition of parties ranging from left to centre right, Berek was appointed as a minister without portfolio and then, in 2025, was made minister in charge of overseeing the implementation of government policy. He has, however, been an extremely low-key figure, rarely speaking in public. Berek is also not a member of parliament, and indeed not even a member of any political party. On Tuesday this week, Tusk unexpectedly announced before a cabinet meeting that Berek, whom he called his “right-hand man”, was leaving the government in order to “move on to other tasks”. The prime minister did not say what those tasks would be, but multiple media outlets reported that Berek would be presented as a candidate to become a judge on the Constitutional Tribunal. Since Tusk’s government came to power in December 2023, it has ignored all TK rulings because three of the tribunal’s judges were appointed illegitimately under the former PiS government. Fifteen months since the change of government, Poland's rule-of-law crisis continues – indeed, many Poles think the situation has got worse.@J_Jaraczewski explains the roots of the crisis, what its impact has been, and how it might be resolved https://t.co/7KOCURV3dU — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 17, 2025 The new ruling coalition also criticised the fact that some TK judges were former PiS politicians. Two of them, for example, were appointed in 2019 shortly after stepping down as PiS MPs. Another, the current TK chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, previously served as a deputy justice minister in the PiS government (though he was never a member of the PiS party). When Tusk’s coalition came to power, it promised to restore the legitimacy of the TK, including by “depoliticising” it. In 2024, it approved legislation that would have banned anyone who had served as a politician in the last four years from becoming a TK judge. However, the measures were referred by the then-president, PiS ally Andrzej Duda, to the TK itself, which subsequently declared them unconstitutional, meaning they did not come into force. Poland’s constitutional court has rejected two government bills seeking to overhaul the court itself, with the aim of reversing the politicisation that took place under the former administration. It found that the measures "violate judicial independence" https://t.co/uBJr1bXFv4 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 30, 2025 At a press conference on Thursday, Tusk confirmed the rumours that he would seek to make Berek a TK judge. He called Berek “one of the most distinguished Polish legal practitioners, who has made his apolitical and nonpartisan nature a hallmark”. Berek has a doctorate in law and, between his stints in government, worked as an assistant professor in the department of constitutional law at the University of Warsaw. “For him, compliance with the law and the constitution has always been paramount,” declared Tusk. “I don’t know anyone better equipped, better prepared, to help rectify the situation we face with the flawed Constitutional Tribunal.” 💬 Premier @donaldtusk w #Warszawa: Nie mamy żadnych innych interesów w tej sprawie. Zależy nam na naprawieniu Trybunału Konstytucyjnego, żeby nie był na smyczy prezydenta i PiS-u, tylko wykonywał swoją robotę. — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) August 13, 2026 The prime minister acknowledged that his government had tried to ban politicians from serving on the TK. But he said that Berek himself had recently told him that, “under the current political circumstances, we must do everything we can to remedy the situation” at the tribunal. “Since methods that are unconstitutional are being used from the other side, I must also demonstrate my determination and that we won’t give in to such methods,” added Tusk. Those remarks, in which Tusk also called Święczkowski’s leadership of the TK “embarrassing”, were a reference to the fact that the current PiS-aligned president, Karol Nawrocki, and Święczkowski have refused to accept four new TK judges chosen by parliament earlier this year. “We have no interests in this matter other than to repair the Constitutional Tribunal so that it is not a tool and is not under the thumb of the president or PiS, but rather that it performs its work as objectively as possible,” said Tusk. A newly sworn-in @TK_GOV_PL judge says he will not take his seat until four colleagues appointed by parliament are allowed to take theirs. He said their appointments had been blocked "unlawfully", in the latest twist in a long-running disputehttps://t.co/X30rm1Gfzs — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 29, 2026 However, there remain major potential stumbling blocks on Berek’s path to the TK, not least doubts over whether Tusk’s coalition partners will support his nomination in the Sejm, the lower house of parliament, which is responsible for nominating new TK judges. Anna Maria Żukowska, the head of The Left’s (Lewica) parliamentary caucus, declared on Tuesday that, if rumours of Berek’s nomination were true, “he won’t get votes from The Left because we promised our voters that politicians wouldn’t end up on the TK”. Given that the government has a majority of just nine in the 460-seat Sejm, it would only require a small number of MPs from Tusk’s coalition to oppose Berek’s nomination for him to lose the vote. On Thursday, Tusk said that he “understands” concerns from some coalition partners but that he would “try to convince those who have doubts”. Jeżeli to się wydarzy (a raczej nie), to do niedawna czynny polityk nie dostanie głosów klubu @__Lewica, gdyż obiecaliśmy naszym wyborcom, że politycy nie trafią do TK. Ale IMHO to bardzo krzywdząca dla @MaciejBerek plotka, on by się jako państwowiec w życiu na coś takiego nie… https://t.co/QWFFmdy4V3 — Anna-Maria Żukowska 💁🏻‍♀️ (@AM_Zukowska) August 11, 2026 The next vacancy on the TK’s 15-judge bench is due to open on 18 September, when the nine-year term of Justyn Piskorski, one of the PiS-era judges regarded as illegitimate by the current government, ends. After that, a further vacancy will open in January. However, even if Berek is approved by the Sejm, the law states that new TK judges must swear an oath “before the president”. Nawrocki has used this requirement to refuse to swear in four of the judges chosen by the Sejm this year. He has, however, sworn in three others. It remains unclear what the president would do in the case of Berek. Earlier this week, his chief of staff, Zbigniew Bogucki, told Radio Zet that Nawrocki would “accept the oath if procedures are followed”. However, he added that he does “not know if [the Sejm] is able to carry out those procedures properly”. World.title: Poland reintroduces VAT cut and daily price caps to lower fuel costs for drivers
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s government has announced that, from Monday, it will reintroduce some of the measures that were used earlier this year to lower prices for consumers at petrol stations amid the energy crisis triggered by the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The package, known in Polish as CPN and which will be in place from 17 August until at least 31 August, includes reducing VAT on fuels from 23% to 8% and introducing retail consumer price caps on fuels set daily by the energy minister. Announcing the measures on Thursday, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said they should result in prices falling by around 1 zloty (€0.23) per litre. Currently, average retail prices are 7.29 zloty for 95-octane petrol and 8.09 zloty for diesel, according to Polish price monitoring service E-Petrol. 💬 Premier @donaldtusk ⤵️ Polska będzie w absolutnej czołówce europejskiej, jeśli chodzi o najniższe ceny paliw. pic.twitter.com/ar3IZbzFHQ — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) August 13, 2026 Tusk acknowledged that CPN will entail “serious costs” for the state budget. When similar measures (which also, unlike now, included cuts in excise duty on fuels) were in place between the end of March and end of June, they cost the state an estimated 4.7 billion zloty. On Thursday, the prime minister renewed his criticism of opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki for last month refusing to sign into law a windfall tax on fuel companies’ excess profits this year. The government said that the tax, which would have raised an estimated 4 billion zloty, was intended to help cover the costs of fuel subsidies. The profits of many fuel companies have boomed during the crisis, with Polish state energy giant Orlen last week announcing record half-year results. Nawrocki’s chancellery, however, has argued that fuel companies would seek to pass the costs of tax increases onto consumers, thereby increasing prices. CPN was first introduced in March in response to soaring fuel prices in the wake of US and Israeli attacks on Iran and subsequent disruption to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies. CPN subsequently helped bring Polish fuel prices to among the lowest in the EU. Since the measures were withdrawn in June, prices at the pump in Poland have risen significantly, placing pressure on the government to again cushion the blow for consumers. E-Petrol reports that prices have recently started to fall, but remain well above the levels seen before the crisis. Economists at PKO, a major bank, wrote on Thursday that higher fuel prices in July, which stemmed from the expiry of CPN and an increase in global oil prices, were the main drivers of inflation accelerating from 2.5% in June to 3.0% last month. Polish state energy giant Orlen posted a record profit in the first half of 2026, as turmoil in the Middle East boosted earnings in the fuel sector. It also saw its highest-ever proportion of revenue from foreign markets https://t.co/uhGWJVQvf3 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 7, 2026 On Thursday, Tusk claimed that the reintroduced CPN would lead to Poland having among “the lowest prices in Europe”, helping “possibly millions of Polish drivers, on critical days, when they return from holidays”. But he also acknowledged that fuel would “still be expensive”. Nawrocki’s chief of staff, Zbigniew Bogucki, however, criticised the government for what he claimed was a belated response to high prices. World.title: Poland says it foiled Russian plot to “execute” US-Ukrainian citizen in Warsaw

We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has detained a Russian national who it says was planning to assassinate a person with joint US and Ukrainian citizenship in Warsaw. The news was first announced by Prime Minister Donald Tusk at a press conference on Thursday afternoon. “Thanks to the truly brilliant action of our security services – the Internal Security Agency (ABW) with the assistance of the police – on 7 August we detained a Russian citizen, recruited by Russian intelligence services, whose task was to execute an American and Ukrainian citizen right here in Warsaw,” he said. “This is the first time someone on Russian orders has decided to attack an American citizen on the territory of another NATO country,” added Tusk. 💬 Premier @donaldtusk w #Warszawa: 7 sierpnia zatrzymaliśmy obywatela Rosji, którego zadaniem było wykonanie egzekucji w Warszawie na obywatelu amerykańskim i ukraińskim równocześnie. Dzięki akcji ABW i Policji udało się temu zapobiec. — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) August 13, 2026 Though the prime minister said he was not allowed to name either the suspect or the target, he revealed that the latter was someone who is “inconvenient for Putin’s regime”. World.title: Faster Than the Metro. New Bus is Now Linking Prague 8 and Prague 6
World.content:
A new bus service running through Prague’s Blanka tunnel has begun operating, offering a direct connection between the northern part of the city and Dejvice.

Bus line 145 connects Čimice and Kobylisy in Prague 8 with Hradčanská and Dejvická in Prague 6. The journey takes around 15 minutes, according to Prague’s public transport authority ROPID.



The same trip by metro requires a change between lines C and A in the city centre and takes around 22 minutes.

Including the time spent walking through stations and using escalators, the journey can take about half an hour.

The first day of operation brought mostly positive results, with many buses arriving on time or even ahead of schedule. The real test will come during regular weekday traffic, when congestion around Prague is heavier.

Where the new bus runs

In the direction from Čimice to Dejvice, line 145 serves:

Sídliště Čimice – Čimice – Libeňská – Řepínská – Podhajská pole – Čimický háj – Písečná – Služská – Kobylisy – Okrouhlická – Vychovatelna – Hradčanská – Vítězné náměstí – Dejvická

The return route follows the same corridor in the opposite direction.

The key feature of line 145 is its use of the Blanka tunnel, allowing buses to avoid the city centre and provide a direct connection between Prague 8 and Prague 6.

The new route is expected to make commuting easier for residents of Čimice, Kobylisy and surrounding neighbourhoods, while providing an alternative to the metro for journeys towards Dejvice and Hradčanská.

World.title: Leo Express to Launch Direct Prague–Brno Trains in December
World.content:
Leo Express is set to begin operating direct trains between Prague and Brno in December, marking the private carrier’s first direct connection between the two cities.

The company has already been serving passengers in the South Moravian Region, but its trains have so far bypassed Brno.

Over the past year, travellers from towns such as Hodonín and Břeclav have been able to use Leo Express services to reach Prague, travelling via Přerov and Olomouc.



The new Prague–Brno service will change that, putting the carrier directly on one of the Czech Republic’s busiest rail routes.

There is, however, one limitation for passengers travelling to Prague.

Leo Express trains do not serve Prague Main Station. In Prague, passengers must use Praha-Libeň station, which may be less convenient for those travelling to the city centre.

Leo Express was founded by businessman Leoš Novotný and has operated passenger trains in the Czech Republic since 2012.

The company has gradually expanded its network in the Czech Republic and abroad, competing with established operators such as České dráhy and RegioJet.

The Prague–Brno connection is expected to become another important part of the company’s Czech network from December.

World.title: Romanian Community to Celebrate Culture and Traditions in Prague
World.content:
The Romanian community in Czechia will come together in Prague on September 6 for the 12th edition of the Romanian Celebration, an annual event highlighting Romanian culture, traditions and the community’s ties with Czech society.

The main event will take place at the Ethnographic Section of the National Museum of the Czech Republic in Kinský Park, Prague 5.

The program will bring together Romanian music, dance, food, literature and activities for children.



Organized by the Association of Romanians in the Czech Republic (ARRC), the event is part of a wider cultural project running from March 1 to November 30, 2026.

Visitors can expect traditional music and dance performances, educational activities for children, cultural exhibitions, book presentations and Romanian gastronomy.

The event is aimed at members of the Romanian community, Romanian-speaking families, children and young people, as well as Czech residents interested in Romanian culture.

According to ARRC, the project aims to preserve and promote Romanian cultural and linguistic identity among Romanians living in the Czech Republic while creating opportunities for greater interaction between the Romanian and Czech communities.

“Through this project, we aim to offer the Romanian community, Romanian speakers, and lovers of the Romanian language a space for meeting, dialogue, and celebration of our cultural values, while also contributing to the consolidation of intercultural relations between Romania and the Czech Republic,” the ARRC leadership said.
