World.title: Czech Fish Farmers Take Emergency Measures Amid Prolonged Drought
World.content:
Fish farmers reduce or suspend supplementary feeding to lower oxygen consumption, reports say.

Fish farmers in the Czech Republic have begun taking emergency measures as a prolonged drought, worsened by high temperatures across Europe, strains water supplies.

Facing water shortages, fish farmers have reduced or suspended supplementary feeding to lower fish oxygen consumption, while ponds are being regularly aerated, according to the report.



Several ponds have also been netted earlier than usual.

In the Třeboň area, which delivers tons of carp for the Czech Christmas table, part of the 200-hectare Koclířov pond has been drained and the fish moved to holding tanks.

More than a third of the water is missing from the region’s famous system of fish ponds due to the drought. The water level in Lake Svět, for example, has fallen by 98 centimetres. High temperatures are also causing water to evaporate more quickly.

The Czech government is expected to address the 2027 budget, upcoming elections and measures to tackle worsening drought.

Prime Minister Andrej Babiš has pledged an extra CZK 4 billion for drought-related measures. If approved, ministers will present plans for implementing them.

World.title: Burgermeister to Open First Prague Restaurant on Wenceslas Square in 2027
World.content:
Berlin burger chain Burgermeister is preparing to enter the Czech market, with its first Prague restaurant expected to open in early 2027.

The company has chosen Wenceslas Square for its debut. The location will also serve as a base for Burgermeister’s planned expansion across the Czech Republic, with more restaurants already in the pipeline.

Burgermeister has built its reputation in Berlin over the past two decades, growing from a single restaurant in a former public toilet into an international chain with 32 locations across Germany and other European markets.



Burgermeister has not yet revealed the exact address or confirmed a specific opening date.

The Prague restaurant will follow the concept that made Burgermeister popular in Berlin. The chain focuses on freshly prepared burgers and fries, with part of its food production handled in-house. Its operations also include its own bakery.

From a former public toilet to an international burger chain

Burgermeister opened its first restaurant in the Kreuzberg district of Berlin in 2006. The location was far from a conventional restaurant site. It occupied a former public toilet beneath the railway tracks near Schlesisches Tor station.

The unusual setting quickly became part of the brand’s identity. Over the years, Burgermeister expanded beyond its original Berlin location and developed into a larger restaurant chain.

Today, the company has 32 branches and is pursuing its goal of building a pan-European network.

World.title: Russell Crowe to Perform in Prague for the First Time in May 2027
World.content:
Oscar-winning actor and musician Russell Crowe will bring his band, The Gentlemen Barbers, to Forum Karlín on May 23, 2027, for their first-ever Prague concert.

Russell Crowe is best known for his roles in Gladiator, A Beautiful Mind and A Good Year, but long before Hollywood, music was a major part of his life.

On May 23, 2027, the Oscar and Golden Globe winner will bring that side of his career to Prague for the first time, performing with his band The Gentlemen Barbers at Forum Karlín.



You can get your ticket here.

The concert will also mark the opening night of the band’s European tour.

The Gentlemen Barbers have been developing their sound over the past four years, although many of the musicians have worked with Crowe for decades. The lineup includes drummer Dave Kelly and trumpeter Stewart Kirwan, both former members of Thirty Odd Foot of Grunts, as well as musicians who have collaborated with Crowe on later projects.

The band also features pianist Stu Hunter, guitarist Chris Kamzelas and bassist James Hazelwood. Irish singer Lorraine O’Reilly, known for her powerful, raspy vocals, has performed with Crowe since they first met while recording a duet for the Bible Code Sundays album Walk Like Kings.

The result is a band that moves between R&B, gospel, country, dark waltzes and singalong anthems, with storytelling at the centre of its music.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by JV Classics (@jvclassics)

“There is an attitude about this band. It’s got a groove. We do a lot of story songs, but we also know we are here to blow out cobwebs and give the audience a good night,” Crowe says.

For Crowe, music has remained a constant alongside his film career. He began performing in bands, touring and releasing records before moving into musical theatre and eventually film. He has continued to perform throughout his decades in Hollywood, despite his demanding acting career.

“I love playing in pubs. It’s what I did growing up. Even though my day job has a huge claim on my time, I’ve never not played music,” he says.

Russell Crowe’s Indoor Garden Party & The Gentlemen Barbers takes place on May 23, 2027, at 8 p.m. at Forum Karlín in Prague.

World.title: How Much Can a Prague Taxi Driver Really Earn Each Month
World.content:
For passengers, a taxi ride can make the job look straightforward. Pick someone up, drive them across Prague, wait for the next booking and repeat.

But the income of a full-time taxi driver depends on far more than the fare shown on the meter or app.

Drivers working through platforms such as Uber and Bolt can generate more than CZK 60,000 in gross monthly revenue when working around 40 to 50 hours a week. What they actually keep, however, is considerably less.



Gross income can exceed CZK 60,000

Official figures for Prague’s taxi sector put the average gross monthly pay at roughly CZK 38,000. Drivers who work full time through ride-hailing platforms can earn more, particularly when they concentrate on periods of high demand.

According to Ondřej Krátký, founder of the Czech taxi platform Liftago, drivers can typically earn about CZK 250 to CZK 350 per hour. At the lower end of the market, however, some drivers make only around CZK 80 an hour, which is difficult to turn into a sustainable income in Prague.

Official statistics may also underestimate the money generated by some drivers because not every journey is paid through an app. Cash payments remain part of the business.

Fuel and commissions take a large share

Most Prague taxi drivers operate as self-employed contractors and use their own cars. That means they are responsible for almost all of the costs associated with the job.

Fuel is one of the largest expenses. Someone driving every day can spend more than CZK 10,000 a month on petrol or diesel alone.

Ride-hailing platforms also take a percentage of each fare. Depending on the service and other conditions, commissions can account for roughly 20 to 25 percent of the fare. Drivers must also cover vehicle maintenance, repairs, commercial insurance and the mandatory social and health insurance payments required of self-employed workers.

Once these expenses are taken into account, the amount left from gross earnings can fall by a third or more.

For a full-time driver, a realistic monthly amount after operating costs can therefore be somewhere between CZK 22,000 and CZK 35,000. The exact figure depends on the car, fuel consumption, working hours, platform commissions and the number and type of trips completed.

Tips make only a small difference

Tips are unlikely to transform a taxi driver’s income in the Czech Republic.

Unlike in countries where tipping is a major part of service workers’ earnings, Czech passengers generally round up the fare or leave a relatively small amount.

Uber allows passengers to tip through its app for up to 30 days after a journey, with the full tip going to the driver. Bolt offers a similar feature.

For most drivers, however, tips remain a minor addition to their monthly income rather than a significant source of earnings.

Timing can make a bigger difference

Drivers can increase their income by choosing when and where they work.

Friday and Saturday nights are among the busiest periods in Prague, particularly in the city centre. When demand rises sharply, ride-hailing platforms can increase fares, allowing drivers to generate more revenue from the same number of working hours.

Major concerts, festivals and other large events can have a similar effect. Airport journeys can also be attractive because they tend to cover longer distances than short trips within the city.

World.title: Czechia Now Ranks Among the World’s 10 Best Countries to Live In
World.content:
Czechia has placed ninth among 192 countries in the 2026 Rumavi Global Relocation Index, which assesses destinations based on factors including safety, healthcare, taxation, living costs and opportunities for people considering a move abroad.

The country scored 69.9 points in the overall ranking, putting it just outside the top five but ahead of Malta and several larger European economies. Estonia took first place with 72.8 points, followed by Singapore, Malaysia, Portugal and Taiwan.

Czechia performed particularly well in the ranking for families, where it placed third worldwide. The index also gave the country strong scores for safety, property rights and climate risk.



Within Europe, Czechia ranked fourth overall. Estonia, Portugal and Lithuania were the only European countries placed higher in the general ranking.

The results are based on the Rumavi Global Relocation Index 2026, a privately produced ranking designed for people considering relocation as well as investors. Rumavi evaluates 192 countries using 24 indicators grouped into four areas: finance and taxes, livability and health, safety and stability, and settling and opportunity.

Czechia scores particularly well for families

The index uses different weightings for different types of people considering a move. For families, safety, education, cost of living and healthcare carry greater weight than tax considerations.

Czechia’s overall result is less impressive for other groups. It ranked 20th among countries assessed for retirees and 25th for digital nomads.

The index also evaluates destinations for entrepreneurs and people primarily interested in tax efficiency, although the rankings can vary significantly depending on the category.

What the index measures

Rumavi says its ranking is intended to measure the practical conditions faced by someone moving to another country rather than simply assessing tourism or passport access.

The 24 indicators cover issues such as affordability, income tax, foreign-income taxation, banking, healthcare, housing, air quality, climate, digital infrastructure, education, business opportunities, language, visa access, property rights and startup ecosystems.

Each indicator is converted to a score between zero and 100, with higher scores representing more favorable conditions for someone relocating. The same data is then weighted differently for six groups: general applicants, retirees, digital nomads, families, entrepreneurs and people seeking tax advantages.

For the general ranking, the most heavily weighted indicators include street safety, foreign-income taxation, cost of living and climate comfort.

Rumavi’s methodology draws on sources including the World Bank, World Health Organization, OECD, World Justice Project, UNODC and other international datasets. Some indicators, including visa access, property rights for non-citizens and aspects of taxation, are classified as Rumavi assessments rather than direct institutional data.

World.title: Polish bus tragedy: expert reveals how and why it happened – and how such crashes can be survived
World.content:
Twelve people died and 47 were injured in the Polish bus tragedy on the M3 motorway near Mezőkeresztes late last Sunday night. The bus, carrying pilgrims from Medjugorje in Bosnia and Herzegovina back to Poland, left the carriageway, plunged into a drainage ditch and overturned. Police preliminarily suspect the driver fell asleep at the wheel. A forensic vehicle expert has now outlined how long the driver may have been unconscious, how the crash unfolded and what might prevent similar tragedies in future.

Polish bus tragedy: how a few seconds proved fatal

Based on evidence at the scene, the driver appears to have lost alertness for only a matter of seconds. Sándor Boncsér, a court-certified automotive engineering expert, told Telex that as little as two to four seconds of micro-sleep could have been enough to cause the catastrophe. At roughly 100km/h, the 24-tonne vehicle would have travelled more than 100 metres in four seconds with no one at the controls. If cruise control was engaged, the speed would barely have dropped before the driver regained consciousness.

Because motorways are cambered slightly to shed rainwater, the bus drifted gradually to the right after the driver nodded off. The Scania’s right-hand wheels left the tarmac, crossed the hard shoulder and mounted the embankment. On the steep slope, traction on the right-side wheels was lost, making it virtually impossible to steer the bus back onto the road.

Polish bus overturns on M3 motorway in tragic accident. Photo: MTI

The absence of a continuous crash barrier on this stretch meant there was nothing to arrest the vehicle’s departure from the carriageway. On the steep embankment, the bus’s centre of gravity shifted laterally, causing it to roll over. The expert added that the roof structure may not have been designed to absorb the mass and kinetic energy involved, contributing to the severity of the crash.

Who stands the best chance of survival?

Seat-belt use significantly affects survival odds. On Tempo 100-rated coaches, motorway regulations require all passengers to wear seat belts, but with 50–60 travellers on board, the driver cannot realistically check who has unbuckled during the journey. Reports that several passengers were thrown from the bus suggest many were not restrained.

Polish bus overturns on M3 motorway in tragic accident. Photo: MTI

How to prevent future tragedies

The most critical factor remains driver alertness. EU rules strictly govern driving and rest periods, although more flexible provisions for tourist-coach drivers have applied since 2024. Technology can also help: modern coaches may be fitted with systems that monitor fatigue, eye movement and steering patterns, alongside lane-departure warnings, active lane-keeping and emergency-brake assist.

Yet technology alone cannot eliminate risk. European Commission data suggest driver fatigue contributes to 15–20 per cent of road accidents. Hungary’s public road authority recorded 716 crashes between early 2020 and March 2026 in which the driver was confirmed to have fallen asleep.

Polish bus overturns on M3 motorway in tragic accident. Photo: MTI

If you missed our previous article concerning the tragedy: ‘People were shouting, trapped beneath the seats’ – exclusive interview, video and latest developments in Polish bus crash

What the driver now faces

The driver’s criminal liability has not yet been determined. Authorities must examine tachograph data, driving and rest periods, speed records and any possible mechanical faults. If convicted of causing a mass-casualty traffic accident resulting in death, he could face two to eight years’ imprisonment, plus fines and a multi-year driving ban. Sentencing will take into account his prior record and whether he breached traffic regulations.

The tragedy’s starkest lesson is that, with a vehicle weighing dozens of tonnes, even a few seconds’ loss of attention can prove fatal. By the time a driver realises the coach has left the road, its motion may already be irreversible.

World.title: Key deal secured for new Danube bridge at Mohács – new photos
World.content:
Construction company Duna Aszfalt has agreed to refund the state HUF 59bn of an advance payment for a bridge it is building across the Danube at Mohács (Southwest Hungary), Transportation and Investment Minister Dávid Vitézy said in a post on Facebook on Monday.

New deal struck concerning the new Danube bridge

Vitézy noted that János Lázár, the head of the transportation portfolio under the former Fidesz-KDNP government, had decided to raise the advance payment rate for the project from 20pc to 98pc just two days ahead of the election in April.

Vitézy said the government was also seeking to recover HUF 76bn in additional costs related to a decision taken by Lázár to build a 20km expressway connecting to the bridge, even though traffic volume was not expected to require the link for 25 years or more.

Public interest in the last place

He called the bridge project a “typical NER story“, using a Hungarian acronym referring to companies that benefitted from big state contracts under the Fidesz-KDNP government: “All other interests superseded those of the public”.

He added that the government would not shelve the bridge project as it could not be reversed. In a separate statement on Monday, Duna Aszfalt confirmed it would refund the advance payment and said future payments for the project would take place on a monthly basis, linked to milestones.

World.title: Orbán-era business ‘mothership’ 4iG under scrutiny as PM Magyar speaks of graft and overpricing – updated
World.content:
The Government has ordered a comprehensive review of 4iG’s contracts with the state, Prime Minister Péter Magyar said in a Facebook post on Monday. Unusual in Hungary for combining telecommunications, IT, digital infrastructure, space and defence under a single corporate umbrella, 4iG has expanded internationally while its space and defence activities have become a major strategic pillar, making it one of the country’s most diversified technology groups.

‘Harsh scrutiny’ over taxpayers’ billions

Mr Magyar said four ministries would take part in the probe of 4iG, which he described as the “mothership” of “NER” companies – a Hungarian acronym for businesses that benefited from large state contracts under the former Fidesz-KDNP administration. He said 4iG had won state IT contracts “in the billions” during the 2010s before “switching into a much higher gear” from 2022, citing the issue of HUF 389 billion in bonds under a National Bank of Hungary (NBH) programme and a capital raise of more than HUF 400 billion at Antenna Hungária, after which 4iG acquired a majority stake in the telecoms operator.

Former Economy Minister Márton Nagy in the centre and Gellért Jászai, the head of the 4iG, in the right. Photo: FB/4iG

In 2023, Mr Magyar added, Antenna Hungária and the Hungarian state acquired Vodafone Magyarország in a deal worth HUF 660 billion, with the state-owned Hungarian Development Bank (MFB) providing financing for 4iG’s stake. He also noted 4iG’s acquisition of the state’s majority stake in automotive group Rába and the subsequent transfer of a stake in the business to a foreign company.

Mr Magyar added that 4iG had been the general contractor for an “overpriced” programme to supply elderly people with remote medical alert bracelets. “We are talking about several thousand billion forints of taxpayers’ money. The Hungarian people have a right to know what happened to their money,” he said, adding that the results of the probe would be published.

If the review raises any suspicion of graft, Mr Magyar said reports would be filed with the relevant authorities. He warned against any efforts to strip assets from the group.

The 4iG story: from telecoms to state-backed conglomerate

The rise of 4iG is not merely the tale of a fast-growing IT firm: within a few years, through a deliberate acquisition strategy, substantial financing and close ties to the state, it has built a conglomerate spanning telecommunications, defence and space.

The central figure in this process has been Gellért Jászai, who as chairman and chief executive – and a defining shareholder – has steered the group’s expansion. After 2020, 4iG moved quickly to consolidate Hungary’s telecoms market, acquiring DIGI, Invitech and a controlling stake in Antenna Hungária, before culminating in the 2023 purchase of Vodafone Hungary in partnership with the state. The Vodafone deal, valued at HUF 660 billion, was underpinned by significant public financing: the 4iG group secured €425 million from the state-owned MFB and a further €750 million via Eximbank, which also acted as an intermediary in the structure.

State involvement did not end with telecoms. In 2025, 4iG and the Hungarian Government agreed to establish a joint defence-industry holding, under which 4iG could acquire a 75 per cent majority stake. That same year, a HUF 50 billion state-funded facility supported the group’s push into military technology. By 2025, the model was delivering substantial results: 4iG reported revenue of HUF 733.9 billion, EBITDA of HUF 275 billion and adjusted profit after tax of HUF 36 billion.

Defence and space: the new frontier

Having consolidated its domestic position, 4iG’s ambitions have turned decisively international. In the United States, the group’s defence and space arm, 4iG Space and Defence Technologies (4iG SDT), completed a $100 million investment in Axiom Space by early 2026, becoming a strategic shareholder in the Houston-based developer of commercial space stations and orbital infrastructure. The investment is intended to give 4iG a foothold in the development of orbital data centres, commercial space stations and other space-industry assets.

If you missed: Why Hungary’s cheapest shop may have closed – and shoppers are already furious

In Israel, 4iG has worked with the state-owned defence giant Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI) on the restructuring of satellite operator SpaceCom. Under a joint proposal, IAI would take an 80 per cent controlling stake, with 4iG retaining 20 per cent and providing part of a $12 million subordinated shareholder loan. Through these partnerships, 4iG aims to market defence and space technologies internationally, leveraging its Hungarian base and state connections.

A regional player with global aspirations

In little more than half a decade, 4iG has transformed from a domestic IT and telecoms operator into a regional, and increasingly global, technology, defence and space group. The Hungarian consolidation phase is largely complete; the next chapter is defined by cross-border investments, strategic shareholdings in US and Israeli space firms, and an explicit goal of becoming a significant international player in high-tech defence and orbital infrastructure.

Update: 4iG to cooperate with govt on contracts probe

4iG will cooperate with the government on a probe of contracts it signed earlier with the state, the group said on Tuesday. “We are convinced that our cooperation with the state of Hungary is undertaken in a framework that complies with regulations and is fair and advantageous for Hungarians,” 4iG said in a statement. “To protect the interests of our shareholders, we believe that a fact-based probe, conducted in a professional manner, is indispensable. In the course of that probe, we will provide all necessary documents and information at our disposal to allow an objective assessment of the facts,” it added.

The price of 4iG shares fell 14.52pc to HUF 1,590 on Monday. The shares traded at HUF 1,570 around 10:00 in the morning on Tuesday, down 1.26pc.

World.title: Hungary’s finest cave bath reopens on national holiday – what to expect on prices, programs
World.content:
Miskolctapolca’s Cave Bath, one of Hungary’s most striking thermal attractions, is set to reopen its doors on August 20, marking the end of a nearly two-year closure following a devastating fire. The city is pulling out all the stops for the occasion, with a packed programme of events planned across Miskolc for the long holiday weekend.

A troubled return

The bath suffered severe fire damage on September 6, 2024, when flames broke out in the aqua therapy section before spreading to other parts of the complex. While the outdoor pools escaped relatively lightly and were brought back into use the following summer, the cave section itself required extensive reconstruction, with work beginning in late 2025. From August 20, visitors will once again be able to bathe in the thermal pools hewn into the natural cave passages, though the medical and therapeutic facilities will remain closed for the time being.

Heartbreaking images after the 2024 fire:

Admission prices at the restored cave bath

An all-day adult ticket to the cave bath will cost 8,500 forints, with reduced rates of 6,400 forints for children, students and pensioners. Miskolc residents benefit from further discounts: 5,100 forints for adults and 3,800 forints for children, students and pensioners.

Three-hour tickets are also available: 6,000 forints for adults and 4,500 forints for concessionary categories, or 2,400 and 1,800 forints respectively for locals.

The outdoor Shell Beach. Photo: Miskolctapolca Cave Bath and Aquatherapy

Family tickets for a full day are priced at 18,700 forints for two adults and one child, and 11,900 forints for one adult and one child; each additional child costs 5,100 forints. The three-hour family rates are 14,000 and 8,900 forints, with extra children at 3,800 forints.

Group tickets (from 15 people) are offered at 7,300 forints for adults and 5,500 forints for children, students and pensioners. Disabled visitors pay a reduced rate of 3,800 forints, according to Pénzcentrum.

If you missed: Hungarian Wizz Air opens new base in another European city!

A city-wide celebration

The reopening will be accompanied by a four-day festival, “Pezsgés Miskolctapolcán” (Fizzing in Miskolctapolca), running from August 20 to 23, with concerts, food events and community activities.

Elsewhere in the city, the airport will host “Legends in the Air” from August 20 to 22, featuring air displays, rare aircraft and family entertainment, including a presentation by aerobatic pilot Péter Bessenyei.

In the city centre, the “Tündöklő” (Radiant) Light Festival on August 20 and 21 will project installations and films onto public buildings and spaces.On August 20, Miskolc Zoo will mark its 43rd anniversary with a day of birthday events, while on the evening of August 22 the Night Run Miskolc will set off from Szent István Square, with 5km, 10km and 21km routes.

World.title: Personal documentary is being made about former PM Viktor Orbán – here’s its main focus
World.content:
A “personal documentary” directed by Réka Pigniczky is being made in Hungarian-Canadian co-production about former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán’s political “transformation and downfall”, with the premiere scheduled for the first half of 2027, the Hungarian film portal Filmhu has reported.

The documentary project titled Orbán and Me was presented on Sunday at the Cinelink Industry Days professional forum at the Sarajevo Film Festival, the website said. Pigniczky’s project was selected, alongside six other films in production, for the professional forum dubbed “Docu Talents From the East”, organised by the Jihlava International Documentary Film Festival in Czechia. On Monday, the jury will award a prize to the most promising project, MTI wrote.

According to the Jihlava Festival’s website, Orbán and Me is “an intimate political documentary” in which Pigniczky — who had previously interviewed Orban — attempted to speak again with the then Prime Minister during the 2026 Hungarian parliamentary elections.

The filmmaker “seeks to understand his transformation from democratic reformer to increasingly inaccessible leader”. Through the attempt to interview Orbán, and the debates within the director’s own family, “the film explores democracy’s fragility, political polarisation, and whether democratic renewal remains possible in Hungary today,” the Jihlava Festival website said.

World.title: How to see a doctor without insurance in Budapest: a tourist’s guide
World.content:
You wake up in your Budapest hotel feeling much worse than you did yesterday. Perhaps you’ve developed a high fever overnight, food poisoning has ruined your sightseeing plans, or you’ve injured yourself exploring the city. As you reach for your phone to find a doctor, you realize something that makes the situation even more stressful. You forgot to buy travel insurance.

Written by: Dorottya Fekete

Collaborative content

If you need to see a doctor without insurance in Budapest, you can still receive medical care at a private clinic, although you will normally pay directly for your treatment.

Remember, your health is important, and resources are available to help you get care even if you’re uninsured. Knowing your options in advance can make it easier to navigate the healthcare system and decide where to seek appropriate care.

Where Can Tourists See a Doctor Without Insurance in Budapest?

Rest assured, there are several ways to see a doctor without insurance in Budapest. Healthcare services are accessible to tourists in Budapest, whether for vacation or business. Waiting times and English-language support can vary between public healthcare facilities, so it’s useful to check what services are available to international visitors before attending.

Private clinics such as FirstMed offer outpatient medical care for international visitors, including English-language communication with doctors and reception staff. Appointments are available during regular opening hours, subject to availability. You’ll understand the recommended care and its rationale, and you’ll receive medical documents in English, which can be useful for follow-up after returning home.

EHIC and GHIC: Do They Replace Private Insurance?

Many travelers wonder whether the European Health Insurance Card (EHIC) or, for UK travelers, the Global Health Insurance Card (GHIC) offers similar access to medical care as travel insurance. But this is not the case. The EHIC/GHIC covers only medically necessary care at public/statutory facilities during a temporary stay and isn’t valid at private clinics. You can also access private medical care smoothly, but you’ll need to pay for the services out of pocket.

Difference between travel insurance and EHIC/GHIC:

EHIC/GHIC:

Provides access to the public healthcare system for medically necessary issues;

Excludes cancellation or travel back to your home country;

Doesn’t cover the costs of private treatment.

Travel Insurance: depending on the terms and conditions of the specific policy, it may

Cover eligible private medical treatment.

Reimburse eligible private healthcare costs;

Include cancellations and return travel/transportation.

Private Healthcare Cost for Tourists in Budapest

Concerns regarding unpredictable out-of-pocket expenses often make travelers hesitant to see a doctor without insurance in Budapest.

Many common health concerns can initially be assessed during a doctor’s consultation. Depending on the diagnosis, the doctor may recommend treatment, prescribe medication, or arrange further testing or follow-up.

To ensure you stay on budget, it is advisable to inquire about payment terms in advance. Ask about consultation fees, additional tests or procedures, and any documentation charges before treatment if you need to understand the expected cost.

Even if you are currently uninsured, keep your invoices and medical records in case you later need them for your records or for an insurance claim. However, any reimbursement will depend on the terms of your insurance policy.

What does a private doctor visit typically include for a tourist?

FirstMed provides outpatient medical care in English for international visitors, including consultations with English-speaking doctors. The clinic provides English-language communication with doctors and reception staff, helping international visitors understand their care. Open every day excluding holidays, the clinic may be able to offer same-day appointments for urgent, non-life-threatening health concerns, depending on availability.

Tourist looking to see a doctor without insurance in Budapest, in front of Hattyúház, building of FirstMed, English-speaking clinic.Source: FirstMed

Depending on your symptoms and the doctor’s assessment, your FirstMed appointment may include:

A consultation with an English-speaking doctor

Discussion of your symptoms and medical history

A physical examination

Recommendation for treatment and further care

Prescriptions for medications available in Hungary

Referral for hospital care if your condition requires emergency or complex treatment.

Additional diagnostic testing or specialist consultations may be recommended and obtained in-house depending on your symptoms and the doctor’s assessment.

What should you bring to your appointment?

Bring your passport or other photo ID, a payment card or cash in local currency (such as HUF), a list of regular medications, details about allergies or chronic health conditions, your EHIC or GHIC if available (for administrative purposes, as it is not accepted for payment), and any available medical documents related to your current illness or injury.

If English isn’t your first language, it can also help to keep a note of your symptoms on your phone, including when they started, any medications you’ve taken, and whether they’ve been improving or worsening.

If you’re feeling unwell, it’s easy to forget important details. Gathering these key items in advance can help your appointment run more smoothly.

Conclusion

Without insurance, medical care in Hungary is available but must be paid for. EHIC/GHIC can provide access to medically necessary healthcare within the public healthcare system, but it does not cover private medical care. For international visitors considering private treatment, English-language communication and appointment availability may be important factors.

At an international private clinic in Budapest like FirstMed, tourists can arrange care without insurance and be seen in English. That lets you focus on recovery rather than paperwork.

Before booking, check the clinic’s current consultation fees for English-language services and ask whether additional tests or procedures may involve extra charges.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) About Seeing a Doctor Without Insurance

How can I find a doctor in Budapest without insurance? You can find a doctor without insurance at both public and private clinics in Budapest. Private international clinics, such as FirstMed, may be an option for visitors who specifically want English-language communication and appointment-based care. Public hospitals might have long wait times for non-emergency cases, and there’s no assurance you’ll find an English-speaking doctor. Do private clinics accept EHIC in Hungary? Unfortunately, EHIC or GHIC cannot be used to pay for treatment at private clinics. EHIC/GHIC cards are intended for access to medically necessary healthcare within the applicable public/statutory healthcare system and are not a form of private health insurance.

If you choose a private clinic for appointment-based care and English-language communication, you will need to pay directly for the medical services you receive. How much does it cost to see a doctor without insurance in Budapest? In Budapest, the costs of seeing a doctor without insurance depend on whether you choose a private clinic or the public system. EHIC/GHIC holders can access medically necessary treatment in the public healthcare network, though some fees or services may apply. Tourists who are not eligible for EHIC/GHIC coverage, or who prefer to use private healthcare, can contact a private clinic to ask about consultation fees and available appointment options. Is an urgent care doctor available without insurance? Private clinics may offer appointments for urgent, non-emergency health concerns, depending on availability. Calling the clinic at least one hour before your arrival allows the staff to prepare for your specific symptoms, secure your slot, and minimize your wait, helping you get back to your travels sooner. Shall I book an appointment, or can I walk in? Some private clinics can see you the same day, but it is highly recommended to schedule an appointment rather than walk in. Calling a clinic even one hour before you arrive allows the staff to prepare for your specific symptoms, reserve a time slot, and minimize your wait. You can also double-check the expected treatment costs.

Need to see a doctor in Budapest?

FirstMed provides English-language outpatient medical care for international visitors, with appointments available during regular opening hours.

Book an appointment with a FirstMed doctor.

World.title: Could the August 20 fireworks be cancelled? Looming peril threatens Budapest
World.content:
As the August 20 fireworks approach, forecast uncertainty invariably rises, for late summer brings a confluence of atmospheric influences to the Carpathian Basin. This volatility, coupled with the sudden onset of violent showers and thunderstorms, could place the national day celebrations in jeopardy. There is precedent: a few years ago the display was called off over fears of an approaching storm, while in 2006 an inhuman gale that broke during the fireworks themselves left five dead and hundreds injured.

Forecasting August 20 remains notoriously difficult

The Carpathian Basin’s hitherto monotonous summer weather is now shifting. This morning, a continuous cloud layer obscured the sun over Budapest, and a brief shower drenched the capital and its environs in the small hours. For weeks there had been no rain to speak of, nor even cloudy skies; a scorching heatwave had baked Hungary and the surrounding region.

Storms after heatwave. Photo: Anadolu/Németi Róbert

A significant atmospheric reorganisation is under way, yet the heat is not retreating – and that combination may render the national holiday genuinely hazardous. Cool, 12–22°C dawns will be followed by daytime highs of 30–35°C, conditions that readily spawn violent showers and thunderstorms. The meteorological service has therefore issued lemon-yellow warnings for several counties, as reported by Blikk. Precisely what to expect on Thursday remains exceptionally difficult to predict.

On multiple occasions, forecasters have only been able to confirm at the last moment that no major storm would materialise; conversely, events have been cancelled on the basis of such warnings.

Ominous precedents

In 2022, for example, forecasts indicated a serious storm threatening the capital. When the prediction ultimately proved erroneous, the Government dismissed the then president and deputy president of the National Meteorological Service. The fireworks were held a week later, on August 27.On August 20, 2006, however, the display was not called off in time. A storm arriving with winds of 120 km/h struck the celebrating capital. Five people died and more than 300 were injured; the Orbán government in 2022 was determined to avoid any repeat of that catastrophe.

Photo: Facebook/Magyarország Kormánya

If you missed: ‘People were shouting, trapped beneath the seats’ – exclusive interview, video and latest developments in Polish bus crash

A radical shift in Hungary’s weather

At present, meteorologists are expecting partly cloudy, sunny conditions on August 20, but showers and thunderstorms could break out almost anywhere owing to the persistent heat and elevated mean temperatures.

According to an analysis by The Weather on Maps, the heatwave-inducing air mass is drifting eastwards and weakening, while a cool oceanic–Arctic air mass is advancing; their frontal boundary will undulate over our region, definitively ending the recent weather monotony. This, however, introduces another uncertainty factor for the fireworks. It is also the change that may bring more substantial rainfall to the upper catchment of the Danube and thus assist Paks.

Ongoing heroic work near the Paks NPP to raise the water level of the drying Danube and provide enough cooling water for the plant. Photo: Facebook/Péter Magyar

On the national holiday, therefore, everyone would do well to keep abreast of the expected weather – and then no one should be caught unawares.

World.title: PM Magyar’s stern message to richest Hungarian Lőrinc Mészáros over scheme to aid very poor, but high-achieving students
World.content:
Prime Minister Péter Magyar called on MBH Bank and Lőrinc Mészáros, who has ties to business interests with stakes in the lender, to reinstate a charity programme benefitting children from low-income households with good grades in a post on Facebook on Monday.

New HQ of Lőrinc Mészáros’s bank too expensive?

Magyar said that the International Children’s Safety Service had announced that MBH Bank had pulled support for the programme, after 32 years, while moving forward with the construction of a new corporate headquarters, “in an untransparent manner”, at a cost of more than HUF 100bn.

Lőrinc Mészáros and former FM Péter Szijjártó. The latter is now a top executive of the Chinese BYD. Photo: FB/Szijjártó

In the name of the state of Hungary, which is also a stakeholder in MBH Bank, Magyar called on Mészáros and MBH Bank to publish the details of the new HQ, including the plans and the name of the general contractor, MTI wrote.

MBH Bank, Hungary’s second-largest commercial lender, is listed on the Budapest Stock Exchange. A little more than 25pc of the bank’s shares are in free float.

Péter Magyar wrote in a Facebook post that Mészáros’s bank had helped 100 low‑income, high‑achieving students under a programme it now plans to cancel.

Hungary’s richest reshaped by the Orbán era: Mészáros wealth surges by 284,400% in 15 years!

The bank responded

The scholarship was open to outstanding students from families whose per‑capita monthly income was below HUF 55,000 (about €151). Recipients received HUF 800,000 a year (roughly €2,200), equivalent to around €183 per month.The bank’s full‑year profit for 2025 stood at HUF 240 billion (€661 million).

In response to a statement by the International Children’s Safety Service, the bank said it was “baffled” that the organisation had taken the matter to the press. MBH Bank stated that its decision to withdraw from the programme had been made last year and that the organisation had been given a year to prepare for the consequences. The bank did not respond directly to Péter Magyar’s remarks, but added that it had spent “tens of millions of forints” on the scheme in recent years.

World.title: Romania’s drone production capacities to rapidly increase in coming years, minister says
World.content:
Romania’s drone production capacity will increase rapidly in the coming years thanks to private companies and public initiatives, said interim economy minister Irineu Darău on Monday, August 17, in an interview with Euronews Romania.

The increase will be noticeable beginning with 2027, the minister said, thanks to the funds made available through the SAFE Act. Local drone production may also benefit from partnerships with Ukrainian companies.

“There are private companies that are starting to innovate a lot in this field and already have foreign partners. I am convinced that all these joint efforts, private and public, will have an effect without a delay,” the official said.

Darău noted that Romania has recently shot down drones that illegally crossed its airspace. While this has been done by military airplanes, the country will soon benefit from a drone-based defense industry.

“We have entered an accelerated phase of innovation, and I am confident that very soon we will have a defense industry also based on drones that will help us. Firmly within the horizon of 2027, our domestic production capacities will increase rapidly,” Irineu Darău said.

Drones have come to dominate the battlefield in Ukraine and have even been used by Iran in its asymmetric conflict with the United States and Israel. Russia and Ukraine have both relied on drones for close- but also long-range strikes on each other.

The number of drone attacks recorded on Ukrainian territory, near the border with Romania, has exceeded 110 since the beginning of the war. In 39 cases, Russian drones were reported to have entered Romanian airspace, including the drone shot down on August 16 in Galați County, according to a Ministry of National Defense statistic consulted by News.ro.

Since the beginning of this year, authorities have recorded 54 instances of attacks near Romania’s border. In 42 of these cases, aircraft from the Air Policing Combat Service were scrambled to monitor and verify the air situation. In approximately 50 cases, drones or drone fragments were identified on Romanian territory.

The incidents took place against the backdrop of an unprecedented intensification, during that period, of drone attacks carried out by Russia against targets in southern Ukraine. The main targets were Ukrainian Danube ports, located near the Romanian border and the Danube Delta.

The attacks also involved swarm launches, which explains the large number of drones detected by Romanian radars near national airspace. Some aircraft were intercepted by Ukrainian air defenses, and their fragments reached Romania or the waters of the Black Sea.

(Photo source: Irineu Darău on Facebook)

World.title: Romania’s Enescu Competition introduces play & conduct format for 2026 semifinals
World.content:
Semifinalists in the cello, violin, and piano sections of the 2026 George Enescu International Competition will perform as both soloists and orchestra leaders in a new “play & conduct” format. Introduced for the first time in the competition’s history, the conductor-free semifinals will take place at the Romanian Athenaeum in Bucharest in September.

The cello semifinal is scheduled for September 5, followed by the violin competition on September 11 and the piano event on September 17. Six contestants from each instrumental section will advance to this stage.

Each semifinal will be divided into two parts. First, at 10 a.m., the contestants will perform works by Romanian composer George Enescu, with free public admission.

Then, the play & conduct round will begin at 4 p.m. and require a ticket. During this stage, each contestant will perform as a soloist with the Radio Chamber Orchestra while simultaneously providing the ensemble’s artistic direction without a conductor.

The musicians will have to communicate their interpretation to the orchestra through gestures, eye contact, breathing, and movement while performing their own parts, the organizers said. They will be assessed on their solo performance, musical communication, and ability to lead the ensemble toward a coherent interpretation.

Cello semifinalists will perform Enescu’s Cello Sonata No. 2 in C Major, Op. 26 during the first part of the competition. For the play & conduct round, they will choose one of Joseph Haydn’s two cello concertos.

The violin contestants will perform either Enescu’s Violin Sonata No. 2 in F Minor, Op. 6 or Violin Sonata No. 3 in A Minor, Op. 25, “in Romanian folk character.” They will then perform and lead the orchestra in one of Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart’s Violin Concertos Nos. 3, 4 or 5.

Piano semifinalists will select one of three works by Enescu: Suite No. 2 in D Major, Op. 10, Piano Sonata No. 1 in F-sharp Minor, Op. 24 or Piano Sonata No. 3 in D Major, Op. 24. Their play & conduct repertoire will consist of Mozart’s Piano Concertos Nos. 20, 21 or 23.

The Radio Chamber Orchestra will perform with guest concertmasters Adrian Iliescu for the cello semifinal, Deborah Nemțanu for the violin event, and Sebastian Câșleanu for the piano section.

Up to 50 contestants can be admitted to the first stage of each instrumental section. Twelve will advance to the second round, six to the semifinals, and three to the final.

Tickets for the afternoon sessions are available through Eventim and at Cărturești and Humanitas bookstores. Students, pupils, and teachers from music schools and universities can attend free of charge with valid identification, subject to availability. People with disabilities and their companions are also eligible for free admission, subject to available seats.

The complete program of the 2026 George Enescu International Competition is available on the competition’s official website.

World.title: Famous hacker caught with false plates in Romania’s mountain resort of Sinaia
World.content:
A famous Romanian hacker nicknamed Virus was caught in traffic in Sinaia, Prahova County, over the weekend despite the fact that his car was equipped with an ingenious system for changing license plates.

The 42-year-old man was pulled over following an alert generated by the automatic license plate recognition system installed on a police vehicle. At first, he presented fake identity documents, apparently issued by Italy, while the license plates appeared to belong to the diplomatic corps, according to Euronews Romania.

During checks, police found that the car was equipped with two sets of license plates, both the fake ones observed in traffic and some real ones, plus a rotating system that allowed them to be changed quickly. In addition, the individual had a suspended driving license.

He was detained, and investigations showed that he was a famous hacker. The man had run a service that allowed cybercriminals to distribute dangerous viruses, which infected more than one million computers around the world, including those belonging to NASA.

The hackers stole passwords and personal data from several people in different countries, accessed their bank accounts and transferred their money. After being pursued for many years and eventually arrested in Colombia, the Romanian was extradited to the US and sentenced in 2023 to three years in prison. The US authorities confiscated USD 3.5 million from him.

The man, whose real name is Ionuț Mihai Păunescu, had served the sentence handed down by US judges in Romania, so he was no longer wanted by the authorities, but he preferred to drive around with two sets of license plates.

“Police officers from the Sinaia Resort Police Station ordered the 24-hour detention of a 42-year-old man from the municipality of Bucharest, who is being investigated for the offenses of driving a vehicle on public roads by a person whose right to drive has been suspended, identity fraud, and putting into circulation or driving on public roads a vehicle with a false registration number,” said Alexandru Niță, spokesperson for the Prahova County Police Inspectorate.

A judge, however, changed the measure to 30-day house arrest.

World.title: Romanian endurance swimmer Avram Iancu swims across English Channel in breaststroke style
World.content:
Avram Iancu, a Romanian librarian turned endurance swimmer, famous for his feats, managed to swim across the English Channel on Monday, August 17, using the breaststroke style. After the crossing, he said he had faced an “absolutely exhausting” challenge, describing it as the toughest swimming experience of his entire career.

“My strength is not my merit, but a gift from God, for which I thank Him! By far, this was the hardest and most difficult swim of my entire career. I am simply collapsed,” Iancu said after the crossing, which lasted 24 hours and 46 minutes.

The swimmer from Petroșani pointed out that this was his third time across the Channel, following his successful crossings in 2016 and 2024, using the crawl stroke. This year's crossing, however, was especially difficult.

“I went through absolutely every state: almost unbearable physical pain and psychological torment that I don’t even want to talk about anymore. This breaststroke style is very, very difficult,” Avram Iancu told Agerpres.

The multisport athlete from Petroșani is the tenth man to swim across the English Channel using the breaststroke. The last crossing was registered 11 years ago. Through this swim, which took place without a wetsuit, librarian Avram Iancu also aimed to mark his 50th birthday.

The athlete’s record includes swimming the length of the Danube in 2017, covering a distance of 2,860 kilometers, from its source to its mouth into the Black Sea.

In July 2022, Iancu became the first Romanian to swim across the Bristol Channel, in Great Britain. A year later, he swam the length of the Rhine River, and in August 2025, the Main Canal in Germany, between the Rhine and Danube rivers. He also swam across Israel’s Sea of Galilee.

World.title: New program offers professional certification to traditional craftspeople in Romania’s Făgăraș Mountains
World.content:
Traditional craftspeople from communities around Romania’s Făgăraș Mountains can obtain nationally recognized professional certification through a new program launched by the Conservation Carpathia Foundation and Sibiu’s ASTRA Museum. Applications for the MeșterEȘTI pentru comunitate program are open until October 31, 2026.

The initiative targets people who have learned and practiced traditional trades through experience but do not hold formal qualifications. Eligible occupations include artisanal carpentry, making handcrafted wooden objects, and traditional construction using logs, adobe, or stone.

The program is open to craftspeople from selected communities in Argeș, Brașov, and Sibiu counties. Applicants must have completed at least eight years of school, already practice the trade for which they are seeking certification, and be able to demonstrate their skills.

The initiative is not a training course for beginners, the organizers said. Participants will undergo a written theoretical examination and a practical assessment, with evaluations starting on September 1.

Those who pass will receive a nationally recognized certificate attesting to the professional skills they acquired outside formal education. The qualification could allow them to access new employment opportunities, including work on restoration and local cultural heritage preservation projects.

“Through this program, we want to contribute to recognizing the work of craftspeople while preserving knowledge and techniques that form part of these communities’ identity,” said Istvan Szabo, community relations director at the Conservation Carpathia Foundation.

“The cultural landscape at the foot of the Făgăraș Mountains can only be preserved if there continue to be people who know how to work with local materials, understand traditional techniques, continue practicing them and can teach them to others,” he added.

The Conservation Carpathia Foundation will offer selected participants grants of between RON 500 and RON 1,300 to cover part of the certification costs. The full cost varies between RON 750 and RON 1,850, depending on the occupation.

Participants will also receive guidance, documentation and preparation materials from ASTRA Museum specialists until November 30.

“By certifying the skills of these custodians of living heritage, we are not only providing official recognition for valuable trades but also helping ensure that they remain a reference point for future generations,” said ASTRA Museum manager Ciprian Ștefan.

ASTRA Museum has been authorized since 2024 as a center for evaluating and certifying skills acquired outside formal education. It has certified more than 90 craftspeople to date, according to the announcement.

After the certification process, the foundation and museum plan to hold an event featuring practical demonstrations and presentations of the participating craftspeople’s work.

World.title: Third of Romanian children asked parents to remove content about them, survey says
World.content:
Nearly one in three Romanian children aged 9 to 16 has asked their parents to remove content posted about them online, according to EU Kids Online data highlighted in 2026 by Horizon Magazine, the European Commission’s research and innovation publication.

Romania recorded the highest percentage in the comparison, at 29%, while Lithuania ranked at the opposite end, with only 3% of children reporting that they had asked their parents to remove such content.

In most of the countries surveyed, up to one-third of children said their parents had posted something about them without first asking for their permission.

These findings offer a different perspective on digital safety. Research suggests that a child’s first breach of digital privacy may occur within the family itself, when parents begin shaping their child’s online identity before the child is able to decide what they want to make public.

The scale of the phenomenon is further highlighted by a 2026 study involving 470 parents who share content about their children online. On average, more than seven of their 20 most recent posts featured at least one of their children.

For adults, photos and videos can be a way to preserve memories, share important moments, or stay connected with family and friends. For children, however, the same post can mean losing control over their own image, having a private moment exposed, or acquiring a digital identity they did not choose.

As such, sharing content featuring children was associated both with a greater sense of closeness reported by parents and with increased parent–child conflict, particularly when children appeared in content posted on TikTok or YouTube.

Isabelle Filliozat, one of Europe’s leading authorities on positive parenting, emotional development and trauma-informed approaches, highlighted respect for children, attention to their needs and recognition of the boundaries they express in relation to the findings.

According to her, parents should not treat their child’s image as content they alone have the right to control. Asking for permission before posting, explaining where the photo will appear, respecting the child’s refusal, and removing the content if the child no longer feels comfortable are all ways for adults to show that the child’s voice and boundaries matter.

In this context, digital consent becomes a tangible expression of respect within the parent–child relationship, as well as one of the first lessons through which children learn that they have the right to protect their image and privacy.

Isabelle Filliozat will make her first appearance in Romania at ParentED Fest, taking place on October 17-18, 2026, at the Aula Magna of the National University of Science and Technology POLITEHNICA Bucharest. Her talk will explore parent–child relationships, emotional development and the challenges facing families in an increasingly digital world.

World.title: Electricity supply of Bucharest subway operator under question due to amassed debts
World.content:
The company operating the Bucharest subway system, Metrorex, has outstanding electricity payments of over RON 11.5 million (EUR 2.2 million) to state-owned energy provider Hidroelectrica and was sent a disconnection notice, according to information published by Club Feroviar.The sum owed represents the value of the electricity supplied to Metrorex, as well as other obligations related to invoices and installments under rescheduled payment arrangements.

The debt reportedly features in a letter sent by interim transport minister Radu Miruță to Metrorex general manager Mariana Miclăuș. According to the document cited by Club Feroviar, Hidroelectrica issued the disconnection notice on August 9, 2026. The letter was sent for information to the Ministry of Transport and Infrastructure and was registered by the institution on August 13. In the same document, the transport minister asked Metrorex management to explain why the invoices were not paid on time and to present the exact situation regarding the debts.

In a Facebook post, Radu Miruță confirmed that Metrorex had not paid its electricity bills for three months. However, the minister said that the supply is not expected to be interrupted, at least at the current stage of negotiations.

“Metrorex consumes EUR 1 million worth of electricity per month and has to pay for it. It has not paid it for three months and has received a notification. I spoke both last week and this evening with the director of Hidroelectrica. We are not in a situation where Metrorex will be disconnected, but an attempt is being made to negotiate a payment rescheduling,” Radu Miruță wrote on Facebook.

In reply, the subway company explained that the debts were mainly caused by the undercompensation of the public service and unpaid amounts owed by the state. In response to the statements made by the transport minister, the company’s management said that the cumulative undercompensation for the period 2018-2025 was estimated at RON 1.16 billion.

Metrorex also said that it currently has payment obligations of RON 419.94 million, of which RON 365.26 million were overdue. The largest debt, roughly RON 350 million, is owed to Alstom Transport, for subway train maintenance.

The situation is complicated by the company’s losses for 2025. Moreover, Metrorex estimated a loss of RON 431.29 million lei for 2026, 38.21% higher than the loss recorded in 2025.

Alongside the debt issue, the transport minister announced the expansion of the Control Body’s mission at Metrorex. “Meanwhile, we have expanded the mission of the Control Body at Metrorex, because the money there is not being used most efficiently,” the minister said.

Back in June, Miruță canceled the order allowing for the increase in the ticket price from RON 5 to RON 7. Instead, he announced checks at the state-owned company and claimed that it was poorly managed.

World.title: Czech Human Rights Agenda Faces Conservative Pushback Under Babis Government
World.content:
Coordination under threat

The human rights agenda is inherently cross-sectoral. Human rights issues arise in healthcare, education, social affairs, criminal procedure and similar areas. If it were transferred to a single ministry, it would lose its inter-ministerial authority, as well as the ability to provide input on government-level work. At the same time, this area is subject to a number of international agreements and state commitments.

“Through the Office of the Government, we had the opportunity to amplify the voices of vulnerable groups, promote dialogue and encourage their participation in public policy-making,” says former commissioner Simackova Laurencikova. “We served as a forum for dialogue among civil society, non-governmental organizations, academia and government agencies, so that these people could genuinely meet, listen to one another and work together effectively. Not just alongside one another, but together.”

In Simackova Laurencikova’s view, this society-wide coordination has been the main reason for the significant progress made on the issue of domestic and sexual violence in recent years. “We succeeded in drafting and enacting a redefinition of rape and in drafting a new, comprehensive law on domestic violence, which, for the first time ever, establishes a uniform definition of what constitutes domestic violence,” she says.

According to Simackova Laurencikova, if officials find themselves in a subordinate position within a ministry, their bargaining power will be significantly curbed. “Let’s say you’re drafting an action plan pointing out that social service facilities are failing to adequately address the protection of the human rights of clients with intellectual disabilities. If the parent ministry then tells you, ‘No, we think the system is set up properly,’ then as a rank-and-file official in that ministry, you have no chance of getting the issue off the ground.”

She also cites a specific example from the past: “When the Ministry of Regional Development was drafting the Building Code, the requirement to make buildings and government offices accessible was omitted from all regulations. From our position at the Office of the Government, we had the opportunity to amplify the voices of vulnerable groups and set the dialogue on the right track.”

Prime Minister Babis has attempted to defend the reorganisation by citing a 2023 analysis by the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) that assesses the state of the public administration. “Even the OECD says to consider placing councils that do not address a government’s priorities, or are not cross-sectoral, under individual ministries,” he said.

A closer reading of the analysis, however, shows that Babis’s interpretation omitted important context. While the document does allow for the transfer of certain specific councils, it in fact calls for strengthening the coordinating role directly under the Office of the Government when it comes to cross-sectoral issues, such as the human rights agenda. Furthermore, the OECD emphasised that any changes must be preceded by an in-depth analysis of effectiveness – an analysis that Babis’s cabinet failed to conduct.

Under pressure from experts, the prime minister finally agreed to a compromise: two new offices will be established within the Office of the Government: one for human rights and the protection of minorities, and one for mental health and addiction. Experts say, however, these will be merely empty shells.

“It will be more like a secretariat. It will lack specialised teams and capacity. All that will remain are secretaries who send out invitations and take minutes at meetings, but expertise on the legislative process, policy concepts and action plans will vanish from the Office of the Government for good,” warns Simackova Laurencikova.

According to information provided to iROZHLAS, even civil servants themselves have not had their concerns raised. “We still have questions about this. Honestly, I don’t know how it’s all going to work,” said one. At the same time, however, they said they considered the current discussions at the various ministries to be constructive, even if not all of them can be so described.

The cabinet’s actions drew an immediate reaction, both from officials and from experts serving on committees and working groups.

“As for advisory bodies such as committees and working groups, we know of dozens of people who have resigned at this stage or are seriously considering standing down. Some of them resigned immediately,” says Medal, spokesperson for Straka, the trade union organisation at the Office of the Government.

Anna Smyslova, another representative of the union, says some agencies are already completely paralysed, including the Committee for the Prevention of Domestic Violence and Violence Against Women. Yet this committee included key figures in the field; of 20 members, eight came directly from the non-profit sector, which provides direct assistance to victims.

Last week, Lucie Fukova, the government commissioner for Roma minority affairs, resigned from her post, citing her disagreement with the transfer of the Roma agenda to the Ministry of Labor and Social Affairs. Following her departure, Vice Chair Marian Dancso and member Tomas Scuka also stepped down as of the end of June. According to a statement provided to the Romea website, there are serious concerns that placing the agenda under the ministry will reduce Roma issues to a purely “social issue” and reinforce harmful stereotypes.

In the last two weeks, iROZHLAS repeatedly requested a statement from the current human rights commissioner, Tatana Mala. She did not respond to any calls, while her assistant, who could be reached by phone, stated that Mala was in meetings.

Only Justice Minister Jeronym Tejc of the ANO party replied, asserting that the equality agenda will not disappear. “The Ministry of Justice is not only in charge of criminal law legislation, but also civil legislation. I believe that where the equality agenda concerns the Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs, we will find common ground,” he said.

He added that when the agenda was located at the Office of the Government, the Ministry of Justice was also significantly involved in legislation related to domestic violence and the physical punishment of children.

World.title: Vigilante Murder Raises Fears of Russian Neo-Nazi Influence in Bulgaria
World.content:
The sadistic murder of a 37-year-old man by a group of teenagers in the city of Plovdiv has sparked a heated debate about neo-Nazi influence on local youth and highlighted the issue of vigilante activity in Bulgaria.

Georgi Kuzev, from the small town Krichim, died of his injuries on August 5, several hours after a beating that was partially livestreamed on TikTok by teenagers who had concocted a scheme to track, lure and then attack alleged paedophiles.

Kuzev was lured to meet a 17-year-old girl who had posed as a 15-year-old in their correspondence. Five teenagers, three boys and two girls, have been charged with murder. However, pictures from the attack which made their way into the media suggest there may have been a larger group of teenagers involved in the attack on Kuzev.

The pictures in which the teenagers pose next to Kuzev’s bloodied body also give a new reading of the events: all of the teenagers are making the gesture of a clenched fist with the thumb bent or pointed upward and then inward. Called the “Tesak gesture”, it is associated with Maxim Martsinkevich (1984-2020), a notorious Russian neo-Nazi activist who was nicknamed Tesak (meaning "Hatchet" or "Cleaver").

World.title: Courting Trump’s Allies, Bosnian Croat Political Party Signs US Lobbying Contract
World.content:
For political analyst Tanja Topic from Banja Luka, it is obvious that Covic listened to his political ally Dodik and followed in his lobbying footsteps. According to her, Dodik’s experience is valuable, and every opportunity to capitalise on American support for Christian values is being used.

“Of course, the work of lobbying firms should not be equated with the positions of the State Department, nor should we blindly believe domestic spin masters who equate these activities with ‘friendship with Trump’,” Topic said. “The purpose of these activities is to lobby for the ‘Croatian issue in Bosnia and Herzegovina’, which implicitly points to a connection with the elections, while the second part concerns the biggest current US interest in BiH – the Southern Interconnection.”

Adnan Huskic, a professor of political science and international relations at the Sarajevo School of Science and Technology (SSST), previously told BIRN that this move by HDZ BiH is logical.

“It is clear that everyone has seen that American power is for sale,” Huskic said. “So they are doing this to increase their standing and their chances for any future plans.”

Karcic says that what Covic wants from Mercury Public Affairs – crisis communications and public affairs experts who can navigate the corridors of Capitol Hill – is to promote the following argument: “We are not against American gas, we are for American gas, but we want it to be managed by an organisation based in Mostar in order to ensure institutional equality.”

According to the signed contract, Mercury Public Affairs is also committed to strengthening the HDZ BiH’s relations with institutions and representatives of the United States, NATO, the European Union and “other relevant international stakeholders”.

For Karcic, in the language of lobbying in Washington, this is a classic “pro-Western shield”.

Karcic noted that the inclusion of a commitment to NATO, the US and the EU creates the impression for American decision-makers that the HDZ BiH is a stable Euro-Atlantic partner. He said this is crucial for the party because it neutralises accusations that its tactical partnership with Dodik’s Serb nationalist party SNSD is weakening the country’s pro-Western course.

“This is an attempt to brand the HDZ in Washington as a bulwark of Western values in Bosnia and Herzegovina, conveying the message that internal stability – as they see it, through Dayton and the constituent peoples [Bosniaks, Croats and Serbs] – is actually a prerequisite for the overall security architecture of this region,” Karcic said.

Bassuener considers the contract fairly standard and noted that it contains reference to the “equality of constituent peoples” and the “preservation of peace, stability, territorial integrity and the multi-ethnic character [of Bosnia and Herzegovina]“, as well as a target of presenting the HDZ BiH’s positions to the US government, elected representatives, the media and the wider public.

“However, it is considerably less explicit than statements already publicly available regarding a third entity, the ‘discrimination’ against Croats, electoral reform and similar issues,” Bassuener said.

Lobbying against Dayton

World.title: No Subsidies for Hormone Therapy for Trans People in Albania
World.content:
A rally in Tirana for the International Day against Homophobia and Transphobia, May 2017. Photo: EPA/MALTON DIBRA.

Albania’s new guideline for gender-affirming hormone treatment for transgender people within the public healthcare system does not provide financing from public funds, according to information gathered by the NGO LGBT Alliance.

This means that people receiving such treatment cannot obtain their medications free of charge, Xheni Karaj, head of the LGBT Alliance, told BIRN.

“The guideline regulates the provision of healthcare and the clinical protocol, but it does not provide for the reimbursement or public provision of hormones,” Karaj said.

The adoption earlier this year of the Clinical Practice Guideline on hormone treatment for trans people sparked a wave of hate speech targeting the LGBTQ+ community, with various posts claiming that the medication would be funded by taxpayers, and that treatment would be made available to minors.

However, official documents and responses from the Ministry of Health make it clear that the guideline does not provide for hormone therapy for minors or fund treatment for people over the age of 18.

The guideline sets out the clinical procedures to be followed by the Endocrinology Service at the Mother Teresa University Hospital Centre in Tirana for the enrollment and monitoring of people seeking treatment.

Evidence gathered by the LGBT Alliance shows that, even for adults covered by the protocol, the actual provision of the services exists only on paper.

“Although the Clinical Practice Guideline has been approved and entered into force, in practice there have been obstacles that have made it impossible for transgender people to actually access this service,” said Karaj.

“The first three cases that were referred received contradictory information from the responsible institutions, which indicates that the guideline is still not being implemented uniformly,” she added.

The Mother Teresa University Hospital Centre, the Deputy Health Minister Eugena Tomini and the head of the Endocrinology Service Agron Ylli did not respond to requests for comment on the issue.

According to the Ministry of Health, the guideline was developed as part of the measures envisaged in the National Action Plan for LGBTQ+ people from 2021 to 2027 and aims to improve access to inclusive, safe healthcare services based on international standards.

“The guideline was developed in cooperation with experts in the field, representatives of healthcare institutions and civil society organisations, with technical support from the Council of Europe,” the ministry said.

Karaj said that the transgender community had not been directly informed about the approval of the guideline, and that another issue that remains unclear is the referral pathway to the Endocrinology Service.

During the drafting of the guideline, Karaj said, the possibility of direct referral to the Mother Teresa University Hospital Centre had been discussed in order to avoid the barriers or discrimination that members of the community have reported at health centres. However, in the first cases reported to the LGBT Alliance, they were instructed to go through their family doctor first.
