This means pupils in grades 2-6 will not have uniforms in September. At the start of the school year, parents will have to buy regular clothes and purchase the uniforms later.

Will school uniforms change anything in Georgia’s education system?

The government is spending 45.66 million lari on school uniforms, saying they will help reduce social inequality. Meanwhile, Georgian schools still do not provide free meals.

According to a 2023 study by Georgia’s National Statistics Office, with support from UNICEF, only 27% of children aged 6 to 17 eat at school every day. Meanwhile, 34.9% do not eat at all during the school day. Among children from low-income families, the figure reaches 44.9%.

The same study found that 83.2% of parents believe schools should provide children with meals during the school day. In some Georgian schools, particularly in the regions, children cannot even buy food because the schools have no canteens.

Against the backdrop of these and other problems, school uniforms appear to be the least pressing issue facing Georgia’s public schools.

“I cannot support spending such a large amount of money on uniforms when schools have yet to address basic problems with toilets, canteens and the quality of education,” says Ana Gvaladze.

“We called the ministry 80 times to get the problem with the toilets at School No. 161 resolved,” adds Sopho Trapaidze.

Taya, who has been studying education issues in depth, says building a school culture is a complex process and involves much more than a set of behavioural rules:

“Schools face many problems today, from poor infrastructure and failures to meet health and hygiene standards to a lack of an emotionally safe environment for children. Children attend dull, grey schools. Sometimes a school has just one teacher, who provides the support that the education system as a whole should provide. So school culture cannot be strengthened through uniforms alone. Likewise, in such an unhealthy environment — and given the problems with crime in the country — uniforms cannot stop bullying.”

Taya notes that bullying does not actually start because of clothing.

“Clothing is just an excuse. If a bully is looking for a victim, they can pick on someone’s height, weight, glasses, shoes, bag or even pen. Uniforms cannot hide social differences. And most importantly, when the minister talked about school culture and a sense of belonging, did he forget that a child who is hungry because their school has no canteen will not develop any sense of belonging?”

Hundreds of thousands of Georgian schoolchildren will start the new academic year in “impoverished” conditions, in buildings that are not suitable for proper education. In recent years, hundreds of schools across the country have been demolished, while construction on many replacements has yet to begin.

School uniforms in Georgia

World.title: Former Georgian PM Irakli Garibashvili accuses Ivanishvili of blackmail
World.content:
Former PM accuses Ivanishvili of blackmail

Jailed former Georgian prime minister Irakli Garibashvili has accused Georgian Dream honorary chairman Bidzina Ivanishvili and the current government of blackmail.

In a statement released from prison on 17 August 2026, the former prime minister claimed he was being pressured to plead guilty to new corruption charges and permanently withdraw from politics at Ivanishvili’s demand. It is the first time that a former close ally of Ivanishvili has openly spoken out against the founder of the ruling party.

Plea deal ultimatum and plan to quit politics

A photograph of a printed letter dated 17 August was posted on the Facebook pages of Garibashvili and his wife, Nunuka Tamazashvili. Only four paragraphs of the letter were made public. It is unclear who wrote the letter or how it was delivered.

According to the published document, the government is offering the former prime minister a compromise. Under the proposed terms, Garibashvili would have to plead guilty to a new corruption-related charge.

The letter sets out the proposal in detail:

“They are offering me the option of pleading guilty in one case, where everything would be arranged by agreement, including a confession, witness signatures and so on. They are offering a plea bargain while retaining the same five-year sentence: that is, as it has been explained to me, the sentences would be combined, but the final term would remain five years.”

According to the document, a corruption conviction would serve as a form of “insurance” for the government, aimed at preventing the former prime minister from returning to politics in the future.

Two options and a political condition

The published letter refers to investigations into several cases. Its author suggests that these could result in corruption charges.

The text outlines two possible courses of action for Garibashvili. The first would involve continuing to contest the case in court.

“Let’s discuss this seriously and see it through to the end,” the document says.

The second option is presented as a compromise. According to the letter, Garibashvili would plead guilty in one of the cases, with the details agreed in advance:

“Let’s plead guilty in one case, where everything will be arranged by agreement: a confession, witness signatures and so on.”

The document also says that a new plea deal would not increase the five-year prison sentence already imposed on Garibashvili. The sentences would be combined, leaving the overall term unchanged at five years.

However, the proposal comes with a political condition.

“After leaving, you cannot engage in politics. If it is decided to ‘renege on the agreements’, then the corruption charges that will be brought will serve as an insurance mechanism, preventing even the thought of returning to politics,” the document says.

The authenticity of the letter has not been independently verified, and its author remains unknown. There is also no confirmation that new cases are in fact being prepared against Garibashvili.

Garibashvili’s first open confrontation with Ivanishvili

This marks Irakli Garibashvili’s first public confrontation with Bidzina Ivanishvili. For many years, Garibashvili was regarded as one of his most loyal political allies.

He served twice as Georgia’s prime minister, first from 2013 to 2015 and again from 2021 to 2024.

Garibashvili was sentenced under a plea agreement reached on 12 January 2026. He was given a five-year prison term and fined one million lari. Two cars and $6.5m were also confiscated from him.

The case concerned the laundering of illicit proceeds on an especially large scale. Garibashvili is currently serving his sentence in a prison in Rustavi.

The new statement means that the former prime minister himself is now linking possible further legal action against him to demands that he stay out of politics. However, the material made public so far presents only Garibashvili’s version of events.

Response from MP Irma Inashvili, named in letter

The letter published by Garibashvili mentions MP Irma Inashvili and Dito Chubinidze. According to the text, they — along with “supporters like them” and campaigns on social media — have raised suspicions.

“Supporters such as Dito Chubinidze and Irma Inashvili, as well as campaigns organised on social media, have raised very serious suspicions and caused us tangible harm,” the document says.

Inashvili denied any involvement in organised campaigns. She said Irakli Garibashvili was her friend, but that she expressed her views publicly and independently.

“I have never planned or conducted any campaigns on social media; I don’t need such campaigns — I already express my views openly in my own name!” Inashvili wrote.

She said Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze was the main target of her criticism.

“I expose Kobakhidze and fight against him,” Inashvili said.

Opposition says Garibashvili being politically neutralised

Opposition figures have described Garibashvili’s letter as a sign of an internal conflict within the government. Their comments amount to political assessments and do not independently corroborate the circumstances described in the letter.

Nika Gvaramia, one of the leaders of the Coalition for Change, said the contents of the letter pointed to a political motive behind Garibashvili’s imprisonment.

“Ivanishvili’s bargaining with Garibashvili — ‘I will punish you even more severely unless you give me guarantees that you will leave politics for good’ — confirms that the motive for his arrest is neither to punish a corrupt official nor to fight corruption in general, nor does it serve any public or state interest. It serves Bidzina’s personal political interests,” Gvaramia wrote.

He also qualified his comments by noting that the authenticity of the letter had not been established. Gvaramia particularly highlighted what he described as an attempt to politically neutralise Garibashvili.

Levan Samushia, a member of the Lelo – Strong Georgia party, linked the statement to the country’s current system of governance. He said any potential threat against Garibashvili’s family warranted a legal response.

“It is clear that Garibashvili is speaking about a possible, alleged threat to his family. This is an issue that requires particular attention and, naturally, provides grounds for launching an investigation,” Samushia said.

Berdia Sichinava, a representative of the Gakharia for Georgia party, said he preferred to wait for further information before reaching a definitive conclusion. Nevertheless, he linked the developments to an internal conflict within Georgian Dream.

“The situation appears alarming because it concerns his family, and at this point clarity is the best means of protecting him and his loved ones,” Sichinava said.

Khatia Dekanoidze, one of the leaders of the United National Movement, described Garibashvili’s case as a warning to current government figures.

“Garibashvili’s case should be learnt by heart by Ivanishvili’s current servants, officials and representatives of the financial sector who justify the government,” Dekanoidze wrote.

Government silent as questions remain unanswered

At the time of writing, reports about Garibashvili’s allegations had not appeared on the websites or Facebook pages of the pro-government Imedi and Rustavi 2 television channels.

Government representatives have yet to respond publicly to the central allegation. They have not said whether Bidzina Ivanishvili had any involvement in sending the letter to Garibashvili. It also remains unclear whether any new investigations into the former prime minister are under way.

Background: From alliance to prison

For many years, Irakli Garibashvili was regarded as one of Bidzina Ivanishvili’s closest political allies. He served twice as Georgia’s prime minister.

On 24 October 2025, Garibashvili was charged with laundering illicit proceeds on an especially large scale. A plea agreement was reached on 12 January 2026, under which the former prime minister was sentenced to five years in prison and fined one million lari. Two cars and $6.5m were also confiscated. He has since been serving his sentence at a penitentiary facility in Rustavi.

Legal proceedings against former senior figures in the ruling team were preceded by internal party disagreements and arrests of officials from various state agencies. There have also been reports of investigative measures involving members of Garibashvili’s family.

The developments suggest that the power struggle within Georgian Dream has entered an increasingly acute phase.

World.title: Georgia does not join EU’s updated sanctions against Iran
World.content:
Georgia did not join EU sanctions against Iran

Georgia did not join the EU partner countries that backed the bloc’s updated sanctions against Iran. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the measures involve three decisions imposing restrictions on Iran.

What are the decisions?

The EU has amended its sanctions regime against Iran. It removed and added several individuals and updated information on one organisation. All other restrictions remain in force.

The EU also adopted a decision on Iran’s military support for armed groups operating in Russia, the Middle East and the Red Sea region. The EU extended the existing sanctions and removed four individuals from the list.

In another decision, the EU added six individuals to its sanctions list over human rights violations in Iran.

The countries of the European Economic Area — Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway — joined the EU measures. So did EU candidate countries Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Moldova, Montenegro, North Macedonia and Ukraine.

Georgia did not join them.

Georgian Dream’s position

Georgian Dream MP Tengiz Sharmanashvili said Georgia only joins international decisions when they serve the country’s interests.

“The question of whether Georgia joins a resolution or takes steps in international affairs is determined by one criterion alone: whether it serves the country’s interests at that particular moment,” he said.

Sharmanashvili noted that two other EU candidate countries, Turkey and Serbia, had also not joined the sanctions against Iran.

“If it goes against Georgia’s interests, we do not care whose interests it serves,” the MP stressed.

Georgia’s Foreign Ministry has not yet responded to a request from Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty to explain why the country did not join the EU sanctions.

The EU’s enlargement reports have already noted Georgia’s limited alignment with the bloc’s foreign policy. According to the 2025 report, Georgia’s alignment with the EU’s Common Foreign and Security Policy had fallen to 40% by October 2025, down from 53% in 2024.

Georgia did not join EU sanctions against Iran

World.title: Controversial changes to NDIS will pass after Labor strikes deal with Coalition
World.content:
The federal government will pass reforms that it says will save the National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS) "from itself" by making it more sustainable and cracking down further on fraud.

The Coalition voted with Labor to pass the sweeping changes in the Senate this evening, which are intended to curb the structural bloat of a scheme that costs more than $50 billion annually.

The overhaul is expected to save an estimated $37.8 billion over the next four years alone.

Health Minister Mark Butler argued the scheme had become a "soft target for shonks, for fraudsters and for sharp practice".

Mr Butler said the 63 amendments, following engagement with the disability community, reflect a "government that is willing to listen".

Powerful testimonies heard at NDIS inquiry The key takeaways from the six-day Senate inquiry into a proposed NDIS shake-up.

"We said when we announced this plan in April that we would engage deeply with the disability community but also with other parliamentarians," he told reporters this afternoon.

NDIS Minister Jenny McAllister said the changes would "deliver a NDIS that is strong, safe and sustainable and has a strong social licence".

The changes include establishing an escalation pathway for high-risk participants.

Ms McAllister said it would ensure an individual requiring 24-hour continuous care could apply for a plan variation to have their needs met, protecting them from support cuts.

Jenny McAllister says the changes will deliver a more sustainable NDIS. (Matt Roberts/ABC News)

The legislation will strengthen anti-fraud measures, introducing new criminal and civil penalties for providers who offer or provide kickbacks.

It will also grant additional whistleblower protections and greater enforcement powers for the National Disability Insurance Agency (NDIA) to ensure swifter regulatory action against unsafe or unethical providers.

The health minister said the new eligibility system, which aims to reduce participants from roughly 760,000 to 600,000 by 2030, is not explicitly spelled out in the bill.

Jordan Steele-John says the government's changes represent the end of the NDIS as it was promised. (ABC News: David Sciasci)

Under the proposal, standardised assessments of functional capacity would determine eligibility for the scheme rather than diagnosis alone.

Mr Butler reassured Australians that the new eligibility standards will be made clear well ahead of their introduction on first January 2028.

The Greens have expressed concern the changes will leave hundreds of thousands without support, arguing they represent the "end of the NDIS as it was promised".

"Labor and the Liberals have got together in a room and have decided to strip us of our rights regardless of our safety or dignity," Greens senator Jordan Steele-John said this afternoon.

Crossbenchers and disability advocates also insisted the changes have come "too far, too fast".

Butler issues state warning over Thriving Kids

Mr Butler acknowledged there was still "substantial" work to do on foundational support systems for children over the age of eight and other adults who will be taken off the scheme as a result of changes.

He remained adamant that the Thriving Kids program was on track to meet its scheduled start of October 1, despite the Queensland state government's refusal to sign up to the scheme.

Asked whether he had used the $25 billion in public hospital funding to state and territories in exchange for supporting the NDIS reform as leverage, Mr Butler reminded them of their commitments.

Mark Butler says amendments made to the bill show the government is willing to listen. (Matt Roberts/ABC News)

"It's a question of honour, really, for states — they signed an agreement earlier this year that set up five years of very significant increases for our public hospital system, but a reaffirmation of the commitment they made in 2023 to work with the Commonwealth to get the NDIS back on track."

"The Queensland government needs to answer for its inability so far to live up to the agreement that the premier signed earlier this year," he added.

The ABC has approached Queensland Minister for Families, Seniors and Disability Services, Amanda Camm, for comment.

The government vowed to fast-track a fix to the unintended "widow tax" created by its changes to negative gearing in exchange for the Coalition's support.

It is part of a broader deal with the Coalition that will also create a pathway to pass Labor's gambling reforms and news media bargaining incentive.

World.title: Sydney Swans say players 'in serious breach' of club standards
World.content:
The Sydney Swans say the players allegedly connected to an incident at a Melbourne hotel "are in serious breach of expected club behaviour and standards".

The ABC understands four players — Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, James Jordon and Riley Bice — are linked to an investigation into an alleged assault at the Pullman Hotel in east Melbourne in the early hours of yesterday morning.

It is not suggested that any of the four players are being accused of sexual assault.

Victoria Police is investigating, stating this morning that "the exact circumstances are yet to be established and … no one has been arrested or formally interviewed at this time".

The club said it interviewed all the players linked to the incident in Melbourne and concluded "firm action" should be taken relating to the breaching of club standards.

(Clockwise from top left) James Jordon, Chad Warner, Riley Bice and Isaac Heeney are understood to be linked to a sexual assault investigation. (ABC News/Getty Images)

"The club also acknowledges that these serious allegations impact others and their wellbeing must be paramount," a statement read.

"The Sydney Swans condemn all forms of abuse and disrespectful behaviour towards women. Any conduct that causes offence or harm to others is unacceptable and falls well short of our expectations. All women deserve to be respected and feel safe.

"We also want to acknowledge that the care and welfare of our AFLW athletes and staff is of the utmost importance to us as a club.

"They have been and will continue to be offered the support they require, and we acknowledge the impact these allegations have on our female athletes, staff members and the wider community."

Heeney, Warner, Bice and Jordon did not appear at Swans HQ with the rest of their team today and were interviewed by the club off-site with lawyers present.

The Swans board will meet tonight to agree on club-imposed sanctions and penalties.

Focus should not be on 'football consequences' AFLW star turned broadcaster Kate McCarthy calls out members of the media focusing on how a police investigation linked to Sydney Swans players could affect the team's finals chances.

"Any further sanctions or decisions regarding the outcome of the police investigation would take place after that process is completed," the statement read.

"During this time, we will provide the appropriate support to the players involved in the incident, along with their partners and families.

"The Sydney Swans hold all players and staff at the club to high standards of behaviour and personal conduct. Representing this club carries significant responsibilities both on and off the field, and we expect those standards to be upheld at all times.

"Our focus remains on cooperating fully with the AFL and authorities, maintaining the integrity of the process, and upholding the high standards expected of everyone who represents this club."

'Deeply concerning' incident: AFL CEO

AFL chief executive Andrew Dillon said the allegations around the Swans were "deeply concerning", stressing that, regardless of the outcome of the police investigation, the incident raised wider concerns around the game.

"The conduct and serious allegations regarding Sydney Swans players are deeply concerning," he said in a statement.

Andrew Dillon said the effects on a club's season had no bearing on the seriousness of the allegations. (Getty Images: Mark Kolbe)

"While the matter remains under police investigation, it raises broader issues for our game and our responsibilities as a sport.

"The woman who made the report to police is entitled to privacy and care, and that should be respected.

"It is important that the police process is allowed to run its course."

Dillon alluded to discussions around the potential sanctions or distractions for the Swans and the potential impact that may have on the second-placed club heading into the AFL finals.

"Sexual assault allegations are serious, regardless of who is involved, what time of year it is, or what they may mean for a season," he said ahead of the team's final home-and-away game on Sunday.

"Our first question should not be what this means for a football club. It should be whether our actions match the standards we stand for and the community expects of us.

"As a sport, and as an industry, we are clear about the standards we expect and the values we stand for and the need to uphold them.

"Being clear about our standards also means being prepared to act when those standards are not met.

"Notwithstanding the ongoing police investigation, the AFL and the Sydney Swans will consider the broader conduct of the players as more information comes to light."

World.title: Mistrial declared in alleged 2007 stabbing murder at Adelaide party
World.content:
A mistrial has been declared in the case of Kimlong Rim, who is charged with murder over the alleged fatal stabbing of a 21-year-old at a birthday party almost 20 years ago.

Mr Rim, 38, had been standing trial in South Australia's Supreme Court after pleading not guilty to the murder of Thea Kheav outside a party at Parafield Gardens, in Adelaide's north, in December 2007.

The court previously heard Mr Kheav was a guest at the 18th birthday party, which he attended with his brothers, before he died.

Justice Rachael Gray said there would be a retrial.

World.title: Unions push for renters to be guaranteed two-year lease
World.content:
Landlords would have to offer renters at least two years on their lease, and the proportion of new public housing would increase fivefold as part of a union proposal being presented to the government.

Under current laws, the minimum for lease agreements varies across states and territories, and some, including New South Wales, have no rules in place at all.

The Australian Council of Trade Unions (ACTU) said a nationwide two-year minimum, with the option for renters to opt for a shorter period, would give renters more stability and allow them to plan.

"Having a standard of at least two years across the country would give renters the security of knowing they can stay in their home for at least that period of time," ACTU president Michele O'Neil said.

" This would deal with some of the fears that people currently have. "

The union also wants a return to a Hawke-style model of construction, increasing the rate of public housing being built from one in 50 new homes to one in 10.

Michele O'Neil says one in 10 new homes should be public housing. (ABC News: Tom Hancock)

Public housing is owned and administered by state and territory governments, and the 2026 State of Housing report found public housing stock declined by 1,143 rental units last year, despite annual dwelling completions for public housing increasing 32 per cent over the same period.

"If we expand public housing, you will see more rental stock available, and that is going to free up stock in the rental market and make private stock more sustainable," Ms O'Neil said.

Property developers are benefiting from Australia's housing crisis State and federal governments are offering incentives for property developers in exchange for more affordable housing. But a Four Corners investigation has uncovered major flaws in the strategy.

"It's the combination of measures that need to be put in place — the tax changes from the budget, public housing expansion, and stronger rental rights."

According to the ACTU Housing Plan, the union will also be pushing for tighter rules around rent gouging and a long-term goal of at least 6 per cent of total housing stock being public.

To get there, it is suggesting removal of GST on the cost of maintaining public housing, and a review of the Commonwealth Rent Assistance setting.

Union confident minimum would not drive away landlords

A note sent by NAB to its investors showed the bank was projecting a 30 per cent increase in rents in Sydney and Melbourne over the next two years, which it said was in response to the government's tax changes for property investors.

The negative gearing and capital gains tax adjustments, announced in the May federal budget, were part of an original push from the ACTU to improve housing conditions for workers.

In parliament on Tuesday, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese pushed back on the suggestion, and said the bank does not forecast rental yields.

In towns where thousands of homes are Airbnbs, renters want a tax Homelessness NSW says it is easier to get a holiday rental than a long-term rental — and that needs to change.

"There are no changes to negative gearing for people who owned a property until budget night," Mr Albanese said.

Ms O'Neil also pushed back on the claim, and said she was confident further restrictions on landlords, including the proposed two-year lease, would not discourage investment.

"I think it is more likely that some professional landlords are being opportunistic, and some professional landlords are using the tax changes as cover that actually will not apply to them to justify unacceptable rent increases," she said.

Modular construction part of productivity solution

Ms O'Neil said the union was looking to modular building in factories as a solution to productivity issues in the housing construction sector.

"We think modular housing is something that is a real opportunity to expand housing in Australia with high-quality housing, but expanding the stock," she said.

Factory-built homes could help Australia reindustrialise, report says Factory-built homes could solve Australia's housing crisis and drive reindustrialisation, report says.

Shadow Housing Minister Andrew Bragg is advocating a dramatic rewrite of the National Construction Code to simplify the building process and speed up construction.

After a productivity roundtable last year, the government also said it would consider streamlining the code.

Ms O'Neil said the union wanted to make sure an increase in housing stock, both public and private, did not come at the expense of quality.

"A high-quality house actually makes it more affordable," she said.

"It's a false economy if you have maintenance issues, or if your house is too hot or too cold; it causes all sorts of problems for health and security.

"We don't want to see any reduction in standards in housing that we build; in fact, we want to make sure that however much income you have, you have a safe home."

Melissa Donnelly named new ACTU boss Melissa Donnelly's appointment comes after former peak union body secretary Sally McManus and president Michele O'Neil announced their resignations late last month.

The union wants the changes to be delivered via the 'A Better Deal For Renters' agreement, which was last updated during a meeting of National Cabinet in 2023.

The agreement committed to standardised genuine grounds evictions, a ban on soliciting rent bidding, and a national standard of no more than one rent increase per year.

It is not yet clear who will replace Ms O'Neil as ACTU president, after she announced her resignation last month.

Last week, ACTU announced public service union boss Melissa Donnelly would take over from Sally McManus as secretary.

World.title: Man who stabbed wife to death has four-year sentence doubled on appeal
World.content:
A man who fatally stabbed his wife of 26 years in the chest outside a Darwin hotel has had his prison term doubled after the Northern Territory's Director of Public Prosecutions successfully appealed his sentence.

The Supreme Court previously heard Dennis Naroldol stabbed his wife through the heart outside the DoubleTree by Hilton Hotel on Darwin's picturesque esplanade in April 2023 after the pair got into a drunken argument.

The 60-year-old last year pleaded guilty to negligent manslaughter and was sentenced in March to four years behind bars, with a three-year non-parole period which expired in April.

Prosecutors appealed that sentence and today the NT Court of Criminal Appeal heard while Naroldol had not yet been released on parole, he was potentially being considered for release to a residential alcohol rehabilitation facility.

Sentence 'clearly and obviously inadequate'

In his submissions, Crown prosecutor Patrick Williams said the sentence imposed by Justice Stephen Southwood was "clearly and obviously inadequate" and "did not reflect the maximum penalty and the taking of a human life".

The court heard Dennis Naroldol and his wife got into a drunken argument before he picked up a 9cm knife and stabbed her in the heart. (ABC News: Ben Gubana)

Mr Williams said the sentence also failed to meet important sentencing requirements, including deterrence, punishment, denunciation and protection of the community.

He pointed to findings by Justice Southwood who described the offending as "brazen" given it occurred in a public place in front of multiple witnesses.

"While the offending was not pre-mediated or planned, it was also not spontaneous," he said.

" The level of force was significant — sufficient for the knife to enter the chest cavity and indeed the heart. "

The court heard Naroldol had previously been convicted of assaulting his wife four times between 1995 and 2020, with all four assaults involving weapons, including one involving the use of a knife.

Chief Justice Michael Grant said, "given the circumstances", the court would deliver its decision from the bench with reasons to follow. (ABC News: Tiffany Parker)

Mr Williams said Naroldol's history of domestic violence and the fact the victim was his wife were relevant considerations, adding to the seriousness of the crime.

He said that was "because of the particularly pernicious nature of domestic violence", which "causes more extended harm to society, to families".

Offending 'unsophisticated and not pre-planned'

In response, defence barrister Emrys Nekvapil SC acknowledged Naroldol's sentence was at the lower end of the appropriate range of sentences, but said it was a "proper" use of judicial discretion.

Mr Nekvapil argued his client's level of intoxication and the fact the attack was "unsophisticated and not pre-planned" were important factors in why the sentence was not inadequate.

Dennis Naroldol's barrister argued his intoxication distinguished his offending from murder "or even reckless manslaughter". (ABC News: Ben Gubana)

"It's the intoxication that means what we're dealing with here is a plea to negligent manslaughter and not … murder by a person with a knife intending to cause serious harm, or even reckless manslaughter," he said.

The court previously heard the pair had been drinking in nearby parkland on the night of the stabbing before Naroldol lay down in the hotel's driveway.

Man jailed for fatally stabbing wife eligible for parole in two weeks Dennis Naroldol, 59, has been sentenced to four years in prison over the fatal stabbing of his wife outside the Darwin DoubleTree Hilton in 2023.

His wife then jabbed him with an umbrella, causing a 9-centimetre knife to fall onto the ground, which he later used to stab her in the chest.

"It's that adventitious circumstance that provides the motive for action," Mr Nekvapil said.

"It's very different from a situation where someone has come along with an intention."

After a brief adjournment, the appeal judges overturned Naroldol's original sentence and re-sentenced him to eight years' imprisonment from the date of his arrest and extended his non-parole period to four years and six months.

"We're in a position to make orders in relation to this matter now, and given the circumstances, we think we should, with reasons to be published in due course," Chief Justice Michael Grant said.

Naroldol will now be eligible for parole in October next year.

World.title: Man dies after stabbing south of Brisbane
World.content:
A man has died following a stabbing in Logan, south of Brisbane, with an investigation underway.

Emergency services were called to Lubach Street at Beenleigh at about 4:45pm following reports a 66-year-old man had sustained puncture wounds.

Police say CPR was commenced when officers arrived; however, the man was declared dead a short time later.

A man and a woman are assisting police with their enquiries, with investigations ongoing.

Anyone with relevant information or CCTV is urged to contact police.

World.title: Thousands of patients received sub-par colonoscopies from same doctor
World.content:
A doctor who was found to have committed professional misconduct oversaw thousands of flawed colonoscopies before she was suspended from practising in July.

Concerns over Dr Liu-Ming Schmidt's conduct led to 1,934 patients across three health services, who had received a colonoscopy performed or supervised by her between 2018 and 2022, being advised to repeat their procedure.

Out of 1,084 patients who had a repeat colonoscopy, 548 of them had polyps, and seven had cancer.

Lynette Taylor was one of the patients who placed her faith in Dr Schmidt when she performed her colonoscopy at Albury Wodonga Private Hospital in 2021.

With a history of bowel cancer in her family, Lynette had always booked in regular colonoscopies.

"She trusted Dr Schmidt. She trusted that she'd highlighted the need for it [the colonoscopy] to be careful, because of the family history of bowel cancer," her daughter Belinda Taylor said.

" She put her faith in Dr Schmidt that those colonoscopies were going to be carried out to the standard that they should have. "

But two years after receiving an all-clear following her screening with Dr Schmidt in 2021, she began losing weight rapidly.

"She was very fatigued all the time and had just lost her spark," Ms Taylor said.

"As part of a review with a specialist, it was suggested that she go back and have another colonoscopy because they were extremely shocked by the way she was presenting physically."

The results left the family in shock. It was stage 4 bowel cancer.

Lynette had regular colonoscopies due to her family history of bowel cancer. (Supplied)

"I immediately started questioning and investigating how could this occur," Ms Taylor said.

" How can you be so diligent about your health and then find out you have stage 4 cancer? "

Lynette died earlier this year, aged 78.

According to an independent expert engaged by the family, the size of the cancer detected in 2023 suggested a polyp was likely present when she had her colonoscopy in 2021, but it was not identified.

In 2022, another of Dr Schmidt's patients was diagnosed with bowel cancer following a series of regular colonoscopies.

One of those procedures lasted for five minutes from start to finish.

Dr Cameron Bell has been a gastroenterologist for more than 30 years and has performed around 30,000 scopes throughout his career. He said there was "no way" a high-quality colonoscopy could be conducted in that time.

Dr Cameron Bell has been a gastroenterologist for more than 30 years. (ABC News: Shaun Kingma )

"A colonoscopy generally takes something like 20 to 30 minutes, depending on the difficulty of the procedure," he said.

"It did make me wonder how that situation developed without anybody putting their hand up and saying, 'Well, that's not appropriate. That wasn't a quality colonoscopy'," Dr Bell told 7.30.

A complaint after the 2022 case was then made against Dr Schmidt to the NSW Health Care Complaints Commission.

Dr Schmidt told a tribunal she had conducted colonoscopies the way she was trained to.

Dr Liu-Ming Schmidt was found guilty of professional misconduct in July. (Supplied: Albury Surgical Group)

'Catastrophic mistake' made during surgery

In 2023, Dr Schmidt was asked to step down from practising medicine for 12 months at the request of the Medical Council of NSW. She agreed, and returned to work a year later, but there were restrictions on her practice.

Her work as a surgeon has also come under scrutiny.

In 2019, 79-year-old William Edmunds was rushed to Albury hospital with a perforated bowel and was operated on by Dr Schmidt.

A coronial inquest found that Dr Schmidt made a catastrophic error during the surgery which caused a mechanical bowel obstruction.

Dr Schmidt gave evidence at the inquest that distorted anatomy and extensive contamination made the initial operation difficult but couldn't explain how or why the error occurred.

In 2023, the coroner concluded Mr Edmunds died from complications of peritonitis, which was contributed to by the surgical error made by Dr Schmidt and recommended the Health Care Complaints Commissioner (HCCC) investigate.

Dr Schmidt operated on William Edmunds in 2019, where she made a catastrophic error. (Supplied)

In the years since Mr Edmunds' death, the HCCC investigated 13 complaints against Dr Schmidt in relation to colonoscopies and her surgical management of patients over a seven-year period.

The NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal found her management of several patients fell significantly below reasonable standards.

In July, she was found guilty of professional misconduct and was suspended for six months.

But Belinda Taylor says the suspension is not enough and is now pursuing a complaint to the NSW HCCC against Dr Schmidt.

"Caring for [Lynette] for the last two years of her life, watching her go through endless treatment, back-to-back appointments, scans, immunotherapy, watching her just deteriorate over those two years ... six months is totally inadequate, and more needs to be done," she said.

Belinda Taylor is now pursuing a complaint to the NSW Health Care Complaints Commission against Dr Schmidt. (Supplied)

Professor Cameron Stewart was a member of the medical council of New South Wales, working directly with the HCCC to investigate and prosecute complaints.

He acknowledges that for those involved a six-month suspension may not be seen as enough.

"These systems I think have worked well in this particular case, but they haven't been as efficient as the families wish ... and I think the public would wish," he said.

For Ms Taylor the outcome for her mother remains unfair and painful.

"My wonderful mum died, and we held her hand as she took her final breaths. And she had said to us that she wasn't ready.

" She was just a beautiful person, and didn't deserve [this] to happen to her. "

The ABC requested an interview with Dr Schmidt and sent questions, but did not receive a response.

World.title: Ministers tread carefully as Trump scales back US drills in South Korea
World.content:
Australia and Japan's defence ministers have side-stepped questions about Donald Trump's pronouncement that he will scale back military exercises with South Korea — as well as the US president's overtures to North Korean dictator Kim Jong Un — while signalling they still see Pyongyang as a serious security threat.

Shinjiro Koizumi and Richard Marles sat down in Canberra today to discuss the rapidly expanding defence ties between the two countries.

Trump scales back military drills with South Korea US President Donald Trump orders the Pentagon to scale back planned joint military exercises with South Korea, citing his good relationship with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.

Both countries are increasingly anxious about China's rapidly swelling military might, as well as the Trump administration's chaotic and unpredictable behaviour.

The US president promised on Monday that he would scale back US participation in the Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises because Seoul had not helped the US war effort in Iran, and this morning suggested that North Korean dictator Kim Jong Un had responded "positively" to the move.

The joint exercises that started yesterday are scheduled to run until later in August, with about 18,000 South Korean military personnel taking part -as well as a small contingent of 13 ADF personnel who are serving as part of United Nations Command.

South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said this morning the annual exercises are defensive and not intended to attack North Korea or raise tensions on the peninsula.

Last week, Mr Lee proposed talks to officially end the war with Pyongyang, although North Korea has routinely tested ballistic missiles and strengthened its military ties with Russia.

'Critical' cooperation

Analysts and US senators on both sides of the aisle have warned Mr Trump's move risks alienating South Korea and undercutting US credibility in Asia, while Korean media have quoted a Japanese foreign affairs official warning "we must not weaken our posture to respond to threats."

But Mr Koizumi was much more careful when asked about the announcement, simply saying that countries like North Korea and Russia were posing an increasingly severe threat to Japan's security, and that US allies needed to deepen cooperation in response.

"The missile enhancement and coercive and unilateral challenge to the status quo by other countries and North Korea … is getting stronger," he told journalists in Canberra.

"Our cooperation with Australia, Japan and the US is ever more important."

Mr Marles also would not be drawn on the US president's announcement, saying "obviously what the United States does is a matter for it."

But he stressed that Australia was still "very concerned" about North Korea's nuclear and missile programs, saying that South Korea was a "critically important" defence partner for Australia.

"In the challenging world we face — and there are many challenges but North Korea is the author of quite [a lot] of them — we greatly appreciate our relationship with South Korea and we very much appreciate our relationship with Japan," he said.

The chief executive of the Australian Institute of International Affairs and a Japan expert, Bryce Wakefield, told the ABC that both countries would be monitoring the US administration's moves very closely.

"Tokyo's response to this development won't be panic, but it reinforces Japan's concern that longstanding alliance arrangements can become bargaining chips in Trump's personal diplomacy," he said.

"We saw this in the US president's first-term approaches to North Korea, and we're now seeing it at a time when North Korea is still testing missiles."

Dr Wakefield said that Canberra would be "uneasy for much the same reason" as Japan.

"Australia puts a lot of stock in exercises and interoperability," he said.

"It will worry less about this particular drill than the signal that the US is now changing regional commitments abruptly, according to Trump's transactional approach."

Shinjiro Koizumi, seen here in Japan, says he strongly supports joint security cooperation with Washington and Seoul. (Reuters: Manami Yamada)

One Japanese government source said the two ministers "referred" to the president's plans in their meeting but said the overwhelming focus was on the way the two countries — often labelled as "quasi-allies" — could continue to quickly build up defence ties.

Japan to test hypersonic missiles in Australia

Australia announced last year that a Japanese company had won a multi-billion-dollar contract for Australia's next generation of warships, and signed a contract for the first three frigates in Melbourne earlier this year.

The two ministers confirmed they were pressing ahead with plans to expand Japan's access to Australia's missile ranges to allow it to conduct sophisticated tests — including with hypersonic missiles.

US allies turning to Japan for defence supplies as Iran war drags on Australia's multi-billion-dollar deal with Japan for its future warships could set a template that will help Tokyo rapidly expand defence exports across Asia.

Japan has moved to rapidly increase defence spending to respond to China's massive military build-up, including by investing in advanced equipment such as long-range missiles and hypersonic weapons.

"We have agreed to progress a better and enhanced arrangement between Australia and Japan for Japan's use of our missile ranges over the next decade across a range of missile capabilities," Mr Marles said.

Mr Koizumi said it would be only the second time Japan would have a missile test range arrangement, behind the United States.

"If the Japan Self Defence Forces are able to conduct test launches of stand-off missiles, such as hypersonic missiles in Australia, it would be a groundbreaking development," he said.

Both ministers also said the two countries were making good progress on a new high-energy laser that they were developing together called the Boobook project — named after an Australian owl.

Mr Marles said tests had been successful and it would offer "greater protection and situational awareness by using laser to optically detect incoming threats."

Mr Koizumi also met with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese in Canberra, but told journalists they did not discuss Mr Albanese's comments about the melons gifted to him by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi — despite the political furore it provoked in Australia last week.

"Before I visited Australia, the Australian side already told the Japanese side … that [the prime minister] did not mean it that way," he said.

World.content:
Updated SportAFLAFL 2026 Melbourne dealt massive finals blow as star forward’s ban upheld Jon Pierik Updated August 18, 2026 — 10:09pm ,first published 11:36am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Three-game AFL striking ban upheld for van Rooyen AAP Melbourne have suffered a major pre-finals blow, potentially losing key forward Jacob van Rooyen for the rest of the AFL season through suspension. The Demons failed in their bid to have van Rooyen’s three-game ban for striking overturned or reduced. Joe Richards remonstrates with Jacob van Rooyen after the incident with Aliir Aliir. AFL Photos



It means he will miss the fifth-placed Demons’ final home-and-away game on Saturday against the Western Bulldogs, and that Melbourne will need to win two finals for him to play again this season. Van Rooyen is having a career-best season, kicking 42 goals in 22 games. The Demons forward was charged with striking after he concussed Port Adelaide defender Aliir Aliir in a marking contest on Saturday night at Adelaide Oval. It was graded as severe impact, careless conduct and high impact. Loading After the 90-minute hearing, where van Rooyen testified that he was trying to mark the ball when he collected Aliir, the tribunal jury deliberated for nearly an hour before upholding the charge.



Melbourne had argued van Rooyen’s attempt to mark the ball was not careless, but the tribunal rejected their case. Tribunal chair Jeff Gleeson KC also turned down a bid from the Demons to have a biomechanist give evidence for van Rooyen. “The swing of Van Rooyen’s left arm constituted the act of a strike. It was a forceful blow. It was not simply a trailing or leading arm that Aliir collided with,” Gleeson said in the verdict, adding the panel found it was careless. “Van Rooyen was initially intending to mark the ball, but we find that shortly before impact, he ceased to intend to mark the ball. We say this despite van Rooyen’s evidence to the contrary. “Even if it was van Rooyen’s sole objective at all times to contest the mark, we find that he did so in a way that failed to take reasonable care to avoid acts which could be reasonably foreseen to result in a reportable offence.



“Van Rooyen had time to move his right arm in response to seeing Aliir and he could have done so to some extent or sufficient extent with his left arm.” Why Viney’s September dreams hang in the balance Jon Pierik Melbourne vice captain Jack Viney faces a race against time to return for the finals despite a successful comeback through the VFL. Viney had 19 disposals, including a goal and a game-high 10 clearances, for Casey in the VFL in his comeback from Achilles tendon and back issues.



Demons vice captain Jack Viney hasn’t played a senior game this season, but is now pushing for a return. Getty Images He had not played a game at all this season, one in which the Demons have rebounded from a horror 2025 to be in the frame for a top-four finish heading into Saturday’s clash against the Western Bulldogs – the final game of the home-and-away campaign. Adding to the Demons’ dilemma is that Casey’s VFL campaign has ended, finishing the year 18th on the ladder. While coach Steven King was delighted with Viney’s return, he said on Tuesday there was much to consider when it came to the midfielder’s possible senior return. “There’s a lot of factors that go into it. Obviously, the team balance. We’ve won six of our last seven, but, I mean, when you have Jack Viney available, it’s only a good thing,” King said.



Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 From football glory to police investigation: The 12 hours that changed everything for the Swans “So, I want to make sure I do the right thing by the team, the club, but more so Jack as well. We want to make sure when he comes in, he’s really ready. Is that this week? We’ll wait and see.” The Demons’ midfield has been purring, so Viney would have to squeeze into a line-up that included dynamic playmaker Kysaiah Pickett, the newly contracted Tom Sparrow, Caleb Windsor and Joel Fitzgerald. The Demons are hoping to be involved in a VFL scratch match this weekend to give several of their fringe players another chance to push for finals selection. “I think we have to acknowledge that VFL and AFL are different sports. The intensity … you can’t replicate an AFL game,” King said.



“In saying that, we are in a position with five on the bench. We’d be able to manage players coming back in like we do. I think every team would have probably one player that spends a little less game time, so that’s definitely an option. “For me, we just have to look at our mix and our balance, and there’s more to it than just one player comes in. It’s the ripple effect, how it affects your team and your squad, and also your opponents who are playing that week.” Viney is contracted until the end of 2028. King said he was delighted that Sparrow had inked a five-year deal, and said skipper Max Gawn, almost certain to be named an All-Australian for the ninth time, should also be bestowed the captaincy.

World.title: The VISA hits the fan
World.content:
When the well-travelled Graham Cochrane (C8) made mention of an unwelcome S.H.I.T. stamp, Granny must confess to feeling rather unworldly, but then Steve Castieau of Bexley came along to explain: “In the 1970s, long-haired overland travellers entering Malaysia from Thailand often had their visas marked S.H.I.T (Suspected Hippy In Transit) accompanied by a stern warning to travel directly to Singapore. Entry into Singapore usually required the inevitable haircut.”

“In 1977, when I was considered to be a long-haired uni layabout by some, I travelled to New Zealand for a camping trip,” says Tim Ingall of Scottsdale Arizona, USA. “It took an hour to clear customs as a suspicious, older customs agent went through my gear looking for drugs including probing each aluminium tent pole. On returning to Australia I anticipated similar customs duty interrogation. Instead, I got a ‘G’day’, followed by a short question: ‘Are you bringing any drugs into the country?’ I answered no and was immediately sent on my way. Good thing I wasn’t doing anything nefarious – or at least that’s my story, and I’m sticking to it 49 years later!”

Stephen Tait of Bellevue Hill noticed that Janice Creenaune (C8) was visiting Dirranbandi, Queensland and is hoping “can she report on the welfare of the Norton Brothers and in particular Les Norton? All are robust and handy employees at the Dirranbandi Pub.”

More on the dreaded restaurant dress code (C8), from Elsa Cant of Merewether. “We presented at a posh hotel in London with my husband wearing a very nice (and expensive) leather jacket. This was deemed not respectable and was taken from him and replaced with a too-small, faded, red suit jacket. Thus, he was now suitably dressed for entry to the restaurant for afternoon tea.” As a waiter?

“Pleasing it is to report the first magpie sighting in full swooping mood on a cyclist here in Mudgee,” says Simon Staines. “Is this the earliest reporting of our beloved and most accomplished songbird in action I ask?”

The Scots College Council has thrown its “resolute” support behind principal Dr Ian Lambert, revealing that boys as young as 10 have now been briefed on the sexual assault charges laid against three of their peers. In a joint statement sent to the prestigious school’s community on Tuesday evening by college chairman the Reverend Glen Pather and Lambert, leadership confirmed staff had spoken with all students in year 5 and above in an “age-appropriate way” following public fallout over the police investigation. Scots College principal Dr Ian Lambert. “We understand that staff and parents want to know what has been said to students, what support is available and what the college teaches about consent, dignity and relationships,” the email read. “All students in year 5 and above have now been spoken to about this matter in age-appropriate ways and in settings suited to their stage of development. In every case, additional support has been offered.”



However, one parent who spoke to the Herald on condition of anonymity said the talks focused heavily on warning students against speaking to the media or commenting publicly. “It was the perfect opportunity to talk about consent and what it means, but focus was on public image,” they said. Responding to broader scrutiny over its culture, the school defended its curriculum, stating it has taught age-appropriate consent and sexuality education from kindergarten to senior school for at least 15 years. The action follows the revelation that a Scots College old boy sent messages to a group chat in which he called the 14-year-old victim of the alleged assault by three students a “willing participant” in the attack, and labelled the students involved “deadshits”.



Related Article Private schools Boss from billionaire family quits over Scots College rape case messages Arthur Tzaneros resigned from his position as boss of freight giant ACFS Port Logistics after the comments were published by this masthead on Monday. The email sent to parents did not explicitly reference the incident, but said “sexual violence is never acceptable”. “Behaviour of the kind alleged is entirely inconsistent with the standards and values of the College. Commentary that minimises sexual violence, blames or targets another person or speculates about the young people involved is also unacceptable. “The College does not claim that education can remove every risk or guarantee every individual choice,” the letter read. “We do, however, accept our responsibility to teach these standards clearly, consistently and over time.”



Related Article Exclusive

Crime Three Scots College boys charged with rape of teenage girl The statement also emphasised that the alleged incident occurred away from the school and outside school hours, noting the college did not witness it and learned of details only through police and media reports. There are growing calls for an overhaul of the embattled Bellevue Hill college’s leadership amid criticism of its handling of the alleged sexual assault of a 14-year-old girl and what they say are deep-rooted cultural issues within the school community. However, the council defended the school’s leader, writing that he leads with its “full authority and support”. “Council fully supports his leadership for the remainder of his tenure as Principal and shares responsibility with him and the Executive team for the decisions arising from this matter,” it said.



School leadership also warned the community against public speculation and sharing material online, cautioning that online commentary “can cause significant harm and may have serious consequences”. World.title: Swans declare players ‘in serious breach’ of standards as club suspensions loom
World.content:
The Sydney Swans have declared they believe a group of players “are in serious breach of expected club behaviour and standards” as the club’s board meets on Tuesday night to decide on punishments over their conduct in Melbourne on late Sunday night into early Monday morning. The development comes after AFL chief executive Andrew Dillon suggested the players could also face AFL sanctions irrespective of the outcome of an ongoing police investigation into a sexual assault allegation. Loading “The Sydney Swans can confirm that the club board will meet tonight to agree on player sanctions and penalties, now that the club has concluded its interviews with all the players involved in the incident in Melbourne,” the Swans said in a statement. “We respect there is an ongoing investigation by Victoria Police and any actions we take are independent of this.”



The Swans said it was appropriate “to take firm action” and highlight that any sanction they take as a club relates “solely” to club’s standards of expected behaviour. “The club believes the players are in serious breach of expected club behaviour and standards, and it is appropriate to take firm action and highlight that any sanction we impose relates solely to those breaches,” the Swans’ statement read. “The club also acknowledges that these serious allegations impact others and their wellbeing must be paramount. “The Sydney Swans condemn all forms of abuse and disrespectful behaviour towards women. Any conduct that causes offence or harm to others is unacceptable and falls well short of our expectations. All women deserve to be respected and feel safe.”



The group of five players, who had remained in Melbourne on Monday behind the rest of the team as it travelled back to Sydney, attended separate meetings with senior club and team officials away from Swans headquarters after driving home to NSW. The meetings were to discuss the events of Sunday night and Monday morning, which led to a police investigation into an allegation of sexual assault at the Pullman East Melbourne hotel. The investigation is being handled by Victoria Police’s sexual crimes squad. “The conduct and serious allegations regarding Sydney Swans players are deeply concerning,” Dillon said in a league statement. “The woman who made the report to police is entitled to privacy and care, and that should be respected,” he said.



“Notwithstanding the ongoing police investigation, the AFL and the Sydney Swans will consider the broader conduct of the players as more information comes to light.” This masthead has contacted the representatives of Isaac Heeney, Riley Bice, James Jordon and Chad Warner after two senior industry sources said they were spoken to by police after an allegation of sexual assault in the early hours of Monday morning. Swans players (clockwise from centre): Isaac Heeney, Riley Bice, Nick Blakey, Chad Warner and James Jordon. Artwork: Michael Howard This masthead is not suggesting any of the players are under investigation by police, just that they are assisting with inquiries. This masthead also contacted a representative of Swan Nick Blakey, who denied Blakey was involved in the incident. But the representative confirmed Blakey had also remained in Melbourne with his four teammates.



Photo: Matt Golding Earlier on Tuesday, two senior competition sources, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the players would be dealt with under the AFL rule that covers bringing the game into disrepute and conduct unbecoming. However, late on Tuesday the league said that rule would not immediately be applied. The players had been out drinking after Sunday night’s win over Essendon and returned to the team hotel in the early hours of Monday. The AFL has the power to suspend them under rule 2.3A, which prohibits conduct unbecoming or likely to prejudice the interests or reputation of the league.



Related Article Updated

AFL 2026 ‘Extremely disappointed’: Cox breaks silence as police release update on Swans investigation Any immediate club or league action would be separate to the Victoria Police investigation. A source close to the group of Swans players, but not authorised to speak publicly, said the players had been fully co-operative with the police probe. They said all five had been prepared to speak with police on Monday, but only one was ultimately quizzed. Police told the group they were not ready to conduct a formal interview or speak with any of the players acting as witnesses.



The source said leading Melbourne criminal lawyer Tony Hargreaves was called in to assist the group before they were told they were free to leave and return to Sydney. No player has been arrested and the AFL’s disciplinary action does not make any finding in relation to the allegation that remains under investigation by police. Instead, the AFL and the club have been examining the conduct of the players before and around the alleged incident, and whether their behaviour fell sufficiently below the standards expected of AFL footballers to warrant sanction under the league’s broad disrepute provisions. One of the most recent examples of an AFL suspension under this rule was for then Bulldog Bailey Smith, who was found guilty of conduct unbecoming and suspended for two matches in 2022. Smith admitted to using an illicit substance late in 2021.



This masthead contacted all 36 of the Swans’ corporate partners. None were willing to comment on the incident, and so far, there is no indication any of the club’s sponsors will be walking away. Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 From football glory to police investigation: The 12 hours that changed everything for the Swans However, a spokesperson for Origin expressed disappointment. “The club informed us about this incident yesterday, and we are incredibly disappointed. While the matter is subject to an investigation, it is not appropriate for us to comment any further,” the spokesperson said. The Swans players are now facing the prospect of missing not only Sydney’s final home-and-away match against North Melbourne on Sunday, but at least part of the Swans’ finals campaign. Sydney have already secured second position on the ladder and a home qualifying final. Any multi-game suspension would carry significant consequences for the club’s premiership aspirations.



The Swans were forced to remain in Melbourne on Sunday night because Sydney Airport’s curfew prevented the team from returning home following its convincing win over Essendon at the MCG. Several players subsequently went out drinking before returning to the Pullman, where the team and its staff were staying. Police attended the hotel on Monday after receiving the report of an alleged sexual assault.

World.title: A handful of Swans players wanted to keep partying. The fallout has rocked the AFL
World.content:
Swans players were filtering back to the Pullman hotel, the former Hilton overlooking Yarra Park, in the hours after midnight. A handful of current players who had been out until early Monday morning wanted to keep partying back at the hotel. They duly moved to a player’s room. Swans coach Dean Cox and CEO Matthew Pavlich. Michael Howard At one stage, a former Swans player and a further friend joined the group for at least a period of this night. After 2am – the exact timeline is difficult to ascertain even from the multiple sources who spoke to this masthead on condition of anonymity – one of the players made a phone call. Soon afterwards, two women arrived at the Pullman to join the party of several of the players.



It is uncertain what happened next, except that an allegation was soon made by one of the women of a sexual assault. The two women left the hotel room and were joined by a third woman in the foyer, where there was a commotion. After the alleged incident, police were called. The allegation will be the subject of police investigations as Victoria Police probe the incident. The allegation has been handed to the sexual crimes squad. The five players who remained in Melbourne during the early stage of the police investigation as the rest of the team returned to Sydney on Monday were Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner and Nick Blakey, plus ex-Demon and tagger James Jordon and mature second year defender Riley Bice.



This masthead has contacted their representatives. This masthead is not suggesting any of the players are under investigation by police, just that they are assisting with inquiries. On Monday morning, at least one senior team official went down to the foyer while the five players who had been in the room with the women were instructed to return to or remain in their own rooms as police began working through the first moments of an investigation that would shake the Swans and the entire AFL ecosystem.



There is no doubt that the players will not play this weekend in what is a dead rubber anyway against North Melbourne, but the expectation of close observers – not the Swans – is that the five will miss a bare minimum of two matches. The penalty is almost certain to be uniform. The Swans are working with the AFL on the matter, but the AFL’s integrity boss, former detective Tony Keane, has remained at arm’s length. The league has left the questioning to the Swans and, in time, to police. On Monday, the five players drove back to Sydney, separately from the rest of the team and travelling officials, in at least two rental vehicles. Sydney Swans players (from left to right) Chad Warner, James Jordon, Isaac Heeney, Riley Bice and Nick Blakey. Artwork: Michael Howard By Tuesday, as club and competition confronted arguably the most damaging episode the Swans have faced since their breadline days in the early ’90s, the five would be interviewed by Sydney’s senior management, one by one.



They had not been formally interviewed by police, as suggested, but police had spoken to some and advised that they would be in touch down the track. A representative of Blakey’s says that the star running defender did not speak to the police even informally. Heeney went down to the police headquarters in Melbourne on Monday in what turned out to be an unnecessary trip as he was not interviewed then either. Editor's pick Updated

AFL 2026 Swans declare players ‘in serious breach’ of standards as club suspensions loom Clearly, the police had to gain witness and/or victim statements from the women before they sought answers from the players, as a matter of process. After the Sunday twilight game victory over Essendon, the club had been forced to stay in Melbourne because of the early curfew at Sydney airport. Swans players and officials went out for drinks after the late game. Senior coach Dean Cox as well as a number of the players were on film outside the Harlow, a bar in Church Street Richmond and, according to one witness, about 15 players – Heeney, Warner, Bice and Jordon among them – went on to trendy Queen Street bar Her. They were, the source said, there until close to 2am.



It is not unusual for Sydney players to go out for a drink after the game, according to club insiders. The Swans, who have a mature team, tend to trust their players and especially team leaders to exercise good judgment. Cox was back at the hotel shortly after he left the Richmond bar not long after midnight, according to CCTV footage shown on Seven. The Swans’ hierarchy – led by new chief executive Matthew Pavlich and their chairman Andrew Pridham – were unsurprisingly described as “filthy” with the reckless decisions in those wee hours, irrespective of whether the matter proceeds into a serious criminal charge or not. Confronted by the media avalanche on Tuesday morning outside the club, Cox said he was “obviously extremely disappointed with what’s happened”.



AFL CEO Andrew Dillon who had hitherto been silent on the scandal on Tuesday night released a statement that foreshadowed strong action. “Sexual assault allegations are serious, regardless of who is involved, what time of year it is, or what they may mean for a season,” Dillon said. “Our first question should not be what this means for a football club. It should be whether our actions match the standards we stand for and the community expects of us. “Being clear about our standards also means being prepared to act when those standards are not met.” With Cameron Houston Be the first to know when major news happens.

Van Rooyen is having a career-best season, kicking 42 goals in 22 games. The Demons forward was charged with striking after he concussed Port Adelaide defender Aliir Aliir in a marking contest on Saturday night at Adelaide Oval. It was graded as severe impact, careless conduct and high impact. Loading After the 90-minute hearing, where van Rooyen testified that he was trying to mark the ball when he collected Aliir, the tribunal jury deliberated for nearly an hour before upholding the charge.



Melbourne had argued van Rooyen’s attempt to mark the ball was not careless, but the tribunal rejected their case. Tribunal chair Jeff Gleeson KC also turned down a bid from the Demons to have a biomechanist give evidence for van Rooyen. “The swing of Van Rooyen’s left arm constituted the act of a strike. It was a forceful blow. It was not simply a trailing or leading arm that Aliir collided with,” Gleeson said in the verdict, adding the panel found it was careless. “Van Rooyen was initially intending to mark the ball, but we find that shortly before impact, he ceased to intend to mark the ball. We say this despite van Rooyen’s evidence to the contrary. “Even if it was van Rooyen’s sole objective at all times to contest the mark, we find that he did so in a way that failed to take reasonable care to avoid acts which could be reasonably foreseen to result in a reportable offence.



“Van Rooyen had time to move his right arm in response to seeing Aliir and he could have done so to some extent or sufficient extent with his left arm.” Why Viney’s September dreams hang in the balance Jon Pierik Melbourne vice captain Jack Viney faces a race against time to return for the finals despite a successful comeback through the VFL. Viney had 19 disposals, including a goal and a game-high 10 clearances, for Casey in the VFL in his comeback from Achilles tendon and back issues.



Demons vice captain Jack Viney hasn’t played a senior game this season, but is now pushing for a return. Getty Images He had not played a game at all this season, one in which the Demons have rebounded from a horror 2025 to be in the frame for a top-four finish heading into Saturday’s clash against the Western Bulldogs – the final game of the home-and-away campaign. Adding to the Demons’ dilemma is that Casey’s VFL campaign has ended, finishing the year 18th on the ladder. While coach Steven King was delighted with Viney’s return, he said on Tuesday there was much to consider when it came to the midfielder’s possible senior return. “There’s a lot of factors that go into it. Obviously, the team balance. We’ve won six of our last seven, but, I mean, when you have Jack Viney available, it’s only a good thing,” King said.



Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 From football glory to police investigation: The 12 hours that changed everything for the Swans “So, I want to make sure I do the right thing by the team, the club, but more so Jack as well. We want to make sure when he comes in, he’s really ready. Is that this week? We’ll wait and see.” The Demons’ midfield has been purring, so Viney would have to squeeze into a line-up that included dynamic playmaker Kysaiah Pickett, the newly contracted Tom Sparrow, Caleb Windsor and Joel Fitzgerald. The Demons are hoping to be involved in a VFL scratch match this weekend to give several of their fringe players another chance to push for finals selection. “I think we have to acknowledge that VFL and AFL are different sports. The intensity … you can’t replicate an AFL game,” King said.



“In saying that, we are in a position with five on the bench. We’d be able to manage players coming back in like we do. I think every team would have probably one player that spends a little less game time, so that’s definitely an option. “For me, we just have to look at our mix and our balance, and there’s more to it than just one player comes in. It’s the ripple effect, how it affects your team and your squad, and also your opponents who are playing that week.” Viney is contracted until the end of 2028. King said he was delighted that Sparrow had inked a five-year deal, and said skipper Max Gawn, almost certain to be named an All-Australian for the ninth time, should also be bestowed the captaincy.

World.title: The VISA hits the fan
World.content:
When the well-travelled Graham Cochrane (C8) made mention of an unwelcome S.H.I.T. stamp, Granny must confess to feeling rather unworldly, but then Steve Castieau of Bexley came along to explain: “In the 1970s, long-haired overland travellers entering Malaysia from Thailand often had their visas marked S.H.I.T (Suspected Hippy In Transit) accompanied by a stern warning to travel directly to Singapore. Entry into Singapore usually required the inevitable haircut.”

“In 1977, when I was considered to be a long-haired uni layabout by some, I travelled to New Zealand for a camping trip,” says Tim Ingall of Scottsdale Arizona, USA. “It took an hour to clear customs as a suspicious, older customs agent went through my gear looking for drugs including probing each aluminium tent pole. On returning to Australia I anticipated similar customs duty interrogation. Instead, I got a ‘G’day’, followed by a short question: ‘Are you bringing any drugs into the country?’ I answered no and was immediately sent on my way. Good thing I wasn’t doing anything nefarious – or at least that’s my story, and I’m sticking to it 49 years later!”

Stephen Tait of Bellevue Hill noticed that Janice Creenaune (C8) was visiting Dirranbandi, Queensland and is hoping “can she report on the welfare of the Norton Brothers and in particular Les Norton? All are robust and handy employees at the Dirranbandi Pub.”

More on the dreaded restaurant dress code (C8), from Elsa Cant of Merewether. “We presented at a posh hotel in London with my husband wearing a very nice (and expensive) leather jacket. This was deemed not respectable and was taken from him and replaced with a too-small, faded, red suit jacket. Thus, he was now suitably dressed for entry to the restaurant for afternoon tea.” As a waiter?

“Pleasing it is to report the first magpie sighting in full swooping mood on a cyclist here in Mudgee,” says Simon Staines. “Is this the earliest reporting of our beloved and most accomplished songbird in action I ask?”
